cards.front:
The force that opposes the relative motion of two surfaces in contact is called:

(A) Gravity
(B) Friction
(C) Tension
(D) Buoyancy
cards.back:
(B) Friction

Mechanics & Motion — Friction — arises due to microscopic irregularities and molecular attractions between surfaces. Types — static (before motion begins, up to a maximum), kinetic (during sliding), rolling (smallest). Friction is useful (walking, braking) but also wasteful (heat losses in machines). Reduced by lubrication, ball bearings and streamlining.

cards.front:
The product of mass and velocity of a body is called its:

(A) Kinetic energy
(B) Momentum
(C) Acceleration
(D) Force
cards.back:
(B) Momentum

Mechanics & Motion — Momentum p = m × v. Unit: kg·m/s. Momentum is conserved in an isolated system — the basis of rockets, recoil, collision analysis. Kinetic energy is ½mv² (scalar, unit joule). Force — rate of change of momentum (Newton's 2nd law: F = dp/dt = ma for constant mass). Acceleration — rate of change of velocity.

cards.front:
The upward force exerted on an object immersed in a fluid is called:

(A) Gravitational force
(B) Buoyant force
(C) Surface tension
(D) Viscous force
cards.back:
(B) Buoyant force

Mechanics & Motion — Buoyancy — the upward push a fluid exerts on a submerged / floating object. Archimedes' Principle: the buoyant force equals the weight of the fluid displaced. An object floats if it is less dense than the fluid (ice on water), sinks if denser. Surface tension is the elastic skin of a liquid surface (water-striders walk on it). Viscous force opposes motion through a fluid (honey is more viscous than water).

cards.front:
The force needed to keep an object moving in a circular path is directed towards the:

(A) Tangent of the path
(B) Centre of the circle
(C) Away from the centre
(D) Same direction as motion
cards.back:
(B) Centre of the circle

Mechanics & Motion — Centripetal force — always directed towards the centre of the circular path. Magnitude F = mv²/r. Sources of centripetal force differ — tension in a string for a swung stone, gravitational pull for a satellite, static friction for a car on a curve, normal force for a bicyclist banking on a turn. 'Centrifugal force' is a pseudo-force experienced in the rotating frame.

cards.front:
The SI unit of pressure is the:

(A) Newton
(B) Pascal
(C) Joule
(D) Watt
cards.back:
(B) Pascal

Mechanics & Motion — Pressure = Force / Area. SI unit — pascal (Pa) = 1 N/m². Atmospheric pressure at sea level ≈ 101,325 Pa = 1013.25 hPa. Common units — bar (10⁵ Pa), mmHg / torr, psi. Newton is force; joule is energy; watt is power. Pressure cookers, hydraulic brakes, blood-pressure cuffs and weather forecasts all use pressure measurements.

cards.front:
An object with a mass of 10 kg on Earth is moved to the Moon. Its weight on the Moon is approximately (taking Moon g = 1/6 of Earth's):

(A) Zero, because there is no atmosphere
(B) About 16.3 N
(C) 98 N
(D) 10 kgf
cards.back:
(B) About 16.3 N

Mechanics & Motion — Mass is the amount of matter (invariant, 10 kg here). Weight = mass × g. On Earth — g = 9.8 m/s², so weight ≈ 98 N. On the Moon — g ≈ 9.8/6 ≈ 1.63 m/s², so weight ≈ 10 × 1.63 = 16.3 N. This is why astronauts can jump much higher on the Moon. 10 kgf is a force unit (~98 N) — effectively the Earth-weight value, not the Moon-weight value.

cards.front:
Newton's third law of motion states:

(A) Force equals mass times acceleration
(B) For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction
(C) A body at rest stays at rest unless acted on by a force
(D) Energy can neither be created nor destroyed
cards.back:
(B) For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction

Mechanics & Motion — Newton's 3rd law — action-reaction pairs of forces act on two different bodies, are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction. Examples — rocket propulsion (exhaust pushed down → rocket pushed up), swimming (arms push water back → water pushes swimmer forward), walking (foot pushes ground back → ground pushes foot forward). 1st law — inertia. 2nd law — F = ma. Energy conservation is a different principle (1st law of thermodynamics).
cards.option2: A body at rest stays at rest unless acted on by a force
cards.option3: Energy can neither be created nor destroyed

cards.front:
Which type of friction is typically the LARGEST?

(A) Static friction (just before sliding)
(B) Kinetic friction (during sliding)
(C) Rolling friction (with wheel)
(D) Fluid friction (in liquid/gas)
cards.back:
(A) Static friction (just before sliding)

Mechanics & Motion — ORDER of FRICTION (largest to smallest, generally): STATIC > KINETIC (sliding) > ROLLING. STATIC FRICTION (μ_s): force required to START moving an object at rest; OPPOSES tendency of motion. f_s ≤ μ_s × N (Normal force). MAX value occurs JUST BEFORE motion begins. KINETIC (sliding) FRICTION (μ_k): force opposing object that's already MOVING. f_k = μ_k × N. ROLLING FRICTION (μ_r): much smaller — wheels deform slightly, only a small contact area is opposing motion. KEY VALUES (typical): μ_s rubber on dry concrete ~1.0; μ_k ~0.7; μ_r tire on road ~0.01. WHY STATIC > KINETIC: at rest, microscopic surface bonds (cold-welds) form between contact points; need extra force to break them. Once moving, fewer/looser bonds form. WHY ROLLING is SMALLEST: only the contact patch (under deformed wheel) experiences friction, not the whole interface. THIS IS WHY WHEELS were a PIVOTAL invention — reduced friction enabling efficient transport. PRACTICE: heavy crate harder to PUSH from rest than to KEEP MOVING (μ_s > μ_k). Rolling on tires cheaper than dragging. APPLICATIONS: bearings (use rolling instead of sliding), lubrication (oils, grease — reduce both μ_s and μ_k). PYQ FREQUENCY: friction types comparison in NEET, JEE-Main, NCERT 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
Friction force on a body sliding on a surface depends on:

(A) Normal force and surface roughness
(B) Area of contact only here
(C) Object's weight regardless of angle
(D) Speed of the moving body only
cards.back:
(A) Normal force and surface roughness

Mechanics & Motion — FORMULA: f = μ × N, where μ = coefficient of friction (depends on SURFACE PAIR — roughness/material) + N = NORMAL FORCE (perpendicular pressure between surfaces). KEY LAWS OF FRICTION: (1) Friction is INDEPENDENT of contact AREA (surprising — same μ × N regardless of whether contact is wide-thin or narrow-thick). (2) Friction is INDEPENDENT of relative SPEED (in basic model — actual at high speeds it varies slightly). (3) Friction is PROPORTIONAL to NORMAL FORCE. (4) Friction depends on the PAIR of surfaces (rubber-on-rubber different from rubber-on-ice). NORMAL FORCE on horizontal surface = mg (weight). On INCLINE at angle θ: N = mg cos θ (less than weight). Hence on slope, friction = μ mg cos θ. WHY independent of area? — even though more contact area = more bonds, pressure (force/area) is correspondingly less; products cancel. EXCEPTIONS: at very high speeds (> 100 m/s), area-dependence emerges; tires deform, etc. PRACTICE: car of mass 1000 kg on flat road; μ_kinetic = 0.3. Friction force = 0.3 × 1000 × 10 = 3000 N. To stop from 30 m/s in ~50 m. UPSC angle: friction as a 'force' concept is foundational; in CSAT physics-style problems. PYQ FREQUENCY: friction-formula problems in NEET, JEE-Main 2-3× per cycle.

cards.front:
Why are TIRES grooved (have tread) instead of smooth?

(A) To channel water away (prevent aquaplaning)
(B) To increase friction (smooth would work)
(C) Look attractive in showrooms only
(D) To reduce rolling friction strongly
cards.back:
(A) To channel water away (prevent aquaplaning)

Mechanics & Motion — TIRE TREAD's PRIMARY FUNCTION: CHANNEL WATER AWAY from the contact patch. On WET ROADS, water can form a thin film between tire and road, causing AQUAPLANING (also called HYDROPLANING) — tire LOSES contact with road, vehicle becomes UNCONTROLLABLE. Tread grooves give water somewhere to go, maintaining contact. SECONDARY: tread also provides EDGES that bite into snow, mud, gravel for off-road traction. ON DRY ROAD: technically a SMOOTH (slick) tire with good rubber compound has MAXIMUM contact area, hence MAXIMUM friction. Race cars use slick tires on DRY tracks (F1). On wet tracks: switch to GROOVED 'wet weather' tires. EVERYDAY CARS: must perform in WET + DRY → tread is COMPROMISE. WORN TIRES (low tread depth, < 1.6 mm by law in India) are dangerous — must be replaced. ROAD-FRICTION FACTORS: (1) Tire compound. (2) Tread pattern + depth. (3) Inflation pressure (under-inflated tires deform, increase rolling resistance). (4) Road surface (asphalt, concrete, gravel). (5) Weather (wet/dry/icy/snowy). MOTOR VEHICLES Act 1988 + Indian rules mandate min tread depth + tire condition checks. UPSC angle: ROAD SAFETY is GS-3; ~1.5 lakh road deaths/year in India (highest globally). PYQ FREQUENCY: tread + friction in NEET, NCERT 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
LUBRICANTS reduce friction by:

(A) Forming a fluid film between surfaces
(B) Cooling the surfaces always
(C) Increasing contact area smoothly
(D) Hardening the contact surfaces
cards.back:
(A) Forming a fluid film between surfaces

Mechanics & Motion — LUBRICANTS — substances that REDUCE FRICTION + WEAR between moving surfaces. MECHANISM: form a thin FILM of FLUID/SOLID between contacting surfaces, preventing direct metal-to-metal contact + the high friction that comes with it. Common types: (1) LIQUID LUBRICANTS — oils (mineral, synthetic, vegetable). Engine oil reduces piston-ring friction. Hydraulic fluid for bearings, machinery. (2) SEMI-SOLID / GREASE — lithium grease, calcium grease — for high-load applications (bearings in vehicles, industrial). (3) SOLID LUBRICANTS — graphite, molybdenum disulfide (MoS₂), boron nitride; used at extreme T or vacuum (no liquid evaporation). (4) GAS LUBRICATION (rare) — air-bearing systems. KEY EFFECTS: reduce friction → (a) less heat generation → cooler operation. (b) less wear → longer machine life. (c) less energy loss → better efficiency. (d) sealing (oils prevent corrosion). (e) noise reduction. INDIAN INDUSTRIAL LUBRICANTS: HPCL, IOC, Shell, Castrol India, etc. ENGINE OILS: 5W-30, 10W-40 (viscosity grades; first number = cold viscosity; second = hot viscosity). KEY: viscosity, oxidation stability, additives. UPSC angle: India is 4th largest LUBRICANT MARKET globally. ENVIRONMENTAL: BIO-LUBRICANTS (plant-based) becoming popular for reduced eco-impact. PYQ FREQUENCY: lubrication purpose in NEET, NCERT, SSC physics 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
A 10 kg block on horizontal floor; coefficient of kinetic friction = 0.2; (g = 10 m/s²). Friction force on the block when sliding is:

(A) 20 N (using μ × m × g)
(B) 100 N (just weight value)
(C) 2 N (a calc error here)
(D) 200 N (a wrong calc value)
cards.back:
(A) 20 N (using μ × m × g)

Mechanics & Motion — Apply f = μ × N. On HORIZONTAL surface: N = m × g = 10 × 10 = 100 N. Friction = 0.2 × 100 = 20 N. KEY METHOD: (1) Identify NORMAL FORCE — for horizontal surface, equals weight. (2) Multiply by COEFFICIENT. EXAM TRAP: confusing weight (100 N) with friction (20 N). Weight pushes DOWN on surface; friction acts ALONG surface, OPPOSING motion. PRACTICE: same block on INCLINE at 30°: N = mg cos 30° = 100 × 0.866 = 86.6 N. Friction = 0.2 × 86.6 = 17.3 N. ON A 60° INCLINE: N = 50 N → friction = 10 N. INCLINE ANALYSIS: (1) Component of weight ALONG incline (driving) = mg sin θ. (2) Component PERPENDICULAR (Normal force) = mg cos θ. (3) Friction OPPOSES motion. (4) Net force on incline (going down): mg sin θ − μ mg cos θ. KEY FORMULA: at angle θ where mg sin θ = μ mg cos θ → tan θ = μ → θ = ARCTAN(μ) is the 'angle of repose' (just begins to slide). For μ = 0.2 → θ ≈ 11.3°. PYQ FREQUENCY: friction-on-incline problems in NEET, JEE-Main 2-3× per paper. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests free-body diagram + force resolution.

cards.front:
Without friction, you would NOT be able to:

(A) Walk forward (foot slips back)
(B) Float in air defying gravity
(C) See or hear anything around
(D) Breathe normally on Earth
cards.back:
(A) Walk forward (foot slips back)

Mechanics & Motion — WALKING relies on FRICTION! When you push backward against ground, FRICTION provides FORWARD reaction. Without friction (e.g., on icy or oily surface), foot SLIPS back, you can't propel forward. NEWTON'S 3RD LAW: foot pushes ground BACKWARD; ground pushes foot FORWARD (forward = friction + reaction). FRICTIONLESS WORLD — what would happen: (1) Cannot WALK (feet slip). (2) Cannot DRIVE cars (tires spin, no traction). (3) Cannot HOLD anything in hand (slips out). (4) Buildings collapse (nails, screws need friction to hold). (5) Knots untie themselves. (6) Pencil/pen couldn't write (lead/ink relies on friction). (7) Velcro, zips don't work. (8) Brakes useless. ESSENTIALS we DON'T need friction for: breathing, seeing, hearing — these are biological/EM phenomena, independent of mechanical friction. ALSO: GRAVITY would still hold us down (no levitation). FRICTION is BOTH HELPFUL and HARMFUL: ADVANTAGES — walking, driving, writing, holding, brakes. DISADVANTAGES — wear/tear of machine parts, energy loss as heat, noise, requirement for lubrication. ICE-SLIPPERINESS: ice has very low friction (μ ~0.03 for ice on rubber). Slipping common on icy roads/floors in winter (esp. in Himalayan regions, J&K, HP, UK). UPSC angle: road safety in winter (advisories against speeding on icy roads). PYQ FREQUENCY: friction's role in everyday life in NEET, NCERT, SSC GA 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
An object of mass 5 kg is at rest on horizontal floor; the coefficient of static friction is 0.5. The MINIMUM horizontal force needed to start moving it is approximately:

(A) 25 N (using μ_s × m × g)
(B) 50 N (just weight value)
(C) 10 N (under-estimate calc)
(D) 5 N (way under-shot calc)
cards.back:
(A) 25 N (using μ_s × m × g)

Mechanics & Motion — Maximum static friction = μ_s × N = 0.5 × (5 × 10) = 25 N. To START moving, applied force must EXCEED 25 N (any tiny excess will get it going). So MINIMUM force = 25 N (technically, just above 25 N). IMPORTANT DISTINCTION: (1) MAX STATIC FRICTION = μ_s × N — force you must overcome to START. (2) KINETIC FRICTION = μ_k × N — force resisting motion ONCE moving (typically smaller). (3) Once moving, applied force needs to be ≥ μ_k × mg for steady velocity; if applied F > μ_k × mg, object accelerates. PRACTICE — same block once moving: μ_k = 0.3 typical (less than μ_s). f_kinetic = 0.3 × 50 = 15 N. So if you apply 20 N: (a) BEFORE motion: 20 N < 25 N → stays at rest. (b) IF motion has STARTED (e.g., gave it a push): 20 N > 15 N → accelerates with net 5 N. EVERYDAY: hard to start pushing a car (engage in static friction), easier to keep it rolling. KEY: 'STICKING' phenomenon — object 'sticks' to surface until static-friction max is overcome; then suddenly slips and moves. ANGLE OF REPOSE: tan θ = μ_s. For μ = 0.5: θ ≈ 26.6° — beyond this incline, object spontaneously slides. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests static-vs-kinetic friction distinction. PYQ FREQUENCY: μ_s × N calculations in NEET, JEE-Main 1-2× per paper.

PYQ FREQUENCY: μ_s × N calculations in NEET, JEE-Main 1-2× per paper.

cards.front:
For the same pair of surfaces and the same normal force, the LARGEST friction is usually:

(A) Kinetic friction during steady sliding motion
(B) Maximum static friction just before motion starts
(C) Rolling friction of a wheel on the same surface
(D) Air drag on the object at low velocity
cards.back:
(B) Maximum static friction just before motion starts

Mechanics & Motion — For the same surfaces, μ_static > μ_kinetic > μ_rolling. That's why a stationary object takes more force to start moving than to keep moving once moving. Rolling friction is ~1/100 of sliding — the reason wheels were transformative. Distractor 1 — common confusion between static and kinetic. Distractor 3 — rolling is the smallest. Distractor 4 — air drag at low speed is negligible compared with surface friction.
cards.option1: Kinetic friction during steady sliding motion
cards.option2: Rolling friction of a wheel on the same surface
cards.option3: Air drag on the object at low velocity

cards.front:
The coefficient of friction (μ) between two given surfaces depends most directly on:

(A) The mass of the object placed on the surface
(B) The roughness and material of the contact surfaces
(C) The macroscopic area of contact between the bodies
(D) The speed at which the object is being moved
cards.back:
(B) The roughness and material of the contact surfaces

Mechanics & Motion — μ depends on what the two surfaces are made of and their roughness/lubrication. It does NOT depend on mass directly (mass changes normal force N, but F = μN keeps μ constant) or contact area (Amontons's 2nd law). For moderate speeds, μ is approximately speed-independent. Distractor 1 — μ stays constant when mass changes. Distractor 3 — area independence is counter-intuitive but well-established. Distractor 4 — μ varies very weakly with speed at everyday speeds.

cards.option2: The macroscopic area of contact between the bodies
cards.option3: The speed at which the object is being moved

cards.front:
A 5 kg block rests on a horizontal floor with coefficient of static friction 0.4 (g = 10 m/s²). The minimum horizontal force required to start it moving is:

(A) 10 N
(B) 20 N
(C) 5 N
(D) 50 N
cards.back:
(B) 20 N

Mechanics & Motion — Normal force N = mg = 5 × 10 = 50 N. Maximum static friction = μ_s × N = 0.4 × 50 = 20 N. Force just exceeding 20 N starts motion. Distractor 10 N = mg/5, an arbitrary fraction. Distractor 5 N = the mass itself, no force calculation. Distractor 50 N = the normal force without applying μ.

cards.front:
Ball bearings reduce friction in a rotating shaft mainly by:

(A) Increasing the surface area of the contact zone
(B) Replacing sliding contact with low-friction rolling contact
(C) Eliminating all friction between the moving parts
(D) Dissipating frictional heat into the surroundings quickly
cards.back:
(B) Replacing sliding contact with low-friction rolling contact

Mechanics & Motion — Ball bearings let the inner shaft roll on small spheres rather than slide directly against the outer race. Rolling friction is ~1/100 of sliding friction → power loss + wear drop dramatically. Used in wheels, motors, pulleys, machine spindles. Distractor 1 — increasing area doesn't lower μ. Distractor 3 — friction is reduced, not eliminated. Distractor 4 — heat dissipation is incidental, not the primary mechanism.
cards.option1: Increasing the surface area of the contact zone
cards.option2: Eliminating all friction between the moving parts
cards.option3: Dissipating frictional heat into the surroundings quickly

cards.front:
Without friction, which set of everyday actions would become impossible?

(A) Heating water on a gas stove and boiling it to steam
(B) Walking on the ground, writing with a pen, braking a vehicle
(C) Throwing a ball upward and watching it return to earth
(D) Filling a bucket from a tap and letting water settle
cards.back:
(B) Walking on the ground, writing with a pen, braking a vehicle

Mechanics & Motion — Walking — the foot pushes back on the ground; the ground pushes forward on you via friction. Writing — pen tip drags on paper, depositing ink. Braking — pads grip the rotor (or tyre grips road) by friction. Distractor 1 — heating is by combustion, not friction. Distractor 3 — gravity, not friction, is what brings the ball back. Distractor 4 — gravity drives water flow; friction is incidental.

cards.front:
Lubricants such as engine oil reduce friction primarily by:

(A) Cooling the rubbing surfaces well below room temperature
(B) Forming a thin fluid film that separates the two surfaces
(C) Hardening the asperities on each contacting surface
(D) Increasing the normal force pressing the surfaces together
cards.back:
(B) Forming a thin fluid film that separates the two surfaces

Mechanics & Motion — A lubricant forms a thin layer that prevents direct contact between asperities; sliding now occurs within the lubricant film, which has very low internal shear resistance. Engine oil, gearbox grease, graphite, and MoS₂ work this way. Distractor 1 — cooling is incidental. Distractor 3 — hardening would not reduce friction. Distractor 4 — increasing N would INCREASE friction (F = μN).

cards.front:
A road is BANKED at the curve so that, at the design speed, the centripetal force is supplied by:

(A) Static friction alone, with the road kept perfectly horizontal
(B) The horizontal component of the normal force on the tilted road
(C) The weight of the vehicle pulling it inward toward the curve
(D) Air drag pushing the car sideways through the bend
cards.back:
(B) The horizontal component of the normal force on the tilted road

Mechanics & Motion — On a banked road, the horizontal component of the normal force provides the centripetal force at the design speed; friction is then NOT needed. Above or below design speed, friction supplies the remainder. Banking thus reduces friction demand → safer at higher speeds and on icy/wet roads. Distractor 1 describes a flat road where friction alone supplies centripetal force. Distractor 3 — gravity acts vertically downward, not horizontally inward. Distractor 4 — air drag is far too small to provide centripetal force.

cards.front:
What is the difference between SPEED and VELOCITY?

(A) Velocity has direction; speed scalar
(B) They are completely identical now
(C) Speed is direction; velocity scalar
(D) Both are vectors with directions
cards.back:
(A) Velocity has direction; speed scalar

Mechanics & Motion — SPEED = SCALAR (magnitude only); how fast something moves regardless of direction. VELOCITY = VECTOR (magnitude + direction); how fast AND in which direction. SAME UNITS: m/s (or km/h). EXAMPLE: a car driving 60 km/h NORTH has velocity 60 km/h NORTH; if it turns and goes 60 km/h SOUTH, its SPEED is unchanged (60 km/h) but its VELOCITY changed. CIRCULAR MOTION: an object moving in a circle at constant speed has CHANGING velocity (because direction continuously changes) — that's why circular motion has acceleration even at uniform speed. DISTANCE vs DISPLACEMENT (analogous distinction): DISTANCE = total path length (scalar); DISPLACEMENT = straight-line change of position (vector). If you walk 3 m east then 4 m north, distance = 7 m but displacement = 5 m NE (Pythagoras). KEY DEFINITIONS: AVERAGE SPEED = total distance / total time. AVERAGE VELOCITY = total displacement / total time. INSTANTANEOUS values use limit as time → 0 (calculus). PYQ FREQUENCY: scalar/vector distinction is a 1-mark guarantee in JEE-Main, NEET, Class 11 NCERT.

cards.front:
The first equation of motion (uniformly accelerated motion) is:

(A) v = u + at (final = initial + accel·time)
(B) s = ut + ½at² (distance covered)
(C) v² = u² + 2as (no time variable)
(D) F = ma (Newton's second law form)
cards.back:
(A) v = u + at (final = initial + accel·time)

Mechanics & Motion — FIRST EQUATION OF MOTION: v = u + at, where u = initial velocity, v = final velocity, a = (constant) acceleration, t = time elapsed. DERIVATION: a = (v − u) / t → v = u + at. The other two equations are: SECOND EQUATION: s = ut + ½at² (gives distance covered). THIRD EQUATION: v² = u² + 2as (eliminates time). KEY ASSUMPTION: all three EQUATIONS OF MOTION assume CONSTANT (uniform) acceleration. They DO NOT apply to non-uniform acceleration (e.g., variable forces). INDIA EXAM CONTEXT: introduced in NCERT Class 9 (basic) and Class 11 (formal vector treatment). FREE FALL APPLICATION: a = g ≈ 9.8 m/s² (downward) — for objects in vacuum near Earth surface. e.g., dropped from rest (u=0) for time t: v = gt; s = ½gt² (the famous 'distance in free fall is half g t squared'). NUMERICAL EXAMPLE: ball dropped from 20 m height: 20 = 0 + ½(10)t² → t² = 4 → t = 2 s. PYQ FREQUENCY: equations of motion appear in JEE-Main, NEET, NCERT-tested SSC ~1-2 per paper.

cards.front:
A car accelerates from rest at 2 m/s² for 5 seconds. Its final velocity is:

(A) 10 m/s (using v=u+at)
(B) 5 m/s (mid-calc value here)
(C) 25 m/s (an over-estimate now)
(D) 2.5 m/s (an under-estimate)
cards.back:
(A) 10 m/s (using v=u+at)

Mechanics & Motion — Apply v = u + at. GIVEN: u = 0 (from rest), a = 2 m/s², t = 5 s. So v = 0 + (2)(5) = 10 m/s. SCALE-CHECK: 10 m/s = 36 km/h — reasonable for a car after 5 seconds of moderate acceleration. INSIGHT: 2 m/s² is similar to a typical sedan's acceleration (real cars accelerate ~2-4 m/s² normally, ~10 m/s² for performance models). 0-100 km/h time = 100/3.6 ÷ a = ~27.78/a seconds; for a=2, that's ~13.9 s (slow); for a=10, that's ~2.8 s (sports car). DISTANCE COVERED in 5 s: s = ut + ½at² = 0 + ½(2)(25) = 25 m. CHECKING with third equation: v² = u² + 2as → 100 = 0 + 2(2)(25) = 100 ✓. PYQ FREQUENCY: 1-step kinematics calculations appear in JEE-Main, NEET, SSC CGL Tier 2 1-2× per paper. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests formula recall + plug-and-chug discipline.

cards.front:
Acceleration due to gravity (g) on Earth's surface is approximately:

(A) 9.8 m/s² (standard value)
(B) 9.8 km/s² (way too high)
(C) 1.6 m/s² (the Moon's value)
(D) 3.7 m/s² (the Mars value)
cards.back:
(A) 9.8 m/s² (standard value)

Mechanics & Motion — g = 9.81 m/s² (often rounded to 9.8 or even 10 in problems). It's the acceleration any object FREE-FALLING in vacuum experiences near Earth's surface (vacuum = no air resistance). VARIATION: (1) at EQUATOR: ~9.78 m/s² (less due to Earth's rotation centrifugal effect + slightly larger radius). (2) at POLES: ~9.83 m/s² (more — Earth slightly flattened). (3) at altitude: g decreases ~0.3% per km up. (4) underground/in mines: g decreases as you approach Earth's center (becomes 0 at the center). g VALUES on OTHER BODIES: Moon 1.62 m/s² (~1/6 Earth); Mars 3.71 m/s²; Jupiter 24.79 m/s²; Sun 274 m/s². CONSEQUENCE — APOLLO MOON: astronauts could leap many metres on the Moon because g is 1/6th. CAVENDISH EXPERIMENT (1798): measured G (universal grav constant), allowing g = GM/R² calculation. EQUATION g = GM/R²: M = Earth's mass (~6 × 10²⁴ kg), R = Earth's radius (~6,371 km), G = 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg². PYQ FREQUENCY: 'value of g' is a 1-mark guarantee in NEET, JEE-Main, SSC CGL.

cards.front:
An object is thrown vertically upward with velocity 20 m/s. The maximum height reached (g = 10 m/s²) is:

(A) 20 m (using v²=u²−2gh)
(B) 10 m (a calc error result)
(C) 40 m (an over-estimate)
(D) 200 m (way too large)
cards.back:
(A) 20 m (using v²=u²−2gh)

Mechanics & Motion — Apply third equation of motion: v² = u² − 2gh (deceleration due to gravity going up; acceleration becomes negative). At MAXIMUM HEIGHT, v = 0 (object momentarily stops before falling). So 0 = (20)² − 2(10)h → 0 = 400 − 20h → h = 400/20 = 20 m. ALTERNATIVE: time to reach max = u/g = 20/10 = 2 s. Distance = ut − ½gt² = 20(2) − ½(10)(4) = 40 − 20 = 20 m ✓. SYMMETRY: time to RISE = time to FALL back to launch height; final speed at launch height = initial speed (energy conservation in vacuum). NEGLECT AIR RESISTANCE: real-world projectiles lose energy to air drag — actual max height is slightly less. ENERGY APPROACH: ½mu² = mgh → h = u²/(2g) = 400/20 = 20 m ✓ (same answer, different method). FUN FACT: world high-jumpers reach ~2 m above their stomach launch — leg muscles can launch the body upward at ~6 m/s. PYQ FREQUENCY: 'max-height' projectile Qs in JEE-Main, NEET 2-3× per paper. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests v=0 condition recognition.

cards.front:
A body covers half its total path length in the LAST second of free fall from rest. The total time of fall is approximately:

(A) About 3.4 seconds (over 2+√2)
(B) Exactly 2 seconds always now
(C) 4 seconds is the answer
(D) 5 seconds for free fall
cards.back:
(A) About 3.4 seconds (over 2+√2)

Mechanics & Motion — Let total time = T seconds. TOTAL DISTANCE = ½gT². DISTANCE in LAST second = total − distance covered in (T−1) seconds = ½gT² − ½g(T−1)². GIVEN: distance in last second = ½ of total. So ½gT² − ½g(T−1)² = ½ × ½gT². Cancel g/2: T² − (T−1)² = ½T² → T² − (T² − 2T + 1) = ½T² → 2T − 1 = ½T². Multiply by 2: 4T − 2 = T². Rearrange: T² − 4T + 2 = 0. Quadratic: T = (4 ± √(16−8))/2 = (4 ± √8)/2 = (4 ± 2√2)/2 = 2 ± √2. Take positive root larger than 1 (last second must exist): T = 2 + √2 ≈ 3.414 s. KEY METHOD: write expression for last-second distance; equate to fraction of total; solve quadratic. NUMERICAL CHECK (g=10): total dist = ½(10)(3.414)² ≈ 58.3 m; distance in last second = ½(10)(3.414)² − ½(10)(2.414)² ≈ 58.3 − 29.1 = 29.2 m ≈ half of 58.3 ✓. PYQ ANGLE: 'distance in nth second' in JEE-Main, NEET, advanced kinematics MCQ. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests algebraic manipulation + kinematic insight.

cards.front:
A particle moves in a straight line with VELOCITY-TIME graph that is a horizontal line. This means:

(A) Constant velocity, zero acceleration
(B) Increasing velocity uniformly here
(C) Particle is at rest stationary
(D) Acceleration is increasing now too
cards.back:
(A) Constant velocity, zero acceleration

Mechanics & Motion — VELOCITY-TIME (v-t) GRAPH: a HORIZONTAL line means velocity does NOT change with time → CONSTANT VELOCITY → ZERO ACCELERATION. KEY GRAPH READING SKILLS: (1) v-t graph SLOPE = ACCELERATION. Horizontal slope = 0 = no acceleration. Steep upward slope = high positive accel. Downward slope = deceleration. (2) AREA UNDER v-t graph = DISPLACEMENT. (3) For STRAIGHT-LINE v-t graph (any slope) → uniform acceleration. (4) For CURVED v-t graph → variable acceleration. POSITION-TIME (s-t) GRAPH: (a) horizontal line = at rest. (b) straight slope = constant velocity. (c) curved (parabola for uniform accel). ACCELERATION-TIME (a-t) GRAPH: horizontal line at non-zero a = uniform accel; horizontal at 0 = constant velocity. PRACTICE — COMBINING graphs: from a v-t graph, you can derive both s-t (integrate) and a-t (differentiate slope). PYQ ANGLE: graph-interpretation Qs are top JEE-Main, NEET kinematics MCQs (1-2 per paper). EXAMINER MINDSET: tests multi-representation fluency in physics.

cards.front:
Newton's FIRST Law of Motion is also known by which of the following names?

(A) Law of Momentum
(B) Law of Inertia
(C) Law of Action-Reaction
(D) Law of Universal Gravitation
cards.back:
(B) Law of Inertia

Mechanics & Motion — Newton's First Law states: 'Every body continues in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by an external force.' This is the LAW OF INERTIA — inertia being the property by which a body resists change in its state of rest or motion. Option A refers loosely to the Second Law (F = dp/dt). Option C is the Third Law (every action has an equal and opposite reaction). Option D is a separate Newton contribution — nothing to do with the three laws of motion.

cards.front:
A force of 20 N is applied to a body of mass 4 kg on a frictionless surface. What is the acceleration produced?

(A) 2 m/s²
(B) 5 m/s²
(C) 80 m/s²
(D) 24 m/s²
cards.back:
(B) 5 m/s²

Mechanics & Motion — By Newton's Second Law, F = ma, so a = F/m = 20/4 = 5 m/s². Worked step by step: given F = 20 N, m = 4 kg. Rearranging F = ma → a = F/m = 20 ÷ 4 = 5 m/s². Distractor 2 m/s² would be (force − mass)/something — pure error; 80 m/s² comes from 20×4 (multiplying instead of dividing — a common slip); 24 m/s² comes from 20+4 (adding instead of dividing — less common but tracks a student who has forgotten the formula entirely).

cards.front:
When a rifle is fired, the rifle RECOILS backward. This illustrates which of Newton's laws?

(A) First Law
(B) Second Law
(C) Third Law
(D) Law of Gravitation
cards.back:
(C) Third Law

Mechanics & Motion — The forward force exerted on the bullet by the rifle PRODUCES an equal and opposite backward force on the rifle — pure Newton's Third Law ('every action has an equal and opposite reaction'). Rocket propulsion uses the same principle. Other common Third Law illustrations: walking (feet push ground back, ground pushes us forward), swimming (arms push water back, water pushes swimmer forward), a bird flying (wings push air down, air pushes bird up). The First Law explains why a stationary rifle stays stationary until fired. The Second Law quantifies the recoil velocity using momentum conservation.

cards.front:
A bus moving at 20 m/s suddenly brakes and comes to rest in 4 seconds. If its mass is 2000 kg, what is the magnitude of the AVERAGE braking force?

(A) 5 000 N
(B) 10 000 N
(C) 40 000 N
(D) 2 500 N
cards.back:
(B) 10 000 N

Mechanics & Motion — Step-by-step: (1) Acceleration a = (v − u)/t = (0 − 20)/4 = −5 m/s² — magnitude 5 m/s². (2) By Newton's Second Law, F = ma = 2000 × 5 = 10 000 N (taking magnitudes). The direction is opposite to the motion (braking). Distractor 5 000 N drops the mass by a factor of 2 (common slip: thinking mass = 1000 kg). 40 000 N mistakenly multiplies by 4 (the time) instead of dividing. 2 500 N divides the mass by the time (nonsensical dimensionally). Always unit-check: N = kg·m/s² — so 2000 × 5 = 10 000 N checks out.

cards.front:
The momentum of a body is defined as:

(A) Mass × velocity (a vector)
(B) Mass × acceleration (a vector)
(C) Mass ÷ velocity (a scalar)
(D) (Mass × velocity)² (a scalar)
cards.back:
(A) Mass × velocity (a vector)

Mechanics & Motion — Momentum p = m·v. Since velocity is a vector, momentum is a vector. Unit: kg·m/s (or N·s). Newton's Second Law in its ORIGINAL form: F = dp/dt (rate of change of momentum = force). When mass is constant, this simplifies to F = ma. Option B is force F = ma (not momentum). Option C has wrong units and definition. Option D confuses with kinetic energy which is (1/2)mv² (a scalar).

cards.front:
Two bodies of masses 4 kg and 6 kg moving in the same direction with velocities 10 m/s and 5 m/s respectively collide. If they STICK TOGETHER after collision, their common velocity is (assume perfectly inelastic collision, no external forces):

(A) 5 m/s
(B) 7 m/s
(C) 15 m/s
(D) 10 m/s
cards.back:
(B) 7 m/s

Mechanics & Motion — By conservation of momentum: m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ = (m₁ + m₂)V. Plugging in: 4(10) + 6(5) = (4+6)V → 40 + 30 = 10V → 70 = 10V → V = 7 m/s. (Derivation shown step-by-step; answer matches option B exactly.) Distractor 5 m/s is simply the slower body's speed (ignoring the collision); 15 m/s is the sum of speeds (nonsense); 10 m/s is the faster body's speed. Momentum conservation — not energy conservation — is what always holds in collisions without external force. Energy is NOT conserved in inelastic collisions (some becomes heat/deformation).

cards.front:
Which statement about the three types of friction — STATIC, KINETIC, and ROLLING — is CORRECT?

(A) Kinetic friction > Static friction > Rolling friction
(B) Static friction (maximum) > Kinetic friction > Rolling friction
(C) All three are always equal in magnitude
(D) Rolling friction > Kinetic friction > Static friction
cards.back:
(B) Static friction (maximum) > Kinetic friction > Rolling friction

Mechanics & Motion — The CORRECT ordering (for the same surfaces and normal force): μ_s (static, maximum) > μ_k (kinetic) > μ_r (rolling). This is why: (i) it takes more force to START pushing a box than to keep it sliding (static > kinetic); (ii) wheels and ball-bearings are used because rolling friction is FAR smaller than sliding/kinetic friction. For typical steel-on-steel: μ_s ≈ 0.74, μ_k ≈ 0.57, μ_r (rolling) ≈ 0.002. This vast gap between kinetic and rolling friction is why the wheel is one of humanity's most impactful inventions.

cards.option2: All three are always equal in magnitude

cards.front:
A block of mass 5 kg is kept on a horizontal surface with coefficient of static friction μ_s = 0.4. What is the MINIMUM horizontal force needed to JUST START moving the block? (Take g = 10 m/s²)

(A) 10 N
(B) 20 N
(C) 50 N
(D) 2 N
cards.back:
(B) 20 N

Mechanics & Motion — The block JUST starts moving when applied force equals the maximum static friction. Step 1: Normal force N = mg = 5 × 10 = 50 N (the block rests on a horizontal surface, so N balances weight). Step 2: Maximum static friction f_s_max = μ_s · N = 0.4 × 50 = 20 N. Step 3: Applied force needed = 20 N (just enough to overcome static friction). Distractor 10 N is half — maybe from μ_s · mg/2 confusion. 50 N is just N (student forgot to multiply by μ). 2 N is μ_s · m without g — dimensional error.

cards.front:
Which of the following is a practical application of Newton's FIRST Law of Motion?

(A) Firing a bullet from a gun producing recoil
(B) Seat belts in cars preventing passengers from continuing forward when the car suddenly stops
(C) Using a hydraulic lift to raise heavy objects
(D) Calculating the acceleration of a falling body
cards.back:
(B) Seat belts in cars preventing passengers from continuing forward when the car suddenly stops

Mechanics & Motion — When a car suddenly brakes, the PASSENGERS' upper bodies continue moving forward at the original velocity (by inertia / First Law) — the seat belt applies the external force that brings them to rest, preventing collision with the windshield. Classic First-Law application. Option A demonstrates the Third Law (action-reaction). Option C is based on Pascal's principle (fluid pressure transmission), not Newton's laws directly. Option D uses the Second Law (F = ma, with F = mg). Other everyday First-Law examples: dust flying off a shaken carpet, a fruit falling from a tree when its branch is shaken, a standing passenger in a bus jerking backward when the bus accelerates forward.

(A) 1 N = 1 kg/s²
(B) 1 N = 1 kg·m/s²
(C) 1 N = 1 kg·m·s
(D) 1 N = 1 kg·m²/s²
cards.back:
(B) 1 N = 1 kg·m/s²

Mechanics & Motion — 1 newton = 1 kg · m / s² (unit of mass × unit of acceleration). This is the standard SI unit check for any physics problem involving force. Option A omits the meter (wrong dimension). Option C has the wrong time-exponent (time should be in the denominator with exponent 2). Option D is the unit of ENERGY — the joule (1 J = 1 kg·m²/s²) — not force. cards.front:
Two astronauts in space — far from any gravitational body and initially at rest — push off from each other. If astronaut A (60 kg) moves off at 2 m/s, what is the velocity of astronaut B (80 kg)?

(A) 2.0 m/s in the same direction as A
(B) 1.5 m/s in the opposite direction to A
(C) 2.67 m/s in the opposite direction to A
(D) 0 m/s — A's velocity alone satisfies momentum conservation
cards.back:
(B) 1.5 m/s in the opposite direction to A

Mechanics & Motion — Conservation of momentum: initial total momentum = 0 (both at rest). After pushing off, momenta must still sum to zero → m_A · v_A + m_B · v_B = 0. So v_B = −(m_A / m_B) · v_A = −(60/80) × 2 = −1.5 m/s. The negative sign means OPPOSITE direction — so B moves at 1.5 m/s in the opposite direction. Distractor C (2.67) swaps the mass ratio: v_B = −(80/60) × 2 = −2.67 — a very common error. A is nonsensical (violates momentum conservation). D forgets that conservation applies to the system, not to a single body alone.

cards.front:
The coefficient of friction between two surfaces is a DIMENSIONLESS number because:

(A) It is defined as the ratio of two forces (friction / normal), so the units cancel
(B) It is a probability value between 0 and 1
(C) It is computed using only integer counting
(D) It is always exactly equal to 1 in SI
cards.back:
(A) It is defined as the ratio of two forces (friction / normal), so the units cancel

Mechanics & Motion — μ = f / N where f is the friction force and N the normal force — both in newtons. Ratio of two quantities with identical units is DIMENSIONLESS. Typical values: rubber on dry concrete ≈ 1.0; steel on steel ≈ 0.57 (kinetic); ice on ice ≈ 0.03; rolling friction for ball-bearings ≈ 0.001. Although μ is typically between 0 and 1, μ > 1 IS possible (e.g. some rubber-on-rubber can reach ~1.2-1.5). Option B is a conceptual misconception — μ is NOT a probability. Option C is wrong — it's a real-valued ratio. Option D is wrong — it varies widely.

cards.option2: It is computed using only integer counting
cards.option3: It is always exactly equal to 1 in SI

cards.front:
When a body slides down an INCLINED plane at a constant velocity, the relationship between the angle of inclination θ and the coefficient of kinetic friction μ_k is:

(A) μ_k = cos θ
(B) μ_k = tan θ
(C) μ_k = sin θ
(D) μ_k = 1/sin θ
cards.back:
(B) μ_k = tan θ

Mechanics & Motion — At CONSTANT velocity down an incline, net force = 0. Forces along the incline: component of gravity down the slope = mg sin θ; friction up the slope = μ_k · N = μ_k · mg cos θ. Setting them equal: mg sin θ = μ_k · mg cos θ → μ_k = sin θ / cos θ = TAN θ. The angle at which this happens is called the 'angle of friction' or 'angle of repose'. Typical engineering: a steel coil on a wooden ramp slides at ~30° → μ ≈ tan 30° ≈ 0.58. The distractors sin θ and cos θ reflect common slips (student forgets to take both components).

cards.front:
Which of the following is the CORRECT description of Galileo's contribution to the study of motion, later formalised by Newton?

(A) Galileo proved that heavier bodies fall faster than lighter ones
(B) Galileo showed that in the ABSENCE of air resistance, all bodies fall with the same acceleration
(C) Galileo invented the calculus used to derive F = ma
(D) Galileo discovered the universal law of gravitation
cards.back:
(B) Galileo showed that in the ABSENCE of air resistance, all bodies fall with the same acceleration

Mechanics & Motion — Galileo's famous (possibly apocryphal) Leaning Tower of Pisa experiment and his inclined-plane experiments showed that heavier and lighter bodies fall with the SAME acceleration when air resistance is negligible — refuting the Aristotelian view that heavier bodies fall faster (option A, which Galileo DISPROVED). This was foundational for Newton's First and Second Laws. Newton and Leibniz independently invented calculus (not Galileo). Newton's universal law of gravitation came later in Principia (1687). A classic 1971 demonstration: Apollo 15 astronaut Dave Scott dropped a hammer and feather on the airless Moon — they hit the surface simultaneously.

cards.option3: Galileo discovered the universal law of gravitation

cards.front:
Which of the following scenarios INCREASES friction, useful in many practical applications?

(A) Lubrication of machine parts with oil
(B) Polishing a surface to be smooth
(C) Using treaded tyres on vehicles and grooves on shoe soles
(D) Using ball-bearings in the wheels of a car
cards.back:
(C) Using treaded tyres on vehicles and grooves on shoe soles

Mechanics & Motion — Treaded tyres and soled shoes INCREASE friction — critical for vehicle braking/cornering and for walking without slipping on wet surfaces. Options A (lubrication), B (polishing), and D (ball-bearings — which convert sliding to rolling friction) all DECREASE friction. A balanced understanding of friction recognises both: we WANT friction for driving/walking, BUT also want to REDUCE it in moving engine parts and bearings. Treads work by channeling water away from the contact patch, preventing hydroplaning. Racing slicks (no treads) have MORE rubber-on-road contact in dry conditions — a specialized case — but are illegal in rain.

cards.front:
The KINETIC ENERGY of a body of mass m moving with velocity v is:

(A) mv
(B) (1/2)mv²
(C) (1/2)mv
(D) m²v
cards.back:
(B) (1/2)mv²

Mechanics & Motion — KE = (1/2)mv². Unit: joule. mv is momentum. If v doubles, KE × 4. If m doubles, KE × 2. Work-energy theorem: net work = change in KE.

cards.front:
The principle of CONSERVATION OF MOMENTUM states:

(A) Momentum is always increasing
(B) In a closed system (no external force), total momentum remains constant
(C) Momentum equals mass times acceleration
(D) Every action has an equal and opposite momentum
cards.back:
(B) In a closed system (no external force), total momentum remains constant

Mechanics & Motion — Conservation of linear momentum — follows from Newton's 3rd law applied to pairs of interacting bodies. Collisions: total momentum before = total after. Rocket propulsion works on this principle (exhaust ejected backward → rocket moves forward).

The SI unit of WORK is:

(A) Newton
(B) Joule
(C) Watt
(D) Pascal
cards.back:
(B) Joule

Mechanics & Motion — Work done = Force × displacement × cos θ. 1 Joule = 1 Newton × 1 metre. Also 1 J = 1 kg⋅m²/s². 1 calorie ≈ 4.184 J. Newton — force. Watt — power (J/s).

A simple PENDULUM has maximum KINETIC energy at:

(A) Extreme positions
(B) Mean (lowest) position
(C) Equal at all positions
(D) Only when stopped
cards.back:

Mechanics & Motion — Pendulum: at extreme positions, velocity = 0 → KE = 0, PE = max. At mean position (lowest), velocity = max → KE = max, PE = min (zero if taken as reference). Total energy is conserved. Time period T = 2π√(L/g).

cards.front:
A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 2 m/s² for 10 seconds. What is the distance covered by the car in this time?

(A) 50 m
(B) 100 m
(C) 150 m
(D) 200 m
cards.back:
(B) 100 m

Mechanics & Motion — Use s = ut + ½at². Given: u = 0 (rest), a = 2 m/s², t = 10 s. So s = 0·10 + ½·(2)·(10)² = ½·2·100 = 100 m. Distractor 50 m comes from forgetting the 'half' factor; 200 m from omitting the ½ and doubling; 150 m from adding an extra velocity term.

A body thrown vertically upward with an initial velocity of 20 m/s reaches a maximum height of (g = 10 m/s²):

(A) 10 m
(B) 20 m
(C) 40 m
(D) 100 m
cards.back:
(B) 20 m

Mechanics & Motion — At max height, final velocity v = 0. Using v² = u² − 2gh: 0 = (20)² − 2·10·h → h = 400/20 = 20 m. A classic shortcut: h_max = u²/(2g) = 400/20 = 20 m. 40 m comes from forgetting the factor of 2; 10 m from dividing by 40 instead of 20; 100 m from using the wrong formula.

cards.front:
A train moving at 72 km/h comes to rest in 20 seconds. What is its deceleration?

(A) 0.5 m/s²
(B) 1 m/s²
(C) 2 m/s²
(D) 3.6 m/s²
cards.back:
(B) 1 m/s²

Mechanics & Motion — Convert 72 km/h to m/s: 72 × (5/18) = 20 m/s. Use v = u + at: 0 = 20 + a·20 → a = −1 m/s². So the deceleration is 1 m/s². Key trap: if you forgot to convert km/h to m/s, you'd get 72/20 = 3.6 (distractor D). 0.5 m/s² arises from a sign/arithmetic error.

cards.front:
A body falls freely from the top of a tower. If it covers 45 m in the last second of its fall, the height of the tower is (g = 10 m/s²):

(A) 80 m
(B) 125 m
(C) 180 m
(D) 245 m
cards.back:
(B) 125 m

Mechanics & Motion — Distance covered in the n-th second (from rest): s_n = u + (a/2)(2n−1). With u = 0, a = g = 10: s_n = 5(2n−1). Given s_n = 45: 5(2n−1) = 45 → 2n−1 = 9 → n = 5 s (total fall time). Total height: H = ½·g·t² = ½·10·25 = 125 m. 180 m results if you wrongly add an extra 5; 80 m comes from miscounting seconds; 245 m from using t = 7.

cards.front:
A projectile is launched at an angle of 45° with a velocity of 20 m/s. What is the horizontal range? (g = 10 m/s²)

(A) 20 m
(B) 40 m
(C) 50 m
(D) 80 m
cards.back:
(B) 40 m

Mechanics & Motion — Range formula: R = (u² sin 2θ)/g. With u = 20, θ = 45° (so sin 90° = 1), g = 10: R = (400·1)/10 = 40 m. The maximum range for a given speed occurs at 45°, so this formula peaks here. 20 m would correspond to θ = 15° or 75°; 50 m comes from mis-substituting u = 25; 80 m from doubling erroneously.

cards.front:
Two cars start from the same point. Car A travels 40 km north and then 30 km east. Car B travels directly to A's final position. What distance does Car B travel?

(A) 35 km
(B) 50 km
(C) 60 km
(D) 70 km
cards.back:
(B) 50 km

Mechanics & Motion — Car A's displacement from origin: 40 km N + 30 km E. Net displacement = √(40² + 30²) = √(1600 + 900) = √2500 = 50 km. Car B travels this straight-line distance. 70 km is Car A's TOTAL path distance (40 + 30) — a common distance vs. displacement trap. 35 km and 60 km result from incorrect Pythagorean arithmetic.

cards.front:
The velocity-time graph of a body shows a straight line with a positive slope passing through the origin. This means:

(A) The body moves with uniform velocity
(B) The body moves with uniform acceleration starting from rest
(C) The body moves with increasing acceleration
(D) The body decelerates uniformly
cards.back:
(B) The body moves with uniform acceleration starting from rest

Mechanics & Motion — Slope of v-t graph = acceleration. A constant positive slope means uniform acceleration (a = constant). Passing through origin means at t = 0, v = 0 (started from rest). Uniform velocity would give a horizontal line (slope = 0). Increasing acceleration gives a CURVE with increasing slope, not a straight line. Deceleration gives a negative slope.

cards.front:
A body moving in a circle of radius r with constant speed v has:

(A) Zero acceleration
(B) Centripetal acceleration v²/r directed towards the center
(C) Tangential acceleration v²/r
(D) Linear acceleration that increases with time
cards.back:
(B) Centripetal acceleration v²/r directed towards the center

Mechanics & Motion — In uniform circular motion, speed is constant but velocity (a vector) constantly changes DIRECTION. This requires acceleration — specifically centripetal (center-seeking) acceleration a = v²/r directed radially inward. Tangential acceleration would exist only if speed were changing. Magnitude of velocity constant ≠ zero acceleration; zero acceleration would require straight-line motion.

cards.front:
A car covers the first half of a journey at 40 km/h and the second half at 60 km/h. The average speed for the whole journey is:

(A) 48 km/h
(B) 50 km/h
(C) 52 km/h
(D) 55 km/h
cards.back:
(A) 48 km/h

Mechanics & Motion — For equal DISTANCES at different speeds, average speed = harmonic mean = 2v₁v₂/(v₁+v₂) = (2·40·60)/(40+60) = 4800/100 = 48 km/h. Common mistake: computing arithmetic mean (40+60)/2 = 50 km/h — WRONG because time spent at each speed is different (slower leg takes longer). The harmonic mean handles this correctly.

(B) 20 m/s
(C) 40 m/s

(B) 20 m/s

cards.front:
Which of the following is a scalar quantity?

(A) Displacement
(B) Velocity
(C) Speed
(D) Acceleration
cards.back:
(C) Speed

Mechanics & Motion — Scalar = magnitude only; vector = magnitude + direction. Speed is the magnitude of velocity — a scalar. Displacement, velocity, and acceleration are all vectors (they have direction). Other scalars: distance, mass, time, energy, temperature. Other vectors: force, momentum, torque, electric field.

cards.front:
Newton's FIRST LAW of motion is also known as the law of:

(A) Inertia (objects at rest stay at rest)
(B) Acceleration (the F=ma form law)
(C) Action-reaction (third-law form)
(D) Conservation of momentum law
cards.back:
(A) Inertia (objects at rest stay at rest)

Mechanics & Motion — NEWTON'S FIRST LAW (Law of Inertia, 1687): 'A body at REST stays at REST, and a body in MOTION stays in MOTION at constant velocity, UNLESS acted upon by a NET EXTERNAL FORCE.' INERTIA = the tendency of an object to RESIST CHANGES in its state of motion. PROPORTIONAL TO MASS — heavier objects have MORE inertia. PRACTICAL EXAMPLES: (1) Sudden BUS BRAKING — passenger lurches FORWARD (their body wants to continue moving). (2) Sudden BUS ACCELERATION — passenger jerks BACKWARD. (3) Rotating tyres carry water/mud outward — tangential velocity. (4) When an apple is snapped from a tree, it falls — but earth pulls it down via gravity (a force). ALL THREE LAWS: (1) Inertia (1st). (2) F=ma (2nd). (3) Action-Reaction (3rd). HISTORICAL: pre-Galileo and Newton, ARISTOTLE believed objects need a continuous force to keep moving (incorrect). Galileo's ramp experiments showed objects in absence of friction would move forever — leading to the principle of inertia. Newton formalized it in PRINCIPIA MATHEMATICA (1687). PYQ FREQUENCY: Newton's laws are 1-mark guarantees in NEET, JEE-Main, NCERT-driven SSC, RRB.

cards.front:
Newton's SECOND LAW: F = ma. If a 5 kg mass accelerates at 2 m/s², the net force is:

(A) 10 newtons (mass × accel)
(B) 2.5 newtons (a wrong calc)
(C) 7 newtons (a sum error here)
(D) 20 newtons (over-estimate)
cards.back:
(A) 10 newtons (mass × accel)

Mechanics & Motion — NEWTON'S SECOND LAW: F = m × a, where F = net force (newtons, N), m = mass (kg), a = acceleration (m/s²). Plug: F = 5 × 2 = 10 N. UNIT — NEWTON: 1 N = 1 kg·m/s² (force needed to accelerate 1 kg at 1 m/s²). EVERYDAY SCALE: an APPLE has weight ~1 N (mass ~100 g, g=10); a person of 70 kg weighs ~700 N. ALTERNATIVE FORMULATION: F = dp/dt — net force = rate of change of MOMENTUM (this form is more general; works for variable-mass systems like rockets). RELATED CONCEPT: WEIGHT W = mg (force due to gravity); on Earth W = m × 9.8 N; on Moon W = m × 1.6 N. INSIGHT: gravitation pulls everything towards Earth's center; Newton derived gravity AND motion laws from observation of falling apple + Moon's orbit. EVEN MORE GENERAL: in special relativity, F = dp/dt with relativistic momentum p = γmv (γ → ∞ as v → c). PYQ FREQUENCY: simple F=ma calculations appear 2-3× per JEE-Main, NEET; 1× per SSC CGL Tier 2.

cards.front:
Newton's THIRD LAW states 'For every action, there is an EQUAL and OPPOSITE reaction.' This explains:

(A) Rocket propulsion forward thrust
(B) Why heavier objects fall faster (no)
(C) Why gravity attracts all objects
(D) Why a moving body slows down
cards.back:
(A) Rocket propulsion forward thrust

Mechanics & Motion — NEWTON'S THIRD LAW: 'F_AB = −F_BA' — when body A exerts a force on body B, body B simultaneously exerts an EQUAL but OPPOSITE force on A. ROCKET PROPULSION: hot gases pushed BACKWARD (action) → rocket pushed FORWARD (reaction). ALL of space-flight depends on this. WALKING: foot pushes ground BACKWARD (action) → ground pushes foot FORWARD (reaction); friction provides the necessary grip. SWIMMING: hands push water BACKWARD; water pushes swimmer FORWARD. JUMPING: legs push ground DOWN; ground pushes person UP. KEY MISCONCEPTIONS: (1) Action-reaction pair always acts on DIFFERENT BODIES (NOT the same body). (2) The pair has SAME MAGNITUDE but the EFFECTS may differ if masses are different — Earth and apple: same force, but Earth's mass is 10²⁵ × bigger, so Earth's acceleration is negligible. (3) Pair acts SIMULTANEOUSLY (no time delay). FAMOUS EXAMPLE: WERNHER VON BRAUN (rocket scientist) said Newton's 3rd law is 'all rocketry'. Saturn V (Apollo 11) generated 35 million N of thrust — by ejecting kerosene+oxygen at ~2,500 m/s. PYQ FREQUENCY: 3rd law applications are top NEET, JEE-Main, NCERT MCQ — 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
MOMENTUM is defined as:

(A) Mass times velocity (p = mv)
(B) Mass times acceleration here
(C) Force divided by mass usually
(D) Velocity squared by 2 always
cards.back:
(A) Mass times velocity (p = mv)

Mechanics & Motion — MOMENTUM (linear momentum, p) = m × v, where m = mass (kg), v = velocity (m/s). UNITS: kg·m/s (or N·s, equivalent). VECTOR QUANTITY — has direction. CONSERVATION OF MOMENTUM: in an isolated system (no external force), TOTAL momentum is conserved. p_initial = p_final. APPLICATIONS: (1) COLLISIONS — billiard balls, car crashes: total momentum before = after. (2) ROCKET PROPULSION: rocket gains forward momentum equal to backward momentum of expelled gases. (3) RECOIL: when a gun fires, bullet gains momentum forward; gun gains equal momentum backward (recoil). NEWTON'S 2ND LAW REFORMULATED: F = dp/dt — force is the rate of change of momentum. So if you DOUBLE the time over which a force acts, you can HALVE the force needed for the same momentum change. EXAMPLE — AIRBAGS: increase impact TIME → reduce average force on driver → less injury. CRUMPLE ZONES in cars: same principle. CRICKET — when a player CATCHES a ball, they pull their hands BACK to extend the stopping time, reducing impact force on hand. PYQ FREQUENCY: momentum definition + conservation in NEET, JEE-Main 2-3× per paper; SSC CGL ~1× per cycle.

cards.front:
A bullet of mass 10 g is fired with velocity 400 m/s from a gun of mass 4 kg. The recoil velocity of the gun is:

(A) 1 m/s (from momentum conservation)
(B) 4 m/s (a calc error result)
(C) 0.4 m/s (under-estimate now)
(D) 10 m/s (an over-estimate)
cards.back:
(A) 1 m/s (from momentum conservation)

Mechanics & Motion — Apply CONSERVATION OF MOMENTUM. Before firing, gun + bullet are at REST → total momentum = 0. After firing, the bullet's forward momentum + gun's backward momentum = 0. Bullet momentum = (10/1000) × 400 = 4 kg·m/s (forward). Gun momentum = 4 × v (backward) = −4v kg·m/s. Setting sum = 0: 4 + (−4v) = 0 → 4v = 4 → v = 1 m/s. So the gun recoils at 1 m/s (much slower than bullet because gun's mass is 400× larger). KEY INSIGHT: (m_bullet × v_bullet) = (m_gun × v_recoil). RECOIL VELOCITY = (m_bullet/m_gun) × v_bullet. SAFETY: military rifles + sporting rifles use heavier stocks, recoil pads, gas-operated mechanisms to reduce recoil to manageable levels. SUMO/CANNON CONTRAST: cannons have wheeled carriages that move backward several meters when fired (e.g., 18th-century naval cannons recoiled 4-5m). KEY METHOD for momentum conservation: (1) identify SYSTEM. (2) write total p_before = total p_after. (3) solve for unknown. PYQ FREQUENCY: gun-recoil + 1D collision Qs in JEE-Main, NEET, SSC CGL Tier 2 — 1-2× per paper.

cards.front:
IMPULSE is defined as:

(A) Force times time (F × Δt)
(B) Force times distance (Work)
(C) Force divided by mass here
(D) Force times velocity (Power)
cards.back:
(A) Force times time (F × Δt)

Mechanics & Motion — IMPULSE (J) = F × Δt = CHANGE IN MOMENTUM (Δp). UNITS: N·s (or kg·m/s, same as momentum). VECTOR QUANTITY. KEY EQUATION: IMPULSE = J = ∫F·dt = Δp = m × Δv. APPLICATIONS: (1) AIRBAGS, CRUMPLE ZONES — same Δp, but extended Δt → reduced average F. (2) BOXING — punch lasts brief time → high force; defender 'rolls with the punch' → extends contact time → reduces force. (3) TRAMPOLINE — extends fall-stopping time, reducing force on body. (4) CATCHING A BALL — pulling hand back = longer contact = less impact. NUMERICAL EXAMPLE: car of mass 1000 kg moving at 20 m/s comes to rest in 5 s. Δp = 1000 × 20 = 20,000 kg·m/s. Average force = Δp/Δt = 20,000/5 = 4,000 N. If instead car stopped in 0.1 s (no crumple zone), Force = 20,000/0.1 = 200,000 N — 50× more dangerous. CONTRAST WITH WORK: work = F × distance (kJ); impulse = F × time (N·s). Work changes KE; impulse changes p. PYQ FREQUENCY: impulse-momentum theorem in JEE-Main, NEET 2× per cycle; SSC ~1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Two bodies of masses 2 kg and 3 kg moving with velocities 4 m/s and 2 m/s respectively (in opposite directions) collide and stick together. The final velocity is:

(A) 0.4 m/s in 2-kg's original direction
(B) 0 m/s (perfect cancellation now)
(C) 2.5 m/s (a wrong calc result)
(D) 1.4 m/s in 3-kg's direction here
cards.back:
(A) 0.4 m/s in 2-kg's original direction

Mechanics & Motion — PERFECTLY INELASTIC COLLISION (objects stick together post-collision). Apply CONSERVATION OF MOMENTUM. Take direction of 2 kg's velocity as positive. Before: p_total = (2)(4) + (3)(−2) = 8 − 6 = +2 kg·m/s. After: total mass = 2+3 = 5 kg; final velocity v_f. So 5v_f = 2 → v_f = 0.4 m/s in the original direction of the 2-kg body (positive). KEY: KE is NOT conserved in inelastic collisions — some energy converts to heat, deformation, sound. LET'S CHECK: KE_before = ½(2)(16) + ½(3)(4) = 16 + 6 = 22 J. KE_after = ½(5)(0.16) = 0.4 J. KE LOST = 21.6 J — significant! That's the deformation energy. TYPES of COLLISIONS: (1) ELASTIC — both p and KE conserved (e.g., billiard balls, atoms). (2) INELASTIC — only p conserved; some KE lost. (3) PERFECTLY INELASTIC — bodies stick; max KE loss for given p. REAL CARS: collisions are ~80-95% inelastic; explains why KE lost goes into deforming metal/airbags. PYQ FREQUENCY: 1D collision problems in JEE-Main 2-3× per paper, NEET 1-2× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests momentum conservation discipline + sign convention.

cards.front:
Newton's First Law of Motion is also known as the:

(A) Law of Acceleration
(B) Law of Inertia
(C) Law of Action and Reaction
(D) Law of Conservation of Momentum
cards.back:
(B) Law of Inertia

Mechanics & Motion — First Law (Inertia, 1687) — 'Every body continues in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless compelled by some external force to change that state.' Galileo first articulated the idea; Newton formalised. Real-world: passengers jerk forward when a bus brakes (their bodies tend to keep moving). Three types of inertia — inertia of rest, inertia of motion, inertia of direction. SI unit of inertia: mass (kg).

cards.front:
Newton's Second Law gives the relation:

(A) F = m·v
(B) F = m·a (rate of change of momentum)
(C) F = m·g·h
(D) F = ½·m·v²
cards.back:
(B) F = m·a (rate of change of momentum)

Mechanics & Motion — Second Law: F = ma, derived from F = dp/dt where p = mv (momentum). For constant mass m, F = m × (dv/dt) = ma. SI unit of force = kg·m/s² = newton (N). 1 newton accelerates 1 kg by 1 m/s². Earth's gravity g ≈ 9.81 m/s², so a 1 kg object weighs ~9.81 N. F = ½mv² is kinetic energy, not force. p = mv is momentum (kg·m/s).

cards.front:
A force of 200 N acts on a body of mass 50 kg. The acceleration produced is:

(A) 2 m/s²
(B) 4 m/s²
(C) 5 m/s²
(D) 10 m/s²
cards.back:
(B) 4 m/s²

Mechanics & Motion — Apply Newton's Second Law: a = F/m = 200/50 = 4 m/s². Friction is assumed negligible. Verify by reverse calculation: F = m·a = 50 × 4 = 200 N ✓. SI unit check: N / kg = (kg·m/s²) / kg = m/s² ✓.

cards.front:
The recoil of a gun when fired is best explained by:

(A) Newton's First Law
(B) Newton's Third Law (and conservation of momentum)
(C) Galilean relativity
(D) Bernoulli's principle
cards.back:
(B) Newton's Third Law (and conservation of momentum)

Mechanics & Motion — Third Law — 'For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.' Bullet pushed forward; gun pushed backward (recoil). Conservation of momentum: total momentum before = 0. After firing: m_bullet × v_bullet + m_gun × (−v_gun) = 0 → v_gun = (m_bullet / m_gun) × v_bullet. Heavier gun → smaller recoil velocity. Same principle: rocket propulsion (gases ejected back, rocket pushed forward).

Same principle: rocket propulsion (gases ejected back, rocket pushed forward).

cards.front:
A 100-g bullet is fired from a 5-kg gun with a muzzle velocity of 400 m/s. The recoil velocity of the gun is:

(A) 4 m/s
(B) 8 m/s
(C) 20 m/s
(D) 12 m/s
cards.back:
(B) 8 m/s

Mechanics & Motion — Conservation of momentum (initial total = 0): m_bullet × v_bullet = m_gun × v_recoil. 0.1 × 400 = 5 × v_recoil. So v_recoil = 40 / 5 = 8 m/s. Direction is opposite to bullet's motion. Notice the units carefully: 100 g = 0.1 kg, otherwise the answer would be 8000 m/s — clearly wrong.

cards.front:
When a person walks on the ground, the FORCE that propels them forward is the:

(A) Force of gravity
(B) Frictional reaction of the ground on the foot (Newton's 3rd Law)
(C) Normal force
(D) Tension in muscles only
cards.back:
(B) Frictional reaction of the ground on the foot (Newton's 3rd Law)

Mechanics & Motion — When walking, your foot pushes BACKWARD on the ground (action). The ground pushes the foot FORWARD with an equal force (reaction) — friction provides this reaction. On a frictionless surface (like ice or polished marble) you can't walk effectively. Astronauts on the moon use a different push because of low gravity — but they also rely on regolith friction. Without friction, only forward momentum carries you, which dies on the next step.

cards.front:
An astronaut floats freely inside a spacecraft orbiting Earth. The reason for this 'weightlessness' is:

(A) There is no gravity at orbital altitude
(B) The astronaut and spacecraft are both in continuous free-fall around Earth
(C) The spacecraft is moving faster than light
(D) Magnetic forces cancel gravity
cards.back:
(B) The astronaut and spacecraft are both in continuous free-fall around Earth

Mechanics & Motion — At ISS altitude (~400 km), Earth's gravity is still ~89% of surface value — so it's NOT 'no gravity'. The spacecraft is in continuous free-fall (orbit = perpetual fall around Earth, balanced by tangential velocity). Inside, both the astronaut AND the cabin accelerate towards Earth at the same g — the astronaut feels no contact force from any surface = 'weightless'. Same effect: a person in a free-falling lift feels weightless.

cards.option2: The spacecraft is moving faster than light

(B) Inertia of rest

cards.front:
An object thrown into the air at an angle (in absence of air resistance) follows a path that is:

(A) A straight line tilted at the launch angle
(B) A parabola, due to constant downward gravity
(C) A perfect circle around the centre of the earth
(D) A spiral, due to the rotation of the earth
cards.back:
(B) A parabola, due to constant downward gravity

Mechanics & Motion — Without air resistance, projectile horizontal velocity stays constant; vertical velocity changes uniformly with g. Resulting trajectory: PARABOLA. Galileo first showed this. Distractor 1 — straight line would need no gravity. Distractor 3 — circular orbit needs continuous central pull (orbital velocity). Distractor 4 — spirals would need rotational drag, irrelevant here.

cards.front:
For a given initial speed, the angle that gives the MAXIMUM RANGE on level ground is:

(A) 30° from the horizontal direction
(B) 45° from the horizontal direction
(C) 60° from the horizontal direction
(D) 90° from the horizontal direction
cards.back:
(B) 45° from the horizontal direction

Mechanics & Motion — Range R = u² sin(2θ) / g. Maximum when sin(2θ) = 1 → 2θ = 90° → θ = 45°. Range R_max = u²/g. Complementary angles (θ and 90°−θ) give the SAME range — e.g., 30° and 60°. Distractor 4 (90° = straight up) gives zero range.

cards.front:
A ball is thrown horizontally from a tower. As it falls, the HORIZONTAL velocity component:

(A) Decreases due to air resistance always
(B) Stays constant in absence of air resistance
(C) Increases as it falls under gravity force
(D) Reverses direction at the highest point
cards.back:
(B) Stays constant in absence of air resistance

Mechanics & Motion — Gravity acts only VERTICALLY. So horizontal velocity component is unchanged in absence of air drag. Vertical velocity grows linearly downward. Two motions are independent → parabolic trajectory. Distractor 1 — true with air resistance, but ideal projectile assumption ignores it. Distractor 3 — gravity is vertical, so doesn't affect horizontal. Distractor 4 — direction doesn't reverse.

cards.front:
Two stones, one dropped from rest and another thrown horizontally, fall from the same height H. They:

(A) Hit the ground at very different times
(B) Hit the ground at exactly the same time
(C) Have very different vertical accelerations
(D) Reach the ground only along straight paths

Mechanics & Motion — Vertical motion is independent of horizontal motion. Both stones experience the same gravity from the same height → same time to fall (T = √(2H/g)). cards.front:
The TIME PERIOD of a SIMPLE PENDULUM depends on:

(A) Length and gravity (T = 2π√(L/g))
(B) Mass of the bob alone here
(C) Amplitude of swing (small)
(D) Color and material used (no)
cards.back:
(A) Length and gravity (T = 2π√(L/g))

Mechanics & Motion — SIMPLE PENDULUM TIME PERIOD: T = 2π × √(L/g), where L = length of pendulum, g = acceleration due to gravity. KEY: T is INDEPENDENT of (a) MASS of the bob (light vs heavy bob = same period, in vacuum). (b) AMPLITUDE for SMALL swings (< ~10°). LARGER amplitudes (> 15°) → period slightly increases (anharmonic). EXAMPLES: (1) PENDULUM LENGTH 1 m, g = 9.8 m/s² → T = 2π × √(1/9.8) ≈ 2.01 seconds. (2) GRANDFATHER CLOCK pendulum is ~99 cm to give T = 2 s (1 sec each way). (3) TOWER OF PISA experiment: Galileo (1583) noticed cathedral lamp swinging — observed period independence of amplitude → invented pendulum clock concept. APPLICATIONS: (1) GRANDFATHER CLOCKS — pendulum's regular T provides time-keeping. (2) FOUCAULT PENDULUM (1851) — demonstrated EARTH'S ROTATION (plane of swing rotates due to rotation of Earth's surface). (3) SEISMOMETERS use pendulum-like masses to measure ground vibrations. KEY: T ∝ √L — DOUBLING length, T ↑ by √2 ≈ 1.414. T ∝ 1/√g — at higher altitude (lower g) or moon (g ~ 1/6), T is LARGER (slower swing). MOON pendulum: ~2.45× slower than on Earth. SPRING-MASS variant: T = 2π × √(m/k) — spring constant k. PYQ FREQUENCY: pendulum formula in NEET, JEE-Main, NCERT 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
In SIMPLE HARMONIC MOTION (SHM), the restoring force is:

(A) Proportional to displacement and opposite
(B) Constant always in any direction
(C) Proportional to velocity squared
(D) Independent of any displacement
cards.back:
(A) Proportional to displacement and opposite

Mechanics & Motion — SIMPLE HARMONIC MOTION (SHM) — characterized by restoring force F = −kx, where k = positive constant (spring stiffness, etc.) and x = displacement from equilibrium. NEGATIVE SIGN means force is OPPOSITE to displacement direction (always pulls back to equilibrium). KEY CHARACTERISTICS: (1) F ∝ −x (linear restoring force). (2) Resulting motion: sinusoidal (sine/cosine wave). (3) Energy ALTERNATES between kinetic and potential — both change in magnitude but TOTAL is conserved (in absence of friction/damping). EXAMPLES: (1) MASS-ON-SPRING — ideal SHM. (2) PENDULUM (small angles) — approximates SHM. (3) TUNING FORK vibrations. (4) MOLECULAR vibrations in solids (atomic 'springs'). (5) AC current oscillates SHM-like. EQUATIONS: (1) x(t) = A × cos(ωt + φ), where A = amplitude, ω = angular frequency, φ = phase. (2) ω = √(k/m) for spring; ω = √(g/L) for pendulum. (3) T (period) = 2π/ω. (4) f (frequency) = 1/T. ENERGY: total = ½ k A² (constant). At extremes (x = ±A), all energy is potential; at center (x = 0), all kinetic. NON-SHM cases: large-amplitude pendulum (anharmonic); F = −kx − bx³ models 'soft' or 'hard' springs. RESONANCE: when driven at natural frequency, amplitude grows large (e.g., bridges, glass shattering). PYQ FREQUENCY: SHM definition in NEET, JEE-Main 1-2× per paper.

(3) T (period) = 2π/ω. (4) f (frequency) = 1/T. ENERGY: total = ½ k A² (constant). At extremes (x = ±A), all energy is potential; at center (x = 0), all kinetic. NON-SHM cases: large-amplitude pendulum (anharmonic); F = −kx − bx³ models 'soft' or 'hard' springs. RESONANCE: when driven at natural frequency, amplitude grows large (e.g., bridges, glass shattering). PYQ FREQUENCY: SHM definition in NEET, JEE-Main 1-2× per paper.

cards.front:
If pendulum's length is INCREASED 4 TIMES, its time period becomes:

(A) 2 times original (T ∝ √L)
(B) 4 times original directly
(C) 16 times original (linear)
(D) Half of original (decreases)
cards.back:
(A) 2 times original (T ∝ √L)

Mechanics & Motion — Apply T = 2π√(L/g) → T ∝ √L. If L → 4L, then T → √4 × T = 2 × T. So new period is 2× original. KEY METHOD: T scales as the SQUARE ROOT of L. INCREASE L by FACTOR k → T increases by √k. PRACTICE: (1) L → 9L → T → 3T (since √9 = 3). (2) L → 100L → T → 10T. (3) L halved (L → L/2) → T → T/√2. RELATED FREQUENCY: f = 1/T → f ∝ 1/√L. SHORTER pendulum vibrates FASTER. PRACTICAL: (a) Wristwatch with mechanical movement uses tiny balance wheel acting like a pendulum. (b) Clocks with longer pendulum → tick more slowly. KEPLER'S 3RD LAW analogy: T² ∝ a³ for orbits (Newton's law of gravity); pendulum is T² ∝ L. SAMPLE COMBINED PROBLEMS: (a) Pendulum length increased 4×; gravity halved. New T = 2 × √2 × T = 2√2 T (combining factors). (b) Pendulum on the Moon (g/6) of length L: T_moon = √6 × T_earth ≈ 2.45 × T_earth. SPACECRAFT effects on pendulum: in zero-gravity (orbiting space station), pendulum DOES NOT swing — there's no restoring force; clocks need different mechanisms. PYQ FREQUENCY: pendulum-length scaling in NEET, JEE-Main 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
RESONANCE in mechanical systems occurs when:

(A) Driving frequency = natural frequency
(B) System has highest possible damping
(C) Input force has zero frequency only
(D) Amplitude is at minimum value here
cards.back:
(A) Driving frequency = natural frequency

Mechanics & Motion — RESONANCE — when an external DRIVING FORCE oscillates at the SAME FREQUENCY as the system's NATURAL FREQUENCY (the frequency at which it freely oscillates), AMPLITUDE BUILDS UP DRAMATICALLY. PHYSICS: with each push at the right time, energy is added → amplitude grows. EXAMPLES: (1) PUSHING A SWING — must push at 'right moment' (period-matched) for swing to grow. Pushing at random times damps it. (2) GLASS SHATTERING from singing — opera singer hits note matching glass's resonant frequency; amplitude grows until fracture. (3) TACOMA NARROWS BRIDGE COLLAPSE (Nov 1940, USA) — wind-induced oscillations at the bridge's natural frequency caused massive amplitude → bridge broke; iconic engineering case study. (4) MILITARY: marching soldiers must NOT march in step on bridges — could resonate (BROUGHTON SUSPENSION BRIDGE, England, 1831 — collapsed under marching troops). (5) RADIO TUNING — adjusts circuit's resonant frequency to match radio station's frequency → maximum signal. (6) MRI MACHINES — radiowaves at NMR resonant frequency cause strong response. (7) MUSICAL INSTRUMENTS — sound box resonates at natural frequency, amplifying string vibrations. SAFETY DESIGNS — minimize resonance via DAMPING (e.g., shock absorbers) + DETUNING (avoid critical natural frequencies). PYQ FREQUENCY: resonance in NEET, JEE-Main 1× per cycle.

cards.option3: Amplitude is at minimum value here

cards.front:
What is the time period of a SECONDS PENDULUM (used in clocks)?

(A) 2 seconds (1 sec each swing)
(B) 1 second (one swing only)
(C) 60 seconds (one minute)
(D) Half a second only here
cards.back:
(A) 2 seconds (1 sec each swing)

Mechanics & Motion — SECONDS PENDULUM — time period exactly T = 2 SECONDS. So takes 1 sec for each ONE-WAY swing (left to right or right to left) — pendulum 'ticks' once per second. LENGTH: from T = 2π√(L/g): L = g × T² / (4π²) = 9.8 × 4 / (4π²) ≈ 0.993 m ≈ 99.3 cm. So a seconds pendulum is ~1 meter long. USES: GRANDFATHER CLOCKS — typical pendulum length ~99 cm, ticks 1/sec. The 'tick' you hear is from the pendulum's reversal point. NOTE: g varies by location → pendulum length must be slightly adjusted: at equator g ≈ 9.78 → L ≈ 0.99 m; at poles g ≈ 9.83 → L ≈ 0.996 m. So a CLOCK SET in Equator if MOVED to POLES would tick slightly FASTER (g higher → T smaller → faster). HISTORICAL: Galileo conceived pendulum clock idea (1602); Christian HUYGENS built first practical pendulum clock (1656) — accuracy ~minutes/day, vs prior clocks at hours/day error. KEY ROLE: pendulum clocks dominated time-keeping for ~300 years (1656-1930) until QUARTZ CLOCKS (1927) and ATOMIC CLOCKS (1955) took over for precision. ATOMIC CLOCKS today: NIST F-2 (USA) accurate to 10⁻¹⁶ — 1 second error in 300 million years. PYQ FREQUENCY: 'seconds pendulum length' in NEET, JEE-Main 1× per 2 cycles.

cards.front:
A spring with k = 100 N/m is attached to a 1 kg mass. The angular frequency of SHM is:

(A) 10 rad/s (using ω=√(k/m))
(B) 100 rad/s (over-shot value)
(C) 1 rad/s (under-estimate calc)
(D) 0.1 rad/s (way under-shot)
cards.back:
(A) 10 rad/s (using ω=√(k/m))

Mechanics & Motion — Apply ω = √(k/m). Plug k=100, m=1: ω = √(100/1) = 10 rad/s. PERIOD: T = 2π/ω = 2π/10 ≈ 0.628 s. FREQUENCY: f = 1/T = 1/0.628 ≈ 1.59 Hz (cycles/sec). KEY FORMULAS for SPRING-MASS SHM: (1) ω = √(k/m). (2) T = 2π × √(m/k). (3) f = 1/T = (1/2π) × √(k/m). PRACTICE: (1) k=400, m=1: ω = 20 rad/s, T = 0.314 s. (2) k=100, m=4: ω = 5 rad/s, T = 1.26 s. (3) Doubling mass: ω → ω/√2 (slower). Doubling k: ω → ω×√2 (faster). ENERGY in SHM: (1) Kinetic: KE = ½ m v² = ½ m × ω² × (A² − x²). (2) Potential (spring): PE = ½ k x². (3) Total E = ½ k A² (constant). At equilibrium: max KE, min PE. At extremes: max PE, zero KE. APPLICATIONS: (1) AUTO SUSPENSION — coil springs damped to reduce bouncing. (2) SHOCK ABSORBERS — critically damped. (3) SEISMOMETERS — mass on spring; ground shake → mass relatively stays, providing measurement. (4) ANALOGOUS to LC circuit (electrical SHM): ω = 1/√(LC). PYQ FREQUENCY: spring-mass calculations in NEET, JEE-Main 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
DAMPING in oscillating systems causes amplitude to:

(A) Decrease over time (energy lost)
(B) Increase over time always
(C) Stay constant indefinitely (ideal)
(D) Oscillate randomly (chaotic)
cards.back:
(A) Decrease over time (energy lost)

Mechanics & Motion — DAMPING — the gradual loss of OSCILLATION AMPLITUDE due to FRICTION, AIR RESISTANCE, or other dissipative forces. Energy of oscillator is gradually converted to HEAT or other forms. EXAMPLES: (1) PENDULUM in air — eventually stops due to air drag + pivot friction. (2) GUITAR STRING — vibration dies down because energy radiates as sound. (3) MASS-SPRING in oil — quickly damped (high viscosity). DAMPING TYPES: (1) UNDERDAMPED — system oscillates but amplitude decreases exponentially (most everyday systems). (2) OVERDAMPED — system returns to equilibrium SLOWLY without oscillating (e.g., slamming a heavy door against thick paint). (3) CRITICALLY DAMPED — fastest possible return to equilibrium without overshoot (used in CAR SHOCK ABSORBERS — comfort + safety). MATHEMATICAL: amplitude A(t) = A₀ × e^(−γt) where γ = damping coefficient. Larger γ = faster decay. APPLICATIONS: (1) DOOR CLOSER mechanisms. (2) AUTO SHOCK ABSORBERS — dampen road bumps. (3) BUILDING VIBRATION DAMPERS in earthquake-resistant skyscrapers (Taipei 101 has a giant 660-ton tuned mass damper — reduces sway during earthquakes/typhoons). RESONANCE + DAMPING: low damping → SHARP resonance peaks (sensitive); high damping → broad/no resonance. PYQ FREQUENCY: damping types in NEET, JEE-Main 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
A seesaw is an example of a:

(A) Second-class lever
(B) First-class lever
(C) Third-class lever
(D) Compound machine
cards.back:
(B) First-class lever

Mechanics & Motion — Lever classes by position of fulcrum (F), load (L), effort (E): 1st class — F between L and E (seesaw, crowbar, scissors, pliers); 2nd class — L between F and E (wheelbarrow, nutcracker, bottle opener); 3rd class — E between F and L (tweezers, fishing rod, human forearm, ice tongs). Mnemonic 'FLE-123' — F in middle for 1st, L middle for 2nd, E middle for 3rd.

cards.front:
The 'mechanical advantage' of a simple machine is defined as:

(A) Input work divided by output work
(B) Load divided by effort
(C) Speed divided by distance
(D) Force times distance
cards.back:
(B) Load divided by effort

Mechanics & Motion — Mechanical Advantage (MA) = Load / Effort. If MA > 1, the machine multiplies force (lift a heavy load with a small effort, e.g., lever, pulley, jack). If MA < 1, the machine multiplies speed / distance (e.g., human arm as a 3rd-class lever — small movement at the joint → large movement at the hand). An ideal (frictionless) machine conserves work — input work = output work.

cards.front:
A single fixed pulley — such as the one on a flagpole — has a mechanical advantage of:

(A) 2
(B) 1
(C) 0.5
(D) Infinite
cards.back:
(B) 1

Mechanics & Motion — A single fixed pulley simply changes the direction of the applied force — pulling down to lift something up — but does not reduce the effort (MA = 1). A movable pulley gives MA = 2 (halves the effort but doubles the distance pulled). Block-and-tackle systems (multiple-pulley sets) can reach MA of 4, 6 or higher.

cards.front:
An inclined plane makes lifting a load easier by:

(A) Reducing the load's weight
(B) Spreading the work over a longer distance (less force, more distance)
(C) Eliminating friction
(D) Adding potential energy
cards.back:
(B) Spreading the work over a longer distance (less force, more distance)

Mechanics & Motion — An inclined plane (ramp) doesn't reduce work done — it lets you use a smaller force over a longer distance. Work = Force × distance is the same. Effort force = (load × height) / ramp length. Shallower ramp → easier push, but longer way. Ramps have been used since ancient construction (Egyptian pyramids, Roman aqueducts, modern freight loading).
