cards.front:
FIRST LAW OF THERMODYNAMICS is essentially:

(A) Heat always flows hot → cold spontaneously
(B) Conservation of energy across transformations
(C) Entropy of universe always increases here
(D) Absolute zero temperature cannot be reached
cards.back:
(B) Conservation of energy across transformations

Heat & Thermodynamics — FIRST LAW = energy conservation. ΔU = Q − W (change in internal energy = heat added − work done by system). Energy cannot be created or destroyed; only converted form-to-form. SECOND LAW = entropy of isolated system never decreases (heat flows hot → cold; you can't make heat engine 100% efficient). THIRD LAW = entropy of perfect crystal at absolute zero is zero (absolute zero is unreachable). ZEROTH LAW = if A in equilibrium with B + B with C, then A is in equilibrium with C (basis of thermometers).

ABSOLUTE ZERO is approximately:

(A) 0 °C is the absolute zero point
(B) −273.15 °C (or 0 K) is absolute zero
(C) −100 °C is the absolute zero
(D) 0 °F is the absolute zero point
cards.back:
(B) −273.15 °C (or 0 K) is absolute zero

Heat & Thermodynamics — Absolute zero = lowest theoretical temperature. Atoms have minimum thermal energy (only quantum zero-point motion). On Kelvin = 0 K; on Celsius = −273.15 °C; on Fahrenheit = −459.67 °F. Cannot be reached (3rd law of thermodynamics). Closest achieved: ~38 picokelvin (10⁻¹² K, NIST 2003 with rubidium atoms). cards.front:
Three modes of HEAT TRANSFER are:

(A) Reflection, refraction, diffraction
(B) Conduction, convection, radiation
(C) Compression, expansion, oscillation
(D) Absorption, emission, transmission
cards.back:
(B) Conduction, convection, radiation

Heat & Thermodynamics — Heat transfer modes: (1) CONDUCTION — through direct contact in solids (metal spoon in tea heats up); (2) CONVECTION — through fluids (air, water) by bulk movement (boiling water, sea/land breeze, heat radiator); (3) RADIATION — via electromagnetic waves, no medium needed (Sun's heat reaches Earth through vacuum; infrared from hot stove). All hot bodies emit thermal radiation (Stefan-Boltzmann law: P ∝ T⁴). Distractor 1 = light wave properties.

cards.front:
A THERMOS FLASK keeps liquids hot/cold by minimizing all 3 modes of heat transfer. The vacuum between its walls reduces:

(A) Radiation, but not convection at all
(B) Conduction + convection (both need medium)
(C) All three modes equally well together
(D) Only convection in the surrounding air
cards.back:
(B) Conduction + convection (both need medium)

Heat & Thermodynamics — THERMOS FLASK design: (1) DOUBLE WALL with VACUUM between — vacuum has no particles → blocks both CONDUCTION and CONVECTION (both need medium). (2) SILVERED INTERIOR walls — REFLECT radiant heat back (reduces radiation transfer). (3) Cork/plastic stopper — bad conductor. Combined → liquid stays hot/cold for hours. Invented by James DEWAR (1892, Scottish chemist) — initially called 'Dewar flask' for cryogenic research.

cards.front:
0 °C is equal to which temperature on the Fahrenheit scale?

(A) 0 °F
(B) 32 °F
(C) 100 °F
(D) −32 °F
cards.back:
(B) 32 °F

Heat & Thermodynamics — Freezing point of water = 0 °C = 32 °F. Boiling point = 100 °C = 212 °F. Conversion: F = (9/5)C + 32. The two scales cross at −40° (−40 °C = −40 °F). The Kelvin scale has the same size unit as Celsius but starts at absolute zero: 0 K = −273.15 °C.

cards.front:
The transfer of heat through a vacuum, as from the Sun to the Earth, is called:

(A) Conduction
(B) Radiation
(C) Convection
(D) Evaporation
cards.back:
(B) Radiation

Heat & Thermodynamics — Radiation — transfer of heat via electromagnetic waves (mostly infrared); needs no medium. Conduction needs direct contact between particles (a hot pan handle). Convection needs a moving fluid (boiling water, wind). Evaporation is a phase change, not a heat-transfer mode. Solar energy reaches Earth entirely by radiation through the vacuum of space.

cards.front:
Water has a very high specific heat capacity, which means that compared to most other substances, it:

(A) Warms up and cools down quickly
(B) Requires more heat to change its temperature
(C) Conducts heat poorly
(D) Has very low boiling point
cards.back:
(B) Requires more heat to change its temperature

Heat & Thermodynamics — Water's specific heat capacity is 4,186 J/kg·K, much higher than most substances. It therefore needs large amounts of heat to raise its temperature by 1 °C, and releases large amounts when cooling. This is why oceans regulate climate, coastal cities have milder weather than inland ones, and water is used as a coolant in car radiators and power plants.

cards.front:
The temperature at which all molecular motion theoretically stops — called absolute zero — is:

(A) 0 °C
(B) −273.15 °C
(C) −100 °C
(D) 0 K at 0 °C
cards.back:
(B) −273.15 °C

Heat & Thermodynamics — Absolute zero is 0 K = −273.15 °C = −459.67 °F. At this limit, classical thermal motion ceases; quantum zero-point energy still remains. Absolute zero has never been reached experimentally, but temperatures within a few billionths of a kelvin have been produced in laser-cooling labs. Lord Kelvin proposed the scale in 1848.

cards.front:
The heat absorbed by a substance during a change of state (like melting or boiling) — without any temperature change — is called:

(A) Specific heat
(B) Latent heat
(C) Entropy
(D) Thermal conductivity
cards.back:
(B) Latent heat

Heat & Thermodynamics — Latent heat ('hidden' heat) — the energy that goes into breaking intermolecular bonds during a phase change, without raising the temperature. Latent heat of fusion of ice = 334 J/g (what makes ice such an efficient coolant). Latent heat of vaporisation of water = 2260 J/g (which is why steam burns are so damaging). Specific heat is the energy per °C of temperature change (no phase change).

cards.front:
Water attains its maximum density at:

(A) 0 °C
(B) 4 °C
(C) 100 °C
(D) −4 °C
cards.back:
(B) 4 °C

Heat & Thermodynamics — Water is unusual — it gets denser from 0 °C up to 4 °C, then less dense above 4 °C. This 'anomalous expansion' is why ice floats (ice is less dense than water) and why ponds freeze from the top downwards — the 4 °C water settles at the bottom, protecting aquatic life through winter. Density of water at 4 °C = 1000 kg/m³.

cards.front:
The first law of thermodynamics is essentially a statement of the:

(A) Conservation of momentum
(B) Conservation of energy
(C) Conservation of charge
(D) Conservation of mass
cards.back:
(B) Conservation of energy

Heat & Thermodynamics — First law: ΔU = Q − W. The change in internal energy of a system equals heat added to the system minus work done by the system. Energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only transformed. The second law introduces entropy and the direction of heat flow (hot to cold, not the reverse). The third law says entropy approaches a constant as temperature goes to absolute zero.

cards.front:
Heat is transferred through SOLIDS primarily by which mechanism?

(A) Convection due to fluid flow across the solid
(B) Conduction by lattice vibrations and free electrons
(C) Radiation by infrared waves moving inside the solid
(D) Evaporation of moisture trapped within the solid
cards.back:
(B) Conduction by lattice vibrations and free electrons

Heat & Thermodynamics — CONDUCTION — heat flows from hot to cold parts of a solid via lattice vibrations (phonons) and, in metals, free-electron motion. No bulk movement of matter. Metals are good conductors because they have many free electrons. CONVECTION (Distractor 1) — works in fluids (liquids/gases) via bulk flow. RADIATION (Distractor 3) — does pass through transparent media but isn't the main mode in opaque solids. Distractor 4 — evaporation is irrelevant to solid heat transfer.

cards.front:
A SEA BREEZE that blows from sea to land during the day is the result of:

(A) Differential conduction of heat through solid earth and water
(B) Convection — land heats faster, hot air rises, cooler air rushes in
(C) Radiation imbalance between the sunlit land and the sunlit sea
(D) Evaporation directly cooling the moist air over the open sea
cards.back:
(B) Convection — land heats faster, hot air rises, cooler air rushes in

Heat & Thermodynamics — Land has lower specific heat than water → heats faster during the day. Air over land becomes hot, rises (low pressure forms). Cooler air over sea (high pressure) flows in to replace it → SEA BREEZE during the day. At night, the reverse — land cools faster → land high pressure → LAND BREEZE blows from land to sea. Both are CONVECTION-driven. Distractor 1 — conduction in earth is too slow. Distractor 3 — radiation difference contributes but the moving air is convection. Distractor 4 — evaporation cools but doesn't drive the breeze.

cards.front:
The GREENHOUSE EFFECT on Earth is caused by:

(A) Direct conduction of heat from the sun's surface
(B) Atmospheric gases trapping outgoing infrared radiation
(C) Convection currents in the upper atmosphere
(D) Volcanic eruptions on the planet's surface
cards.back:
(B) Atmospheric gases trapping outgoing infrared radiation

Heat & Thermodynamics — Earth absorbs short-wavelength sunlight, re-radiates it as longer-wavelength INFRARED. Greenhouse gases (CO₂, water vapour, methane, nitrous oxide, ozone) absorb this IR and re-emit some back toward Earth → surface stays warmer than it would in a transparent atmosphere. Without GHG: Earth would average ~−18 °C (uninhabitable). With natural GHG: ~+15 °C (just right). Anthropogenic CO₂ rise from ~280 ppm (pre-industrial) to >420 ppm today is enhancing the effect → global warming. Distractor 1 — conduction doesn't operate across vacuum of space. Distractor 3 — convection is irrelevant to this. Distractor 4 — volcanism is a smaller separate factor.

Why are cooking utensils made of materials like ALUMINIUM and COPPER but with WOODEN handles?

(A) Wood looks attractive while metal is durable for cooking
(B) Metal conducts heat well to food while wood insulates the hand
(C) Wood is cheaper than metal, reducing manufacturing cost
(D) Wood is heavier than metal, so it stays steady on stove
cards.back:
(B) Metal conducts heat well to food while wood insulates the hand

Heat & Thermodynamics — Metals (Cu, Al, steel) — high thermal conductivity → quickly transfer stove heat to food. Wood (and modern plastics) — low conductivity → handle stays cool enough to grip safely. The combination optimises function: efficient cooking + safe handling. cards.front:
Why is the BOTTOM of a cooking pot painted BLACK and the OUTSIDE often kept SHINY?

(A) Black bottom looks elegant and shiny outside reflects oil splatter
(B) Black absorbs heat efficiently from the flame; shiny reduces heat loss
(C) Both are purely cosmetic features unrelated to thermal physics
(D) Black paint and shiny finish are both heat resistant materials
cards.back:
(B) Black absorbs heat efficiently from the flame; shiny reduces heat loss

Heat & Thermodynamics — BLACK surfaces are good ABSORBERS of radiation (black-body). The pot's bottom blackens with carbon over time; this enhances absorption of radiative + flame heat → faster cooking. SHINY (polished metal) surfaces are poor absorbers AND poor emitters → reduce radiative heat loss from the pot's outside to the kitchen. Result: more energy goes into the food, less is wasted. Stefan-Boltzmann law governs radiative heat: Q = εσA(T⁴ − T_amb⁴), where ε (emissivity) is high for black, low for polished. Distractor 1, 3 are aesthetic non-explanations. Distractor 4 — heat resistance isn't the mechanism.

cards.front:
A black body is a body that:

(A) Reflects all incident radiation back to its source
(B) Absorbs all incident radiation across all wavelengths
(C) Emits radiation only at one specific wavelength only
(D) Has zero emission of thermal radiation at all temperatures
cards.back:
(B) Absorbs all incident radiation across all wavelengths

Heat & Thermodynamics — BLACK BODY — idealised body that absorbs ALL incident electromagnetic radiation (no reflection, no transmission). At thermal equilibrium, by Kirchhoff's law of radiation, it also EMITS the maximum possible radiation for its temperature → the spectrum follows Planck's distribution. Stars approximate black bodies; the cosmic microwave background is a near-perfect black body at 2.725 K. Wien's law: peak wavelength × T = constant. Hotter stars peak in blue/UV, cooler stars in red/IR. Distractor 1 = white body / mirror. Distractor 3 = laser / monochromatic emitter. Distractor 4 = unphysical at any T > 0.

(A) Convection

(C) Radiation

cards.front:
The boiling of water in a kettle, sea breezes, and atmospheric circulation are all examples of heat transfer by:

(A) Conduction
(B) Convection (bulk movement of fluid carrying heat)
(C) Radiation
(D) Insulation
cards.back:
(B) Convection (bulk movement of fluid carrying heat)

Heat & Thermodynamics — CONVECTION — heat carried by bulk movement of fluid (gas or liquid). Two types: NATURAL — driven by buoyancy (warm fluid rises, cool fluid sinks) — boiling water, sea/land breezes, monsoon. FORCED — driven by external pump/fan — central heating, hair dryer, AC. Convection currents drive ocean circulation (thermohaline), Earth's mantle (plate tectonics), climate patterns. Doesn't work in solids (no fluid motion).

cards.front:
Newton's law of COOLING states that the rate of heat loss of a body is:

(A) Independent of temperature difference
(B) Proportional to the temperature DIFFERENCE between the body and its surroundings (for small differences)
(C) Proportional to body's mass squared
(D) Independent of surrounding temperature
cards.back:
(B) Proportional to the temperature DIFFERENCE between the body and its surroundings (for small differences)

Heat & Thermodynamics — Newton's Law of Cooling: dT/dt = −k(T − T_surroundings). Holds approximately when T − T_s is small (and the body's emissivity is constant). For larger differences, Stefan-Boltzmann (T⁴) dominates. Solution: T(t) = T_s + (T₀ − T_s) e^(−kt). Applications: forensic time-of-death estimation, cooling rates in metallurgy, radiator design. Hot tea cools faster than warm tea because dT is bigger.

Among Ag, Cu, Al, Fe — which is the BEST conductor of heat?

(A) Iron (Fe)
(B) Silver (Ag) — highest thermal conductivity (~430 W/m·K)
(C) Aluminium (Al)
(D) Copper (Cu)
cards.back:
(B) Silver (Ag) — highest thermal conductivity (~430 W/m·K)

cards.front:
The FIRST LAW of thermodynamics is essentially a statement of:

(A) Conservation of energy (ΔU = Q − W)
(B) Entropy always increases (a 2nd law)
(C) Temperature is universal scale
(D) Heat flows from hot to cold (a 2nd law)
cards.back:
(A) Conservation of energy (ΔU = Q − W)

Heat & Thermodynamics — FIRST LAW OF THERMODYNAMICS: ENERGY CANNOT BE CREATED OR DESTROYED — only converted between forms. Mathematical: ΔU = Q − W (change in internal energy = heat added − work done by system). KEY APPLICATIONS: (1) STEAM ENGINE: heat input → work output + waste heat. (2) AUTOMOBILE ENGINE: chemical energy (fuel) → kinetic + thermal energy. (3) HUMAN BODY: food energy → mechanical work + body heat. PERPETUAL MOTION machines of FIRST KIND (creating energy from nothing) are FORBIDDEN by the 1st law. SIGN CONVENTION: Q positive when ADDED to system; W positive when DONE BY system on surroundings. ENERGY FORMS: kinetic, potential, thermal, chemical, electrical, nuclear, light, sound — all interconvertible. CONNECTION TO E=mc²: even mass and energy are interchangeable in relativity (1st law extends). HISTORICAL: developed by JOULE (1840s) — paddle-wheel experiment showed mechanical work converts to heat (1 calorie ≈ 4.18 joules). HELMHOLTZ formalized as 'conservation of energy' (1847). PYQ FREQUENCY: 1st law statement is a 1-mark guarantee in NEET, JEE-Main, NCERT-driven SSC. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests recognition of energy-conservation principle.

cards.front:
The SECOND LAW of thermodynamics is associated with which physical quantity?

(A) Entropy (always increases in isolated systems)
(B) Internal energy (a 1st law thing) (option here)
(C) Pressure of the gas mixture (option here)
(D) Volume of the system always (option here)
cards.back:
(A) Entropy (always increases in isolated systems)

Heat & Thermodynamics — SECOND LAW: in any spontaneous process in an ISOLATED SYSTEM, ENTROPY (S) ALWAYS INCREASES (or stays constant for reversible processes). ΔS_universe ≥ 0. ENTROPY = measure of DISORDER or NUMBER OF MICROSTATES (Boltzmann: S = k·ln Ω). EQUIVALENT STATEMENTS of 2nd law: (1) KELVIN-PLANCK — no engine can convert heat ENTIRELY into work (always some waste heat). (2) CLAUSIUS — heat flows SPONTANEOUSLY from HOT to COLD (never reverse, without external work). (3) ENTROPY STATEMENT — universe entropy increases. CONSEQUENCES: (a) NO 100% EFFICIENT heat engine. (b) HEAT FLOWS one direction (without input). (c) PERPETUAL MOTION 2nd kind (extracting work from heat with no waste) FORBIDDEN. CARNOT EFFICIENCY (max possible): η = 1 − T_cold/T_hot (in Kelvin). EXAMPLE: car engine ~30% efficient; Carnot maximum (~700K combustion / 300K ambient) = 1 − 300/700 ≈ 57%. ENTROPY in EVERYDAY: ice melts spontaneously (water more disordered than ice); ice doesn't form spontaneously (needs energy input). DEATH OF UNIVERSE: 'Heat Death' — eventually all energy becomes uniform low-grade heat; no work possible (theoretical, ~10¹⁰⁰ years). PYQ FREQUENCY: 2nd law + entropy in NEET, JEE-Main 2-3× per paper.

cards.front:
The ZEROTH LAW of thermodynamics establishes the concept of:

(A) Thermal equilibrium and temperature
(B) Entropy as a state function here
(C) Conservation of mass-energy
(D) Maximum efficiency of an engine
cards.back:
(A) Thermal equilibrium and temperature

Heat & Thermodynamics — ZEROTH LAW: 'IF two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a THIRD system, then they are in thermal equilibrium with EACH OTHER.' This establishes the concept of TEMPERATURE — a property that determines whether two systems will exchange heat. WHY 'ZEROTH'? Discovered/articulated AFTER the first and second laws (early 20th century by R.H. Fowler), but considered MORE FUNDAMENTAL — needed to define temperature itself; hence numbered 'zeroth' so as not to disturb the existing 1st-2nd numbering. PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE: thermometers work because of zeroth law — when a thermometer reaches equilibrium with object A and shows X°C, and reaches equilibrium with object B and ALSO shows X°C, A and B are at the same temperature (would not exchange heat if put together). TEMPERATURE SCALES: (1) CELSIUS — 0°C (water freezes), 100°C (water boils, at 1 atm). (2) FAHRENHEIT — 32°F (freeze), 212°F (boil); F = 9/5 C + 32. (3) KELVIN — absolute scale; 0 K = absolute zero (−273.15°C). T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15. KELVIN is used in scientific equations (especially gas laws, thermodynamics). PYQ FREQUENCY: zeroth law in NEET, JEE-Main 1× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests definition of temperature.

cards.front:
The THIRD LAW of thermodynamics states that as temperature approaches absolute zero:

(A) Entropy of a perfect crystal approaches zero
(B) Energy becomes zero entirely also
(C) Heat capacity becomes infinite always
(D) Pressure must always reach zero
cards.back:
(A) Entropy of a perfect crystal approaches zero

Heat & Thermodynamics — THIRD LAW: as TEMPERATURE T → 0 K (absolute zero, −273.15°C), the ENTROPY of a PERFECT CRYSTAL → 0. Statement by NERNST (1906) — known as Nernst Heat Theorem; PLANCK extended it. INTUITION: at absolute zero, atoms have minimum thermal motion; only one possible microstate (all atoms in their ground state, perfectly aligned in crystal lattice) → entropy log(1) = 0. CONSEQUENCES: (1) Absolute zero is UNATTAINABLE — you can approach but never reach it (would require infinite work). (2) ENTROPY at any finite T can be measured ABSOLUTELY, not just relatively. (3) Heat capacity → 0 as T → 0 (Debye/Einstein models). LOWEST T EVER ACHIEVED in lab: ~38 picokelvin (38 × 10⁻¹² K, achieved 2021 in Bose-Einstein condensate experiments). NOT TO BE CONFUSED with TEMPERATURE LIMITS in nature — Cosmic Microwave Background ≈ 2.7 K (universe's residual heat from Big Bang). NEUTRON STARS interior ~10⁹ K (extremely hot); white dwarfs cool over billions of years. APPLICATION — CRYOGENICS: liquid nitrogen (77 K), liquid helium (4 K) — used for MRI superconductors, low-T research, biological sample preservation. PYQ FREQUENCY: 3rd law in NEET, JEE-Main 1× per 2 cycles.

cards.front:
A CARNOT engine operating between 600 K and 300 K has maximum efficiency of:

(A) 50% (using 1 − T_cold/T_hot)
(B) 30% (under-estimate calc)
(C) 100% (over-estimate amount)
(D) 200% (impossibly large value)
cards.back:
(A) 50% (using 1 − T_cold/T_hot)

Heat & Thermodynamics — CARNOT EFFICIENCY (theoretical maximum for any heat engine between two reservoirs): η = 1 − T_cold/T_hot, where T in KELVIN. Plug T_cold = 300 K, T_hot = 600 K: η = 1 − 300/600 = 1 − 0.5 = 0.5 = 50%. INTERPRETATION: at most 50% of input heat can be converted to work; the other 50% is rejected as waste heat to the cold reservoir. KEY: T must be in KELVIN (NEVER Celsius); using Celsius gives wrong answers. CARNOT CYCLE — ideal reversible 4-step cycle: (1) Isothermal expansion (Q absorbed at T_hot). (2) Adiabatic expansion (T drops to T_cold). (3) Isothermal compression (Q rejected at T_cold). (4) Adiabatic compression (T rises back to T_hot). REAL ENGINES: less efficient than Carnot (irreversibilities, friction, finite-rate heat transfer). Internal combustion engines: ~25-30% efficient (T_hot ~ 2500 K, T_cold ~ 600 K → Carnot max ~76%). DIESEL: ~40%. STEAM TURBINES: ~35-40%. COMBINED CYCLE GAS TURBINE (CCGT): ~60% efficient (highest commercial). PYQ FREQUENCY: Carnot efficiency calculations in NEET, JEE-Main 2-3× per paper. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests Kelvin discipline.

cards.front:
A REFRIGERATOR works on which thermodynamic principle?

(A) Reverse of heat engine cycle (heat pump)
(B) Heating water using current here
(C) Vacuum sucks heat away always
(D) Cold air settles at the bottom
cards.back:
(A) Reverse of heat engine cycle (heat pump)

Heat & Thermodynamics — REFRIGERATOR (and AC) — operates as a HEAT PUMP — REVERSE of a heat engine. Instead of converting heat → work, it uses WORK INPUT to PUMP HEAT from a COLD reservoir (inside) to a HOT reservoir (outside). This DOESN'T VIOLATE 2nd law because work is added (overall entropy of universe still increases). REFRIGERATION CYCLE — 4 stages: (1) COMPRESSOR — refrigerant compressed (T rises). (2) CONDENSER (at back) — refrigerant gives off heat to room air (T drops to liquid). (3) EXPANSION VALVE — pressure drops; refrigerant cools rapidly. (4) EVAPORATOR (inside fridge) — refrigerant absorbs heat from food (T rises to gas), then back to compressor. COEFFICIENT OF PERFORMANCE (COP): COP = Q_cold / W_input. Typically 2-5; can be > 1 (no contradiction; you're MOVING heat, not creating energy). REFRIGERANTS: historically CFCs (Freon, R-12, R-22) — banned due to ozone-layer depletion (Montreal Protocol 1987). Now HFCs (R-134a, R-410A) — climate impact concern; HFOs (R-1234yf) increasingly used. INDIA: ENERGY EFFICIENCY star ratings (BEE) for ACs and refrigerators — 5-star = most efficient. PYQ FREQUENCY: refrigeration in NEET, JEE-Main 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
ABSOLUTE ZERO temperature in Celsius is approximately:

(A) −273.15°C (lower limit of T)
(B) 0°C (the freezing point ice)
(C) −100°C (cold but not absolute)
(D) −500°C (way too cold here)
cards.back:
(A) −273.15°C (lower limit of T)

Heat & Thermodynamics — ABSOLUTE ZERO = 0 KELVIN = −273.15°C = −459.67°F. The COLDEST POSSIBLE TEMPERATURE — at which all molecular thermal motion theoretically ceases. WHY UNREACHABLE? 3rd law of thermodynamics: it would require infinite work/cooling steps. REAL EXPERIMENTS: lowest LAB temperature ~38 picokelvin (NASA Cold Atom Lab on ISS, Bose-Einstein condensates, 2021). DERIVATION: by extrapolation of CHARLES'S LAW (V ∝ T) — V → 0 at T → −273.15°C; gases would have zero volume at absolute zero. SCALES BUILT ON ABSOLUTE ZERO: KELVIN (K), RANKINE (°R, used in some US engineering). KELVIN is the SI unit of temperature. CONNECTION to QUANTUM MECHANICS: at very low T, particles obey QUANTUM STATISTICS — bosons can occupy same state (Bose-Einstein condensates), fermions can't (Fermi gas). SUPERCONDUCTIVITY emerges at T < critical temperature (e.g., niobium at 9.3 K, YBa₂Cu₃O₇ at 92 K — 'high-Tc' superconductor). COSMIC LIMITS: CMB ≈ 2.725 K; deep space ≈ 2-3 K (uniform cosmic background). RECENT (2024) — discoveries of room-temperature superconductors remain CONTROVERSIAL. PYQ FREQUENCY: absolute zero is a 1-mark guarantee in NEET, JEE-Main, NCERT-driven SSC.

cards.front:
A convex lens forms a real, inverted, and magnified image of an object. Where must the object be placed?

(A) Between focal point F and 2F
(B) Beyond 2F always alone alone
(C) At focal point F itself alone
(D) Between F and the lens.
cards.back:
(A) Between focal point F and 2F

Light & Optics — CONVEX LENS — image properties depend on object distance: (i) Object at INFINITY → image at F, real, inverted, highly diminished (a point). (ii) Object beyond 2F → image between F and 2F, real, inverted, DIMINISHED. (iii) Object AT 2F → image at 2F, real, inverted, SAME SIZE. (iv) Object between F and 2F → image beyond 2F, real, inverted, MAGNIFIED ← matches the question. (v) Object AT F → image at infinity, undefined. (vi) Object between F and lens → image on same side, virtual, erect, MAGNIFIED (magnifying glass). KEY FORMULA: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f (sign convention: distances measured from optical centre; f positive for convex). REAL-WORLD: SLIDE PROJECTORS work in setting (iv) — film slide is between F and 2F so we get a magnified inverted image (the slide is loaded upside-down to invert back). EYE LENSES: human crystalline lens is convex, focal length ~22 mm, focuses real images on retina. EXAMINER MINDSET: testing the standard ray-diagram/image-table — appears in NCERT Class 10 ch. 10.

cards.front:
A concave lens always produces an image that is:

(A) Virtual, erect, and diminished always
(B) Real and inverted alone alone
(C) Real and magnified alone alone
(D) Virtual and magnified alone alone
cards.back:
(A) Virtual, erect, and diminished always

Light & Optics — CONCAVE (diverging) LENS — regardless of object position, image is ALWAYS: (1) on the SAME SIDE as object (virtual); (2) ERECT (upright); (3) SMALLER than object (diminished); (4) BETWEEN F and the optical centre. Why? Concave lens diverges parallel rays, so they appear to emerge from a virtual focal point on the SAME side as the incident light — image cannot form on opposite side. KEY FORMULA: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f (f is NEGATIVE for concave); magnification m = v/u always less than 1. REAL-WORLD APPLICATIONS: (a) Spectacles for MYOPIA (short-sightedness) — concave lens diverges light entering the eye, shifting the focal point back to the retina. (b) Peephole/door-viewer (combined with convex). (c) Galilean telescope's eyepiece. PYQ ANGLE: NCERT Class 10 PYQs test exactly this 'always diminished' nature. EXAM TRAP: students confuse with concave MIRROR (which can give real magnified images) — concave LENS is fundamentally different.

cards.front:
The power of a lens is +5 dioptres. What is its focal length and type?

(A) 20 cm convex (converging) lens
(B) 5 cm convex alone alone alone
(C) 20 cm concave alone alone alone
(D) 5 cm concave alone alone alone
cards.back:
(A) 20 cm convex (converging) lens

Light & Optics — POWER P = 1/f (where f is in METRES). P = +5 D → f = 1/5 = 0.20 m = 20 cm. POSITIVE power = converging = CONVEX lens. NEGATIVE power = diverging = concave. UNIT: dioptre (D) = m⁻¹. EYE-PRESCRIPTION ANGLE: when an optician writes '−2.50 D' for your spectacles, that's a concave lens of focal length 1/2.5 = 0.40 m = 40 cm to correct myopia. '+1.50 D' = convex, 67 cm focal length, corrects hyperopia. CAMERA LENSES: a 50mm camera lens has f = 0.05 m → P = 20 D — a 'fast' lens. ZOOM lenses combine multiple convex/concave elements; effective P shifts as elements move. INSIGHT: lens-maker's equation 1/f = (n−1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂) means thicker lenses = shorter f = higher power. A 'plus 5' lens means it bends light enough to converge parallel rays at 20 cm — useful for reading glasses and small magnifiers. EXAM TIP: convert dioptre↔metres carefully; mistakes always come from forgetting the metres convention.

A 'plus 5' lens means it bends light enough to converge parallel rays at 20 cm — useful for reading glasses and small magnifiers. EXAM TIP: convert dioptre↔metres carefully; mistakes always come from forgetting the metres convention.

cards.front:
A simple microscope uses which type of lens, and what kind of image does it produce?

(A) Convex lens producing virtual magnified image
(B) Concave lens, real diminished image.
(C) Convex lens, real inverted image.
(D) Concave lens, virtual erect image.
cards.back:
(A) Convex lens producing virtual magnified image

Light & Optics — A SIMPLE MICROSCOPE (magnifying glass) is a single CONVEX lens of short focal length. Object placed BETWEEN F and the optical centre → image is VIRTUAL, ERECT, MAGNIFIED — viewed comfortably at the near point (~25 cm). MAGNIFICATION formula: M = 1 + D/f, where D = least distance of distinct vision (25 cm). For f = 5 cm → M = 1 + 25/5 = 6×. COMPOUND MICROSCOPE: uses TWO convex lenses (objective + eyepiece) for higher magnification (~1500× max for light microscopes). HISTORY: Anton van Leeuwenhoek (Dutch, 1670s) built ~270× single-lens microscopes and discovered bacteria, sperm cells. INDIA NOBEL TRIVIA: C.V. Raman discovered Raman scattering using a similar setup (lenses + spectroscope). LIMIT: optical microscopes can't resolve below ~200 nm (diffraction limit, Abbe's law). For finer detail, electron microscopes (~0.1 nm resolution). EXAM ANGLE: NCERT Class 10 lens applications — staple PYQ.

cards.front:
An object is placed 30 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 20 cm. Where does the image form?

(A) 60 cm on opposite side of lens
(B) 30 cm on same side alone
(C) 10 cm on opposite side alone
(D) 12 cm on opposite side alone
cards.back:
(A) 60 cm on opposite side of lens

Light & Optics — LENS FORMULA: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f. SIGN CONVENTION (Cartesian): u is NEGATIVE (object on left, light goes right), f POSITIVE for convex. Plug: 1/v − 1/(−30) = 1/20 → 1/v + 1/30 = 1/20 → 1/v = 1/20 − 1/30 = (3−2)/60 = 1/60 → v = +60 cm. Positive v means image on the OPPOSITE side (right), real and inverted. MAGNIFICATION m = v/u = 60/(−30) = −2 → image is 2× and inverted. INSIGHT: object at 30 cm (= 1.5f) lies between F and 2F, so we expect a real, inverted, magnified image beyond 2F (= 40 cm) — answer 60 cm matches that prediction perfectly. PROJECTOR APPLICATION: this exact setup (object near 2F) is used in slide projectors for screen-size magnification. EXAM TIP: Cartesian sign convention is the SSC/IBPS standard — object distance ALWAYS negative when light travels left-to-right.

cards.front:
Which defect of vision is corrected by a CONVEX (converging) lens?

(A) Hypermetropia (far-sightedness)
(B) Myopia (short-sightedness) alone
(C) Astigmatism (cylindrical defect)
(D) Cataract (lens opacity defect)
cards.back:
(A) Hypermetropia (far-sightedness)

Light & Optics — VISION DEFECTS — quick map: (1) MYOPIA (short-sight) → eye too long OR lens too convex → image forms BEFORE retina → fix with CONCAVE lens (diverges incoming light). (2) HYPERMETROPIA / HYPEROPIA (far-sight) → eye too short OR lens too flat → image forms BEHIND retina → fix with CONVEX lens (converges to bring image forward to retina). (3) PRESBYOPIA = age-related hypermetropia from lens stiffening (~age 40+); fixed with reading glasses (convex) or bifocals. (4) ASTIGMATISM = cornea is non-spherical (cylindrical) → fixed with CYLINDRICAL lens. (5) CATARACT = lens becomes cloudy → fixed by SURGERY (replaced with synthetic IOL — intraocular lens). INDIA STAT: ~80% of preventable blindness in India is from cataract; ~6 million surgeries/year. PYQ FREQUENCY: SSC, RRB Group D include vision-defect Qs every 2-3 cycles. NCERT CLASS 10 — Ch. 11 covers all of this. EXAMINER MINDSET: testing whether you can map a defect to its physical cause AND its corrective lens.

cards.front:
Two thin lenses of powers +3 D and −1 D are placed in contact. What is the power of the combination?

(A) +2 D combined power
(B) −2 D alone alone alone
(C) +4 D alone alone alone
(D) −4 D alone alone alone alone
cards.back:
(A) +2 D combined power

Light & Optics — LENSES IN CONTACT: powers ADD algebraically. P_total = P₁ + P₂ + … For thin lenses in contact (separation d≈0), this simple addition holds. P = +3 + (−1) = +2 D. The combination acts as a CONVEX lens (positive power). FOCAL LENGTH: f = 1/P = 1/2 = 0.5 m = 50 cm. WHY? Each lens contributes its own bending; the second lens picks up where the first left off. Mathematically: 1/f_combined = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂. APPLICATION — ACHROMATIC DOUBLET: a convex crown-glass lens (+) glued to a concave flint-glass lens (−) — combined power positive but cancels chromatic aberration (different colours focusing at different points). Used in high-end telescopes, microscopes, camera lenses. INVENTOR: John Dollond (1758, England). PYQ ANGLE: lens-combination Qs appear in CGL Tier 1 every 2-3 sessions; both qualitative ('which type') and quantitative ('what power'). KEY: this is also why eye prescriptions can correct multiple defects at once — combined lens powers.

cards.front:
The SPEED OF LIGHT in vacuum is approximately:

(A) 3 × 10⁵ m/s
(B) 3 × 10⁸ m/s
(C) 3 × 10¹⁰ m/s
(D) 3 × 10⁶ m/s
cards.back:
(B) 3 × 10⁸ m/s

Light & Optics — c = 299,792,458 m/s ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum. In water c reduces to ~2.25 × 10⁸ m/s (n = 1.33). In glass ~2 × 10⁸ m/s (n ~1.5). Light TRAVELS SLOWER in denser media.

A CONVEX lens is also called a:

(A) Diverging lens
(B) Converging lens
(C) Zero-power lens
(D) Cylindrical lens
cards.back:
(B) Converging lens

Light & Optics — Convex — thicker at centre, converges parallel rays to a focal point. Used in magnifying glass, human eye lens, camera lens. CONCAVE lens is diverging (thinner at centre).

The defect of vision in which a person cannot see DISTANT objects clearly is called:

(A) Hypermetropia (long-sightedness)
(B) Myopia
(C) Presbyopia
(D) Astigmatism
cards.back:
(B) Myopia

Presbyopia — age-related inability to focus on near objects. Astigmatism — irregular curvature of cornea, corrected with cylindrical lens. short-sightedness.

cards.front:
The phenomenon of splitting of WHITE LIGHT into its component colours (VIBGYOR) by a prism is called:

(A) Reflection
(B) Dispersion
(C) Diffraction
(D) Polarisation
cards.back:
(B) Dispersion

Light & Optics — Dispersion — different wavelengths of white light refract by different amounts through a prism, producing spectrum VIBGYOR. Violet bends the most, Red the least. Newton's classic experiment.

cards.front:
The RAINBOW is formed due to:

(A) Reflection only
(B) Refraction, internal reflection, and dispersion inside water droplets
(C) Diffraction of sunlight by clouds
(D) Polarisation by dust particles
cards.back:
(B) Refraction, internal reflection, and dispersion inside water droplets

Light & Optics — Sunlight refracts as it enters a water droplet, disperses into colours, undergoes total internal reflection at the back of the droplet, and refracts again exiting — producing the rainbow. A secondary (fainter) rainbow forms with two internal reflections; colour order is reversed.

cards.front:
The SKY appears BLUE because:

(A) Air absorbs other colours
(B) Molecules of air scatter blue light more than other colours
(C) The ocean reflects onto the atmosphere
(D) Nitrogen molecules are blue in colour
cards.back:
(B) Molecules of air scatter blue light more than other colours

Light & Optics — Rayleigh scattering — scattering intensity ∝ 1/λ⁴ → shorter wavelengths (violet, blue) scatter much more than red/orange. Our eyes are more sensitive to blue than violet, hence blue sky. At sunset, longer path through atmosphere → blue is scattered away before reaching eye, leaving red/orange.
cards.option2: The ocean reflects onto the atmosphere
cards.option3: Nitrogen molecules are blue in colour

cards.front:
The power of a lens is measured in:

(A) Watt
(B) Dioptre
(C) Candela
(D) Lumen
cards.back:
(B) Dioptre

Light & Optics — Power (P) = 1 / focal length in metres. Unit: Dioptre (D) = m⁻¹. A +2 D lens has focal length 1/2 = 0.5 m (converging). Negative dioptre = diverging (concave) lens. Spectacle prescriptions use this unit.

cards.front:
When light is reflected off a smooth (specular) surface, the laws of reflection state that:

(A) Angle of incidence > angle of reflection
(B) Angle of incidence = angle of reflection (both measured from normal); incident ray, reflected ray, normal lie in one plane
(C) Reflected ray bends towards the surface
(D) Light always travels through the mirror
cards.back:
(B) Angle of incidence = angle of reflection (both measured from normal); incident ray, reflected ray, normal lie in one plane

Light & Optics — Two laws of reflection: (1) angle of incidence (i) = angle of reflection (r) — both from the NORMAL to the surface, not from the surface itself. (2) the incident ray, reflected ray and normal at the point of incidence are co-planar. Hold for both regular (specular, polished) and diffuse (rough) reflection at every point — but rough surfaces have varied normals, so reflected rays scatter.

cards.option2: Reflected ray bends towards the surface
cards.option3: Light always travels through the mirror

cards.front:
A CONCAVE mirror, when an object is placed BEYOND its centre of curvature C, forms an image that is:

(A) Virtual, erect, magnified
(B) Real, inverted, diminished — between F and C
(C) Real, erect, equal in size
(D) Virtual, inverted, equal in size
cards.back:
(B) Real, inverted, diminished — between F and C

Light & Optics — Concave (converging) mirror image table: object at infinity → image at F (point); beyond C → between F and C (real, inverted, diminished — used in telescope mirrors); at C → at C (real, inverted, same size); between C and F → beyond C (real, inverted, magnified — projector); at F → at infinity (highly magnified); between P and F → behind mirror (virtual, erect, magnified — shaving / makeup mirror).

cards.front:
A CONVEX mirror always forms an image that is:

(A) Real and inverted
(B) Virtual, erect, diminished — irrespective of object position
(C) Sometimes real, sometimes virtual
(D) At infinity always
cards.back:
(B) Virtual, erect, diminished — irrespective of object position

Light & Optics — Convex (diverging) mirror always forms a virtual, erect, diminished image, located between P (pole) and F (behind mirror). That's why convex mirrors are used as REAR-VIEW MIRRORS — wider field of view, all images upright. Side-view mirrors carry warning 'Objects in mirror are closer than they appear' because of the 'diminished' effect. Other uses: security mirrors at shop corners, ATM cabin mirrors, blind-spot mirrors.

cards.front:
The relation between focal length (f) and radius of curvature (R) of a spherical mirror is:

(A) f = R
(B) f = R/2
(C) f = 2R
(D) f = R²
cards.back:
(B) f = R/2

Light & Optics — For a spherical mirror, focal length is half the radius of curvature: f = R/2. Both f and R are measured from the pole P. Sign convention (Cartesian): distances measured from P; positive direction = direction of incident light. Concave: f and R negative; Convex: f and R positive (in the most common convention). Mirror formula: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f. Magnification m = −v/u = h_image / h_object.

cards.front:
An object 4 cm tall is placed 30 cm from a concave mirror of focal length 20 cm. Image distance v is:

(A) −12 cm
(B) −60 cm (real, inverted, magnified)
(C) +60 cm (virtual)
(D) −10 cm
cards.back:
(B) −60 cm (real, inverted, magnified)

Light & Optics — Cartesian sign convention: u = −30 cm (object on left of mirror), f = −20 cm (concave). Mirror formula: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f → 1/v − 1/30 = −1/20 → 1/v = −1/20 + 1/30 = (−3 + 2)/60 = −1/60 → v = −60 cm. Negative → real image on same side as object. Magnification m = −v/u = −(−60)/(−30) = −2 → image is inverted (negative sign), 2× size = 8 cm tall. Positioned 60 cm from mirror.

Magnification m = −v/u = −(−60)/(−30) = −2 → image is inverted (negative sign), 2× size = 8 cm tall. Positioned 60 cm from mirror.

cards.front:
A 'real image' formed by a mirror or lens is one that:

(A) Cannot be obtained on a screen
(B) Can be obtained on a screen — light rays actually meet at the image point
(C) Always upright
(D) Forms behind the mirror
cards.back:
(B) Can be obtained on a screen — light rays actually meet at the image point

Light & Optics — Real image — light rays actually converge → projectable onto a screen. Always inverted (top-bottom flipped). Formed by concave mirrors/converging lenses when object is beyond the focal point. Examples: cinema projector, camera, eye, microscope, refracting telescope. Virtual image — rays only APPEAR to come from a point (extending divergent rays backwards) → not projectable. Formed by plane mirrors, convex mirrors, diverging lenses, and concave mirrors with object inside f.

cards.front:
The image formed in a plane mirror is:

(A) Real, inverted, smaller
(B) Virtual, erect, same size; laterally inverted; image distance behind = object distance in front
(C) Real and same size
(D) Virtual but inverted
cards.back:
(B) Virtual, erect, same size; laterally inverted; image distance behind = object distance in front

Light & Optics — Plane mirror — virtual, erect, same size as object. Image distance behind mirror = object distance in front. Laterally inverted (left↔right swap; top-bottom NOT swapped — that's why text appears mirror-flipped). Used in periscope (combination of two), kaleidoscope, optical instruments. Plane mirror is essentially a spherical mirror with R = ∞, so f = ∞ → image at the mirror level (using mirror formula 1/v = 1/f − 1/u gives v = −u).

cards.front:
The FIRST LAW of REFLECTION states that the angle of incidence:

(A) Equals the angle of reflection
(B) Is twice the angle of reflection
(C) Is half the angle of reflection
(D) Is independent of reflection angle
cards.back:
(A) Equals the angle of reflection

Light & Optics — LAWS OF REFLECTION (memorize): (1) ANGLE OF INCIDENCE (i) = ANGLE OF REFLECTION (r), measured from the NORMAL (perpendicular to surface). (2) Incident ray, reflected ray, and normal LIE IN THE SAME PLANE. KEY: angles measured from NORMAL (NOT from the surface). NORMAL = imaginary line PERPENDICULAR to surface at point of incidence. BOTH LAWS apply equally to PLANE MIRRORS, CURVED MIRRORS, and even DIFFUSE reflection from rough surfaces (locally for each tiny smooth part). REGULAR vs DIFFUSE REFLECTION: (1) REGULAR (specular) — smooth surface (mirror, polished metal, still water) → parallel rays remain parallel; CLEAR IMAGE. (2) DIFFUSE — rough surface (paper, cloth, walls) → parallel rays scatter in many directions; NO IMAGE. WHY WE SEE OBJECTS: light from sources reflects DIFFUSELY off everyday objects → reaches our eyes → brain forms image. ANIMAL EYE-SHINE: many nocturnal animals (cats, dogs, deer) have TAPETUM LUCIDUM behind retina — reflects light back through retina → glow in dark. PYQ FREQUENCY: laws of reflection in NEET, NCERT 1-2× per cycle.

cards.option2: Is half the angle of reflection

cards.front:
Image formed by a PLANE MIRROR is:

(A) Virtual, erect, same-size, laterally inverted
(B) Real, inverted, magnified, behind
(C) Virtual, inverted, larger than object
(D) Real, erect, smaller than object
cards.back:
(A) Virtual, erect, same-size, laterally inverted

Light & Optics — PLANE MIRROR image properties: (1) VIRTUAL (cannot be projected on screen; rays only appear to come from behind mirror). (2) ERECT (right-side up). (3) SAME SIZE as object. (4) AT EQUAL DISTANCE behind mirror as object is in front. (5) LATERALLY INVERTED — left-right flipped. (NOT top-bottom flipped — this is a common misconception.) LATERAL INVERSION explains: (a) text appears reversed in mirror. (b) AMBULANCE has 'AMBULANCE' written in REVERSE on its front so drivers see it correctly in their REARVIEW MIRROR. (c) Right hand appears as left hand in mirror. SAMPLE MIRROR experiments: 'YOGA' written in mirror image looks like 'AGOY' (mirror flip). NUMBER 1881 looks like '1881' in mirror (palindrome by mirror). USES of PLANE MIRRORS: bathroom mirror, full-length dressing mirror, periscopes (with two), kaleidoscopes (with three at angles). MULTIPLE-MIRROR IMAGES: number of images = (360°/θ) − 1, where θ = angle between two mirrors. e.g., θ=90° → 3 images; θ=60° → 5; θ=30° → 11. KALEIDOSCOPE typically uses 60° angle → 6 images forming a star pattern. PYQ FREQUENCY: plane mirror properties in NEET, NCERT, JEE-Main 1-2× per cycle.

(4) AT EQUAL DISTANCE behind mirror as object is in front. (5) LATERALLY INVERTED — left-right flipped. (NOT top-bottom flipped — this is a common misconception.) LATERAL INVERSION explains: (a) text appears reversed in mirror. (b) AMBULANCE has 'AMBULANCE' written in REVERSE on its front so drivers see it correctly in their REARVIEW MIRROR. (c) Right hand appears as left hand in mirror. SAMPLE MIRROR experiments: 'YOGA' written in mirror image looks like 'AGOY' (mirror flip). NUMBER 1881 looks like '1881' in mirror (palindrome by mirror). USES of PLANE MIRRORS: bathroom mirror, full-length dressing mirror, periscopes (with two), kaleidoscopes (with three at angles). MULTIPLE-MIRROR IMAGES: number of images = (360°/θ) − 1, where θ = angle between two mirrors. e.g., θ=90° → 3 images; θ=60° → 5; θ=30° → 11. KALEIDOSCOPE typically uses 60° angle → 6 images forming a star pattern. PYQ FREQUENCY: plane mirror properties in NEET, NCERT, JEE-Main 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
A CONCAVE MIRROR is also called a CONVERGING MIRROR because:

(A) It converges parallel rays to focus
(B) It diverges all incoming rays
(C) It produces only virtual images
(D) It reflects light without bending
cards.back:
(A) It converges parallel rays to focus

Light & Optics — CONCAVE MIRROR — reflective surface CURVED INWARD (like the inside of a sphere). Parallel rays of light entering a CONCAVE mirror converge to a single point — the FOCAL POINT (F). Hence 'CONVERGING' mirror. FOCAL LENGTH (f) = distance from mirror to focal point; f = R/2 (where R = radius of curvature). KEY POINTS on CONCAVE mirror: (1) POLE (P) — center of mirror surface. (2) CENTER OF CURVATURE (C) — center of the sphere from which the mirror is cut. (3) FOCUS (F) — halfway between P and C. (4) PRINCIPAL AXIS — line through P and C. IMAGE FORMATION depends on object distance: (a) Object beyond C: real, inverted, smaller. (b) At C: real, inverted, same size. (c) Between F and C: real, inverted, larger. (d) At F: image at infinity (parallel rays). (e) Between F and P: virtual, erect, larger (used for shaving/makeup mirrors!). USES OF CONCAVE MIRRORS: (1) SHAVING/MAKEUP mirrors (object closer than F gives magnified erect image). (2) DENTIST MIRRORS. (3) HEADLIGHTS, FLASHLIGHTS, search lights — light source at focus → parallel beam emerges. (4) SOLAR cookers, solar furnaces. (5) ASTRONOMICAL TELESCOPES (Newtonian, Cassegrain). (6) Reflectors in operating-theater lights. PYQ FREQUENCY: concave mirror in NEET, NCERT 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
An object 4 cm tall is placed 30 cm in front of a CONCAVE MIRROR of focal length 15 cm. Image position is:

(A) 30 cm in front (at 2F, real)
(B) 15 cm in front (at focus)
(C) 30 cm behind (a virtual)
(D) Infinity (at very far distance)
cards.back:
(A) 30 cm in front (at 2F, real)

Light & Optics — Apply MIRROR FORMULA: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f (Cartesian convention; u = object distance, v = image distance, f = focal length, with appropriate signs). For CONCAVE MIRROR: f is NEGATIVE (in many conventions); u is NEGATIVE (object in front). Plug u = −30, f = −15: 1/v + 1/(−30) = 1/(−15) → 1/v = 1/(−15) + 1/30 = −2/30 + 1/30 = −1/30 → v = −30 cm. v negative → image is in FRONT of mirror (REAL image). DISTANCE: 30 cm. INTERPRETATION: object at 2F → image also at 2F (same distance), inverted, real, same size. MIRROR FORMULA: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f. MAGNIFICATION: m = −v/u = h_image/h_object. Plug m = −(−30)/(−30) = 30/(−30) = −1 → image inverted, same size as object (4 cm). KEY CASES for concave mirror: object at 2F → image at 2F, real, inverted, same size. Object beyond 2F → image between F and 2F, real, inverted, smaller. Object between F and 2F → image beyond 2F, real, inverted, larger. Object at F → image at infinity. Object inside F → image behind mirror, virtual, erect, larger (e.g., shaving mirror). NUMERICAL PRACTICE in NEET, JEE-Main 2-3× per paper. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests sign convention + formula application.

cards.front:
REAR-VIEW MIRRORS in cars and side mirrors typically use:

(A) Convex mirrors (wider field of view)
(B) Concave mirrors (image inverted)
(C) Plane mirrors (limited area only)
(D) Cylindrical mirrors (rare in cars)
cards.back:
(A) Convex mirrors (wider field of view)

Light & Optics — CONVEX MIRRORS (curved outward) used in vehicle side/rear-view mirrors. WHY: (1) Convex mirrors give a WIDER FIELD OF VIEW than plane mirrors of same size — see more area, important for spotting other vehicles. (2) IMAGE always virtual, erect, smaller (diminished). KEY: USA + Europe convex side mirrors are LEGALLY MANDATED on passenger cars to have a small flat 'spot mirror' nearby; some Indian cars also have this. CAUTION SIGN: 'OBJECTS IN MIRROR ARE CLOSER THAN THEY APPEAR' — because convex mirror DIMINISHES image, brain underestimates distance. CONVEX MIRROR uses (memorize): (1) VEHICLE side mirrors. (2) Mirrors at BLIND CORNERS (intersections, hospital corridors, supermarkets — security against theft). (3) MAGNIFYING glass reverse — convex mirror gives smaller image; concave gives larger. CONTRAST OF MIRROR USES: CONVEX (always virtual, erect, smaller) → wide-view applications. CONCAVE (varies by distance) → magnify (shaving), focus (headlights, telescopes). PLANE → simple reflection (regular mirrors). KEY: convex mirror has POSITIVE focal length (per many conventions; it's a DIVERGING mirror — extends rays outward). PRACTICE — UPSC / NEET style: identify mirror used in given application. (a) Telescope objective → CONCAVE. (b) Vehicle side mirror → CONVEX. (c) Bathroom mirror → PLANE. PYQ FREQUENCY: mirror-applications in NEET, NCERT, SSC 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
The relationship between FOCAL LENGTH (f) and RADIUS OF CURVATURE (R) of a SPHERICAL MIRROR is:

(A) f = R/2 (focal length is half radius)
(B) f = 2R (focal length twice radius)
(C) f = R (equal value here)
(D) f = R² (squared relation)
cards.back:
(A) f = R/2 (focal length is half radius)

Light & Optics — f = R/2 — focal length is HALF the radius of curvature. This is the PARAXIAL approximation valid for SMALL ANGLE incidence near principal axis. PROOF: A ray parallel to the axis hitting the mirror at small angle from axis reflects through F. Geometry: triangle with apex at C (center), one side along axis (length R), other side from F (length R−f). For small angle: F is at midpoint between P and C → f = R/2. KEY: HOLDS for both CONCAVE (f, R both negative in Cartesian) and CONVEX (f, R both positive). EXAMPLES: (1) Mirror with R = 20 cm → f = 10 cm. (2) Mirror with R = 40 cm → f = 20 cm. (3) PLANE MIRROR — R = ∞ → f = ∞ (parallel rays remain parallel, never converge). KEY for SPHERICAL ABERRATION: at LARGER angles from axis, paraxial approximation BREAKS DOWN; rays don't all converge to single point → image becomes blurred. PARABOLOIDAL mirrors (mathematical paraboloid shape) avoid this — ALL parallel rays focus to single point. USE: telescopes, headlights, satellite dishes use parabolic reflectors. WHY SPHERICAL (not paraboloidal) used in many cases? Easier and cheaper to make spheres than paraboloids. INDUSTRIAL MIRROR MAKING: silvering process — coat glass back-surface with silver/aluminum. PYQ FREQUENCY: f = R/2 in NEET, NCERT, JEE-Main 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
A PERISCOPE used in submarines works on the principle of:

(A) Total internal reflection in prisms or two-mirror system
(B) Refraction through convex lens only (option here)
(C) Diffraction of light through gaps (option here)
(D) Polarization of light by sunlight (option here)
cards.back:
(A) Total internal reflection in prisms or two-mirror system

Light & Optics — PERISCOPE — instrument that allows OBSERVATION OVER OBSTACLES. SIMPLE PERISCOPE: two PLANE MIRRORS at 45° in a tube, top mirror reflects external scene DOWN; bottom mirror reflects DOWN-incoming light HORIZONTALLY into observer's eye. Each mirror angle = 45°; total ray-deviation = 180° (back to viewer). MILITARY PERISCOPES (submarines): use PRISMS (right-angled, isoceles) instead of mirrors — utilize TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION inside the prism (each face acts as a perfect reflector, no metallic coating needed). WHY PRISMS BETTER: (a) No silver/aluminum coating to wear off / get damaged. (b) Higher reflectivity (~100% vs ~95% for mirrors). (c) More durable. SUBMARINE PERISCOPES: 10-15 m long; can periscope-up while submerged at periscope depth (~15 m); used for visual observation of surface. MODERN SUBMARINES: replacing periscopes with NON-PENETRATING ELECTRO-OPTICAL MASTS — cameras + sensors + radio + GPS in a mast that doesn't penetrate the pressure hull (no need for vertical sight tube through submarine). EXAMPLES: USA Virginia-class subs, India's INS ARIHANT. PERISCOPE in TANKS/ARMORED VEHICLES — for safe observation. CIVILIAN USES: observing crowds, tall barriers. PYQ FREQUENCY: periscope in NEET, NCERT, SSC GA 1× per cycle.

cards.option3: Polarization of light by sunlight (option here)

cards.front:
FIRST LAW OF REFLECTION states that:

(A) Angle of incidence > angle of reflection
(B) Angle of incidence = angle of reflection (equal)
(C) Light bends towards normal (refraction)
(D) Light always travels in straight line
cards.back:
(B) Angle of incidence = angle of reflection (equal)

Light & Optics — LAWS OF REFLECTION: (1) Angle of INCIDENCE = Angle of REFLECTION (both measured from NORMAL, the perpendicular at point of contact). (2) Incident ray, reflected ray, normal — ALL LIE IN THE SAME PLANE. INSIGHT — these laws apply to EVERY type of mirror (plane, concave, convex) and every smooth reflecting surface, even WATER + glass. WHY mirrors work: smooth surface → all parallel rays reflect at same angle (REGULAR reflection). Rough surface → rays scatter (DIFFUSE reflection — why we can see non-mirror objects). Distractor 3 is REFRACTION (light bending when entering different medium — Snell's law).

cards.option3: Light always travels in straight line

cards.front:
An image formed by a PLANE MIRROR is:

(A) Real, inverted, magnified here also
(B) Virtual, erect, same size, laterally inverted
(C) Real, erect, diminished here also
(D) Virtual, inverted, magnified here
cards.back:
(B) Virtual, erect, same size, laterally inverted

Light & Optics — PLANE MIRROR image: VIRTUAL (formed BEHIND mirror; rays only appear to come from there but don't actually meet); ERECT (upright); SAME SIZE as object; LATERALLY INVERTED (left-right swap; that's why letters appear backwards in mirror — try writing your name + see it in mirror). DISTANCE: image is at SAME distance behind mirror as object is in front. EXAM PYQ: AMBULANCE writes its name MIRROR-REVERSED so that drivers ahead, looking in their rear-view mirror, see it correctly! REAL vs VIRTUAL — real images can be projected on screen (formed by actual ray convergence); virtual cannot (rays only appear to converge).

cards.front:
A CONCAVE mirror is used as:

(A) Rear-view mirror in vehicles
(B) Shaving mirror + reflector in torches
(C) Convenience-store wide-angle mirror
(D) Bathroom-tile flat decoration
cards.back:
(B) Shaving mirror + reflector in torches

Light & Optics — CONCAVE mirror = converging mirror (curves IN, like inside of spoon). USES: (1) SHAVING mirror — when face is INSIDE focal length, image is VIRTUAL, ERECT, MAGNIFIED (you see yourself bigger). (2) Headlight / TORCH reflector — bulb at FOCUS produces parallel reflected beam (high-intensity directional light). (3) Solar cookers + furnaces (concentrate sunlight at focus). (4) Doctor's HEAD MIRROR (forehead-mounted, focuses light into ear/throat). (5) Telescope (Newtonian / Cassegrain types). CONVEX mirror — diverging; gives wider field of view (used in vehicle rear-view, road junctions, ATM corners). REVERSE EXAM TRAP: rear-view mirrors are CONVEX (not concave).

cards.back:

(A) f = R (they are equal)
(B) f = R/2 (focal at half radius)
(C) f = 2R (twice radius value)
(D) f = R² (squared relation)
cards.back:
(B) f = R/2 (focal at half radius)

Light & Optics — For SPHERICAL MIRRORS (small aperture, paraxial approximation): f = R/2 (focal length is HALF the radius of curvature). RADIUS = distance from POLE to centre of curvature; FOCUS lies midway between. INSIGHT — for LENSES, the relation is different: f depends on both surface radii + refractive index (lens-maker's equation). LARGE-APERTURE mirrors deviate from f = R/2 due to spherical aberration → use parabolic mirrors for telescopes.

MIRROR FORMULA relating object distance (u), image distance (v), focal length (f) is:

(A) u + v = f (sum is focal)
(B) 1/v + 1/u = 1/f (reciprocal sum)
(C) uv = f (product is focal)
(D) u − v = f (difference) here

(B) 1/v + 1/u = 1/f (reciprocal sum)

cards.front:
Periscope (used in submarines + tanks) primarily uses:

(A) Single concave mirror at angle
(B) Two plane mirrors at 45° (parallel)
(C) Triangular convex mirrors only
(D) Just one large flat plane mirror

Light & Optics — PERISCOPE — uses TWO PARALLEL plane mirrors, each tilted 45° to the line of sight. Light from above (e.g., surface) hits TOP mirror → reflects down through tube → hits BOTTOM mirror → reflects horizontally to viewer's eye. Used in: submarines (to see above water while underwater); tanks (driver to see outside while protected); trench warfare (seeing over walls). IMAGE in periscope = same size, erect, SAME orientation (no lateral inversion because two reflections cancel). INSIGHT — modern periscopes use PRISMS (using TIR — total internal reflection) for sharper images. Submarines now use ELECTRONIC PERISCOPES (cameras + monitors) — no mast through the hull.

(A) Changes speed when entering a different medium
(B) Bounces off the surface of medium (option here)
(C) Gets absorbed inside the medium (option here)
(D) Splits into colours by prism only (option here)
cards.back:
(A) Changes speed when entering a different medium

Light & Optics — REFRACTION = bending of light when it passes from one medium to another, due to CHANGE IN SPEED. Speed in vacuum: c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s. In water: ~2.25 × 10⁸ m/s. In glass: ~2 × 10⁸ m/s. REFRACTIVE INDEX n = c/v_medium (n_water ≈ 1.33; n_glass ≈ 1.5; n_diamond ≈ 2.42). When light enters denser medium → SLOWS + bends TOWARDS NORMAL; lighter → speeds + bends AWAY. SNELL's LAW: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂. INSIGHT — refraction explains: pencil bending in water, pool depth illusion (looks shallower), lens function, mirages, RAINBOWS (refraction + reflection in raindrops, splitting white light by wavelength).

cards.front:
TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION occurs when light tries to go from:

(A) Denser to lighter medium beyond critical angle
(B) Lighter to denser medium at any angle
(C) Vacuum into a denser medium (option here)
(D) Same medium back to itself here (option here)
cards.back:
(A) Denser to lighter medium beyond critical angle

Light & Optics — TIR — when light goes from DENSER to LESS DENSE medium AT ANGLE > CRITICAL ANGLE, ALL light is reflected back into the denser medium (no refraction; refraction angle = 90° at critical angle). Critical angle θ_c: sin θ_c = n₂/n₁. For glass-air: sin θ_c = 1/1.5 → θ_c ≈ 42°. WATER-air: ~49°. APPLICATIONS: (1) FIBRE-OPTIC cables (light bouncing along glass core); (2) DIAMOND sparkle (high n → low critical angle → light trapped + multiply reflected — gives 'fire'); (3) SHEEN of MIRAGES (hot road appears reflective — air layers of varying density act as TIR boundary); (4) PRISMATIC binoculars (TIR replaces silvered mirrors — better quality). KEY exam fact.

cards.front:
A CONVEX LENS (converging) of focal length 10 cm. Object placed at 30 cm. Image is:

(A) Real, inverted, smaller than object
(B) Virtual, erect, larger than object
(C) Real, inverted, larger than object
(D) Virtual, erect, smaller than object
cards.back:
(A) Real, inverted, smaller than object

Light & Optics — Object at u = −30 cm; f = +10 cm (convex lens). Lens formula 1/v − 1/u = 1/f → 1/v = 1/10 + 1/(−30) = (3−1)/30 = 2/30 → v = 15 cm. POSITIVE v → REAL image on opposite side. Magnification m = v/u = 15/(−30) = −0.5 → INVERTED + DIMINISHED (half size). INSIGHT — for CONVEX lens: object beyond 2F → real, inverted, smaller (camera, eye); at 2F → real, inverted, same size; between F + 2F → real, inverted, larger (projector); at F → image at infinity; between F + lens → virtual, erect, larger (magnifying glass). CONCAVE lens always gives virtual, erect, smaller image (used in spectacles for myopia).

cards.front:
A pencil dipped in water APPEARS BENT. This is due to:

(A) Refraction of light at water surface
(B) Reflection of light from water alone
(C) Diffraction of light around water
(D) Polarization of light in water here
cards.back:
(A) Refraction of light at water surface

Light & Optics — Pencil bend illusion = REFRACTION. Light from submerged part REFRACTS at water surface (denser → lighter; bends AWAY from normal); brain projects light back in straight line → underwater part appears at different position → SHIFTED. APPARENT depth = real depth × (n₂/n₁); for water, apparent depth = real × (1/1.33) ≈ 75% real → pool seems shallower than it is. SAME REASON: stars APPEAR TWINKLING (atmospheric refraction varies with air density); SUN looks ELLIPTICAL near horizon (atmospheric refraction); fish in water look closer to surface than they are (anglers learn to compensate).

cards.front:
MYOPIA (short-sightedness) is corrected by:

(A) Concave (diverging) lens spectacles
(B) Convex (converging) lens spectacles
(C) Cylindrical lens used for astigmatism
(D) Bifocal lens with two focal lengths
cards.back:
(A) Concave (diverging) lens spectacles

Light & Optics — MYOPIA — eyeball too LONG; image forms BEFORE retina. Distant objects blurry. Corrected by CONCAVE (diverging) lens — diverges incoming light, image moves back to retina. Common in students (excessive close work). HYPEROPIA / HYPERMETROPIA (long-sightedness) — opposite: eyeball too short; image forms AFTER retina; near objects blurry. Corrected by CONVEX (converging) lens. PRESBYOPIA — age-related; lens loses flexibility, can't focus near; corrected by reading glasses (convex). ASTIGMATISM — cornea irregular shape, blurry at all distances; corrected by CYLINDRICAL lens. POWER of lens (in DIOPTRES, D) = 1/f (in metres). +2 D = convex of 50 cm focal length; −2 D = concave.

cards.front:
A RAINBOW is formed due to:

(A) Dispersion + reflection inside water droplets
(B) Reflection alone from water surface
(C) Polarization of sunlight by atmosphere
(D) Diffraction by clouds in atmosphere
cards.back:
(A) Dispersion + reflection inside water droplets

Light & Optics — RAINBOW formation: sunlight enters raindrop → REFRACTS (slows down + bends, also DISPERSES — different colours bend differently because different λ have different refractive indices); reflects off back of droplet (TIR); refracts again on exit. Result: 7 colours (VIBGYOR — Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red) emerge at angles. Rainbow appears in arc on OPPOSITE side of Sun (sun behind observer). RED on outer arc; VIOLET inner. SECONDARY rainbow — fainter, larger, colours REVERSED — due to 2 internal reflections. INSIGHT — Newton's discovery that white light is composite (Opticks, 1704). Same dispersion in PRISM. SCATTERING (different): blue sky (Rayleigh — short λ scattered more); red sunset (long λ travels more horizontal atmosphere).

cards.front:
Refractive index of DIAMOND (~2.42) is one of the HIGHEST. This causes:

(A) Multiple TIRs inside → dazzling 'fire'
(B) Diamond to absorb most of the light
(C) Diamond to scatter blue light only
(D) Light to pass straight without bending
cards.back:
(A) Multiple TIRs inside → dazzling 'fire'

Light & Optics — Diamond's HIGH refractive index (~2.42) → very LOW critical angle (sin θ_c = 1/2.42 → θ_c ≈ 24.4°). Light entering diamond easily exceeds critical angle when trying to escape → undergoes TIR multiple times before finding a face to exit at low enough angle. Result: light bounces around inside, exits with high intensity → 'BRILLIANCE'. CUTTING DIAMOND with precise angles + facets (e.g., 58 facets in BRILLIANT CUT) maximises this. Also, dispersion in diamond is high → splits white light → colourful 'FIRE' or sparkle. JEWELLERY 4Cs = Cut, Clarity, Colour, Carat. DIAMOND SIMULANTS: cubic zirconia (n = 2.17, lower fire), moissanite (n = 2.65, more fire than diamond).

cards.option3: Light to pass straight without bending

cards.front:
WHY does the SKY appear BLUE?

(A) Reflection of sea below
(B) RAYLEIGH SCATTERING
(C) Absorption of blue by water vapour
(D) Chemical action of ozone
cards.back:
(B) RAYLEIGH SCATTERING

Light & Optics — RAYLEIGH SCATTERING — when SUNLIGHT enters the atmosphere, it is scattered by molecules (and small particles) whose size is much SMALLER than the wavelength of light. Rayleigh showed that the INTENSITY of scattering is INVERSELY PROPORTIONAL to the FOURTH POWER of the wavelength (I ∝ 1/λ⁴). Since BLUE (λ ≈ 470 nm) has a much shorter wavelength than RED (λ ≈ 650 nm), blue is scattered ~(650/470)⁴ ≈ 3.7× MORE than red. Violet is scattered even more, but (1) the Sun emits less violet, and (2) our eyes are less sensitive to violet than blue → net result, we perceive a BLUE sky. WHY IS THE SUNRISE / SUNSET RED-ORANGE? At those times the Sun is low on the horizon, so light travels through a LONGER atmospheric path. By the time light reaches us, most of the blue has been scattered away — leaving the longer (red/orange) wavelengths dominant. WHY IS DEEP SEA / SKY-AT-NIGHT DARK? No atmosphere to scatter (space above) — starry field dominates. WHY DOES THE SUN LOOK WHITE AT NOON? Overhead path is shortest → minimal scattering of any colour → all wavelengths reach you. WHY CLOUDS ARE WHITE? Water droplets in clouds are MUCH BIGGER than light wavelength → cause MIE SCATTERING (wavelength-independent), scattering all colours equally → white. WHY DANGER SIGNALS ARE RED? Red has longest visible wavelength → least scattered by air/dust/fog → visible farthest. WHY MILK IS WHITE? Suspension of fat globules — Mie scattering of all colours. atmospheric molecules (N₂, O₂) scatter SHORTER wavelengths (blue) about 5-6× more than longer wavelengths (red); ∝ 1/λ⁴.

cards.front:
MYOPIA (short-sightedness), where a person cannot see DISTANT objects clearly, is corrected by using:

(A) Convex lens (converging)
(B) CONCAVE LENS (diverging)
(C) Cylindrical lens
(D) Bifocal lens
cards.back:
(B) CONCAVE LENS (diverging)

Light & Optics — MYOPIA (Greek ‘myo’ = ‘shut’; also called NEAR-SIGHTEDNESS / SHORT-SIGHTEDNESS) — the eye can see NEAR objects clearly but DISTANT objects appear blurred. CAUSE: (a) eyeball is too ELONGATED front-to-back, OR (b) cornea/lens curvature too strong — so that parallel light rays from distant objects converge to a focal point BEFORE the retina, giving a blurred image on the retina. CORRECTION: CONCAVE LENS (also called DIVERGING / MINUS-power lens) — diverges incoming rays slightly so they focus further back, landing exactly on the retina. Power of lens: NEGATIVE (e.g., -2.5 D). HYPERMETROPIA (far-sightedness) — opposite — distant OK but near objects blurred. Cause: eyeball too SHORT, so image forms BEHIND the retina. Correction: CONVEX / CONVERGING / PLUS-power lens (+ve D). PRESBYOPIA — age-related loss of flexibility of crystalline lens (usually after age 40); need BIFOCAL or progressive lenses. ASTIGMATISM — cornea/lens has unequal curvature in different meridians (oval instead of spherical), causing blurred/distorted vision; corrected by CYLINDRICAL LENS. CATARACT — opacification of the crystalline lens; treated by SURGICAL removal + insertion of Intraocular Lens (IOL). HUMAN EYE: near-point ~25 cm (‘least distance of distinct vision’); far-point = infinity; pupil diameter 2-8 mm; retina has RODS (120 million, B&W / low light) + CONES (6-7 million, colour — R, G, B); blind spot (optic disc, no photoreceptors); FOVEA CENTRALIS (sharpest vision). it moves the image BACKWARD onto the retina by diverging incoming parallel rays.

cards.front:
The phenomenon by which we see a RAINBOW requires:

(A) Reflection only
(B) Refraction only
(C) DISPERSION + REFRACTION + TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION of sunlight in water droplets; observer stands with back to Sun; primary rainbow ~42° angle, red outside, violet inside
(D) Scattering by dust particles
cards.back:
(C) DISPERSION + REFRACTION + TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION of sunlight in water droplets; observer stands with back to Sun; primary rainbow ~42° angle, red outside, violet inside

Light & Optics — RAINBOW — formed by the combined interaction of SUNLIGHT with tiny WATER DROPLETS in the atmosphere (after rain); the formation involves THREE phenomena: (1) REFRACTION — sunlight enters water droplet, is bent (dense medium → less speed → bending toward normal); (2) DISPERSION — the 7 colours of white light bend by DIFFERENT amounts (violet most, red least) because refractive index n(violet) > n(red) — splits into VIBGYOR; (3) TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION — at the back surface of the droplet, rays reflect internally; (4) REFRACTION again upon exit. The net effect: each colour emerges at a slightly different angle; red at ~42° above anti-solar point, violet at ~40°. Thus a PRIMARY RAINBOW = semicircular arc at ~42° radius centred on the ANTI-SOLAR POINT (point opposite the Sun from observer). RED on the OUTER arc, VIOLET on the INNER. OBSERVER must stand with their BACK to the Sun, Sun behind them. SECONDARY RAINBOW — fainter, larger arc at ~51° radius; formed by TWO internal reflections; COLOUR ORDER REVERSED (red inside, violet outside). Between primary and secondary: ALEXANDER'S DARK BAND (less light scattered). On a 360° horizon (from an aeroplane) you can see a full circular rainbow. MNEMONIC for order: VIBGYOR (Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red). NEWTON, 1666, performed the CLASSIC PRISM EXPERIMENT — split sunlight into colours + recombined them → proved white light = mixture of all colours. PRISMATIC dispersion is the BASIS of SPECTROMETERS.

cards.front:
A CONCAVE MIRROR is used in:

(A) Rear-view mirrors of vehicles (wider field)
(B) SHAVING MIRRORS, CAR/TORCH HEADLIGHTS, DENTIST'S MIRROR, SOLAR COOKERS, REFLECTING TELESCOPES
(C) Kaleidoscope (plane mirrors)
(D) Compound microscope (lens-based)
cards.back:
(B) SHAVING MIRRORS, CAR/TORCH HEADLIGHTS, DENTIST'S MIRROR, SOLAR COOKERS, REFLECTING TELESCOPES

Light & Optics — CONCAVE (CONVERGING) MIRROR — a mirror whose reflecting surface CURVES INWARD (like the inside of a spoon). Properties: (1) Parallel rays converge at the FOCAL POINT (F). (2) Image characteristics depend on object distance: (a) object BEYOND C (centre of curvature) → image real, inverted, DIMINISHED; (b) object AT C → same-size, real, inverted; (c) object BETWEEN F and C → real, inverted, MAGNIFIED; (d) object AT F → image at infinity; (e) object BETWEEN POLE and F → VIRTUAL, ERECT, MAGNIFIED. USES: (1) SHAVING / MAKEUP MIRROR — face within F → magnified erect image. (2) DENTIST'S MIRROR — small tooth within F → enlarged view. (3) TORCH / HEADLIGHT / SEARCHLIGHT REFLECTOR — bulb placed AT F → reflected light emerges as parallel beam. (4) SOLAR COOKER / SOLAR CONCENTRATOR — parallel sunlight converges at F → intense heat. (5) REFLECTING TELESCOPE (NEWTONIAN, CASSEGRAIN) — parabolic concave mirror used as primary; avoids chromatic aberration of lenses (faced by REFRACTING telescopes like Galilean/Keplerian). MIRROR FORMULA: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f (v = image distance, u = object distance, f = focal length). MAGNIFICATION m = -v/u = h'/h. NEWTON'S CARTESIAN SIGN CONVENTION: distances measured from pole; positive to the right, negative to the left (typically). For CONCAVE mirror, f < 0 (if light travels left-to-right conventionally). CONVEX (DIVERGING) mirror uses: REAR-VIEW (wider field, diminished image always), SECURITY/SHOP mirrors, STREET light reflectors. PLANE mirrors: image same size, erect, virtual, laterally inverted, distance = object distance. because it forms a MAGNIFIED / ERECT image when object is within focal length, and a PARALLEL BEAM when source is at focus.

cards.front:
The phenomenon where LIGHT bends AROUND edges of an obstacle/slit is called:

(A) Reflection
(B) Refraction
(C) DIFFRACTION
(D) Polarisation
cards.back:
(C) DIFFRACTION

Light & Optics — DIFFRACTION — the BENDING of waves around the corners of an obstacle or through an aperture; a phenomenon distinctive of WAVES (NOT particles). Light diffraction is usually small because visible wavelength (~500 nm) is much shorter than everyday obstacles, but becomes noticeable with slits/gaps of comparable size. HISTORIC EXPERIMENTS: (1) FRANCESCO GRIMALDI (1660s) — first observed + named ‘diffractio’; light passing through small aperture shows fringes of dark/light (not pure geometric shadow). (2) THOMAS YOUNG (1801) — famous DOUBLE-SLIT EXPERIMENT: sunlight through two parallel narrow slits produces an INTERFERENCE pattern of bright & dark fringes on a screen; proved WAVE nature of light (Newton had argued it was corpuscular). Formula: bright fringes at d·sinθ = n·λ. (3) FRESNEL, FRAUNHOFER — further developed diffraction theory. (4) X-RAY DIFFRACTION — Von Laue (1912), Bragg (father+son, 1913) — discovered X-rays diffracted through crystals obey nλ = 2d·sinθ; basis of crystallography (e.g., Watson-Crick DNA 1953 using Rosalind Franklin's X-ray data). RELATED optics phenomena: INTERFERENCE (superposition of two coherent waves → constructive/destructive); POLARIZATION (confining wave oscillations to one plane — only transverse waves can be polarized, so light can but sound cannot); TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION (at interface with a less dense medium beyond critical angle — basis of OPTICAL FIBRES, DIAMONDS' sparkle, MIRAGE). WAVE-PARTICLE DUALITY of light: Newton said particle; Young diffraction said wave; Einstein's photoelectric effect (1905, Nobel 1921) said particle (PHOTONS); Quantum mechanics unifies both — light is BOTH. de Broglie (1924) extended to matter waves. most pronounced when the obstacle/slit size is comparable to the wavelength of light; YOUNG’s double-slit experiment (1801) proved wave nature of light.

cards.front:
A MIRAGE (the shimmering ‘water on hot desert road’ illusion) is caused by:

(A) Reflection by dust clouds
(B) Scattering by hot air
(C) TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION of light + refraction by layers of AIR of differing densities
(D) Illusion in the human eye
cards.back:
(C) TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION of light + refraction by layers of AIR of differing densities

Light & Optics — MIRAGE — an OPTICAL PHENOMENON caused by the REFRACTION and TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION of light as it passes through LAYERS of AIR with different DENSITIES (and hence different refractive indices). MECHANISM (inferior mirage — common on hot desert roads): (1) Near the SURFACE, air is hot → EXPANDED → LESS DENSE → LOWER REFRACTIVE INDEX. (2) Higher up, air is cooler → DENSER → HIGHER index. (3) Light rays from the sky travelling obliquely downward PASS from denser → rarer layers progressively. (4) When the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle in any layer, TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION occurs → rays bend upward again. (5) To the observer, these bent rays LOOK LIKE they came from a point on the ground → image of sky appears on the road surface, resembling WATER / REFLECTION. Inverted images of distant objects (trees, cars) may also appear. TWO TYPES: (a) INFERIOR MIRAGE — image appears BELOW the real object (classic desert/road mirage). (b) SUPERIOR MIRAGE — image appears ABOVE the real object; seen over cold seas/ice (POLAR regions) — this is the origin of the ‘FLYING DUTCHMAN’ ghost ship, the ‘FATA MORGANA’ of the Straits of Messina, and ‘looming’ effects. MORE OPTICAL PHENOMENA of refraction through atmosphere: (1) APPARENT POSITION of stars / Sun DIFFERS from real position (we see Sun 2 minutes BEFORE it rises and 2 minutes AFTER it sets due to atmospheric refraction, so the ‘day’ is 4 min longer than geometric). (2) TWINKLING OF STARS — atmospheric turbulence causes rapid refractive index changes; planets (extended disks) twinkle less. (3) CIRCULAR/OVAL appearance of Sun-Moon near horizon — differential refraction of top vs bottom. (4) REFRACTION at air-glass-water interfaces makes pencils look bent in water, letters appear displaced under glass slab, swimming pools look shallower than they are. hot/less dense air near the ground refracts light upward, bending images of the sky.

cards.front:
The PRIMARY colours of LIGHT (ADDITIVE) are:

(A) Cyan, Magenta, Yellow
(B) RED, GREEN, BLUE (RGB)
(C) Red, Yellow, Blue
(D) Red, Orange, Yellow
cards.back:
(B) RED, GREEN, BLUE (RGB)

Light & Optics — PRIMARY COLOURS OF LIGHT — RGB (Red-Green-Blue). Known as ADDITIVE primaries because adding them gives brighter colours (up to white). This is how TV screens, computer monitors, phones, LED displays work — millions of tiny pixels, each having R, G, B sub-pixels of controlled intensity. ADDITIVE COMBINATIONS: R + G = YELLOW; G + B = CYAN; R + B = MAGENTA; R + G + B = WHITE. These combinations (C, M, Y) are called SECONDARY colours of light. HUMAN colour VISION — retina has 3 types of CONE cells (photoreceptors) sensitive to roughly RED (L, long wavelength), GREEN (M, medium), BLUE (S, short). Brain combines signals to perceive colour. Colour-blindness (Daltonism) usually = defect in one cone type (most commonly red-green). Wavelength ranges: RED ~625-750 nm, GREEN ~500-565, BLUE ~450-485. SUBTRACTIVE PRIMARIES — CYAN, MAGENTA, YELLOW (CMY) or CMYK (with blacK) — basis of PRINTING and PAINT. Subtractive because pigments ABSORB some wavelengths and REFLECT only a subset. CMY combinations: C + M = Blue; M + Y = Red; C + Y = Green; C + M + Y = Black (in theory; in practice muddy-brown, hence K). In paint, PRIMARY colours traditionally taught to children are RED-YELLOW-BLUE — but strictly CMY is the scientifically correct subtractive primaries. The colour of AN OBJECT depends on which wavelengths it reflects (absorbs others): a red apple absorbs all light except red wavelengths, reflecting red. A BLACK object absorbs all; WHITE reflects all. In darkness, objects have NO colour (no light to reflect). OPPONENT-PROCESS THEORY (Hering): colour vision also processed as R-G, B-Y, and black-white pairs in neural pathways. basis of TV/monitor pixels, human colour vision (cones), additive mixing produces White when all three overlap.
