cards.front:
LASER stands for:

(A) Large Area Signal Emission Ray
(B) LIGHT AMPLIFICATION by STIMULATED EMISSION of RADIATION
(C) Linear Array of Shining Electron Rays
(D) Luminous Automatic Streaming Energy Radiation
cards.back:
(B) LIGHT AMPLIFICATION by STIMULATED EMISSION of RADIATION

Light & Optics — LASER (acronym) — Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation. Concept predicted by EINSTEIN (1917, stimulated emission theory). First MASER (Microwave amplification by stimulated emission) built by Charles Townes (1953). First LASER built by THEODORE MAIMAN (1960, ruby laser, USA). Nobel for laser-adjacent work — Townes, Basov, Prokhorov 1964; Schawlow 1981; Ashkin, Mourou, Strickland 2018 (chirped pulse amplification); Abacus (2023) for attosecond. PROPERTIES: (1) MONOCHROMATIC — single wavelength (very narrow spectral width); (2) COHERENT — all photons in-phase (spatial + temporal coherence); (3) HIGHLY DIRECTIONAL — very little divergence (can travel km with minimal spread); (4) VERY HIGH INTENSITY (concentrated energy, can reach terawatts in pulsed mode); (5) polarised. MECHANISM: (a) active medium (ruby, He-Ne, semiconductor, CO₂, Nd:YAG, dye, free-electron, fibre); (b) pumping source (flashlamp, electric discharge, another laser) excites atoms to higher energy states → POPULATION INVERSION; (c) when an excited atom is hit by a photon of the right wavelength, it undergoes STIMULATED EMISSION — releases a photon identical in phase, direction, wavelength; (d) mirrors in a RESONANT CAVITY amplify this into a coherent beam; (e) one mirror is partially transparent, letting the beam exit. TYPES of lasers by ACTIVE MEDIUM: (i) SOLID-STATE — Ruby, Nd:YAG, Ti:Sapphire, Fiber. (ii) GAS — He-Ne, CO₂ (cutting metals), Argon, Excimer (eye surgery). (iii) LIQUID — Dye lasers. (iv) SEMICONDUCTOR — Laser diode (CD/DVD/Blu-ray, fibre-optic comms, pointers). USES: FIBRE-OPTIC communication, BARCODE scanners, BLUE-RAY/DVD/CD readers, LIDAR, SURGERY (LASIK eye surgery, cancer ablation, angioplasty), INDUSTRY (cutting, welding, 3D printing, marking), MILITARY (range-finding, directed-energy weapons), SCIENTIFIC research (spectroscopy, laser cooling to microkelvin), HOLOGRAPHY, light shows, GRAVITATIONAL WAVE DETECTION (LIGO). a device producing a coherent, monochromatic, highly directional beam of light.

cards.front:
The COLOUR of a BLUE OBJECT under BLUE LIGHT will appear:

(A) Black
(B) Green
(C) BLUE
(D) White
cards.back:
(C) BLUE

Light & Optics — COLOURED OBJECTS under DIFFERENT COLOURED LIGHTS — key principle: an object appears the colour of the LIGHT IT REFLECTS. A blue object ABSORBS red, orange, yellow, green, indigo, violet and REFLECTS BLUE. Under WHITE LIGHT (containing all colours), you see its reflected blue → it looks blue. Under MONOCHROMATIC BLUE LIGHT, the only wavelength available is blue — which the object does reflect → still appears BLUE. Under MONOCHROMATIC RED LIGHT, only red is available; but the blue object ABSORBS red → no reflection → appears BLACK. A WHITE OBJECT reflects all wavelengths → looks the COLOUR of the incident light (blue under blue light, red under red light, white under white). A BLACK OBJECT absorbs all → appears BLACK under any illumination. ADDITIONAL EXAMPLES (tested often): (1) A red flower under green light → looks BLACK. (2) A yellow shirt under red light → looks RED (yellow reflects red+green; red alone reflects → red; hence it appears red — tricky! Need to think: yellow = reflects both red and green). (3) A yellow shirt under blue light → looks BLACK (yellow absorbs blue). (4) Rose in magenta light → looks BRIGHT RED/MAGENTA (rose reflects red; magenta = red+blue; red reflected, blue absorbed → red). COLOUR FILTER principle — a RED filter lets only red light through, absorbing others. A PIECE OF WHITE PAPER seen through red+green filters stacked → dark (neither red nor green passes both). COLOUR CONSTANCY — the human brain's remarkable ability to perceive an object's colour as roughly constant under different illuminations; the brain uses context + white-balance. Famous test: ‘THE DRESS’ (2015 internet phenomenon — blue/black vs white/gold due to perceived white balance). because the object is reflecting the blue wavelength (it only reflects blue; since blue is available in incident light, it remains visible).

cards.front:
The SPEED OF LIGHT in VACUUM is approximately:

(A) 3 × 10⁵ km/s
(B) 3 × 10⁴ km/s
(C) 3 × 10⁶ km/s
(D) 3 × 10⁷ km/s
cards.back:
(A) 3 × 10⁵ km/s

Light & Optics — SPEED OF LIGHT in vacuum (c) — EXACTLY 299,792,458 m/s (by definition since 1983; used to DEFINE the metre: ‘the distance light travels in 1/299,792,458 seconds’). Approximate value: 3 × 10⁸ m/s = 3 × 10⁵ km/s = 3,00,000 km/s. Light takes: (a) 1.3 seconds from Moon to Earth (384,400 km away); (b) 8 minutes 20 seconds from Sun (150 million km / 1 AU); (c) 4.2 years from nearest star PROXIMA CENTAURI; (d) 8 min 20 s from the Sun, so when you SEE the Sun, you're seeing it as it was 8 min ago; (e) 100,000 years to cross the Milky Way galaxy; (f) 2.5 million years to reach us from Andromeda. SPEED depends on MEDIUM — in a MEDIUM, light slows down: v = c/n, where n = REFRACTIVE INDEX. Typical n: VACUUM = 1.000; AIR ~1.0003 (nearly vacuum); WATER ~1.33; GLASS ~1.50; DIAMOND ~2.42 (very high, hence brilliant sparkle due to total internal reflection); ICE = 1.31. In DIAMOND, light travels at ~1.24 × 10⁸ m/s (less than half c). HISTORICAL MEASUREMENTS: (1) OLE RØMER (1676) — first estimation using Jupiter's moon IO eclipses; got ~2.2 × 10⁸ m/s. (2) JAMES BRADLEY (1729) — stellar aberration; 3.01 × 10⁸. (3) ARMAND FIZEAU (1849) — toothed wheel method; 3.13 × 10⁸. (4) LEON FOUCAULT (1862) — rotating mirror; 2.98 × 10⁸. (5) ALBERT MICHELSON (1879 onward, multiple) — rotating prism, interferometer; won NOBEL 1907 for these measurements. SPECIAL RELATIVITY (EINSTEIN 1905) — c is the ULTIMATE SPEED LIMIT for information, matter, energy; c is INVARIANT in every inertial frame — foundational principle. E = mc². NOTHING can travel faster than c in vacuum (though phase velocity, group velocity, and apparent superluminal effects exist in special cases without transmitting info faster than c). i.e., 3,00,000 km/s = 3 × 10⁸ m/s.

cards.front:
A ray of light travelling in air enters a denser medium such as glass. The ray bends:

(A) Away from the normal
(B) Towards the normal
(C) Along the normal
(D) Perpendicular to the normal
cards.back:
(B) Towards the normal

Light & Optics — When light enters a denser medium, its speed decreases and it bends towards the normal (Snell's law: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, so if n₂ > n₁, then θ₂ < θ₁). Going the other way — denser to rarer — the ray bends away from the normal and can undergo total internal reflection beyond the critical angle.

Going the other way — denser to rarer — the ray bends away from the normal and can undergo total internal reflection beyond the critical angle.

cards.front:
Which lens is used to correct short-sightedness (myopia)?

(A) Convex lens
(B) Concave lens
(C) Cylindrical lens
(D) Bifocal lens
cards.back:
(B) Concave lens

Light & Optics — In myopia the image forms in front of the retina; a diverging (concave) lens spreads the rays so the focus moves back onto the retina. Hypermetropia (long-sight) needs a converging (convex) lens. Cylindrical lenses correct astigmatism. Bifocals combine two powers for patients with presbyopia (difficulty focusing at reading distance in older age).

Bifocals combine two powers for patients with presbyopia (difficulty focusing at reading distance in older age).

cards.front:
The image formed by a plane mirror is:

(A) Real and inverted
(B) Virtual and erect
(C) Real and erect
(D) Virtual and inverted
cards.back:
(B) Virtual and erect

Light & Optics — A plane mirror always forms a virtual, erect image of the same size as the object, located at the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front. The image is laterally inverted (left becomes right) but not vertically inverted. A real image is one that can actually be caught on a screen — a plane mirror cannot produce one.

cards.front:
The focal length of a convex lens is 25 cm. Its power, in dioptres, is:

(A) +2 D
(B) +4 D
(C) +25 D
(D) +0.25 D
cards.back:
(B) +4 D

Light & Optics — Power P = 1 / f(in metres). Here f = 25 cm = 0.25 m, so P = 1/0.25 = +4 D. Convex lens → positive power; concave lens → negative. A prescription of '-2 D' means a concave lens of focal length 0.5 m.

cards.front:
Inside an optical fibre, light travels along the core by repeated:

(A) Diffraction
(B) Total internal reflection
(C) Refraction at the end face
(D) Scattering
cards.back:
(B) Total internal reflection

Light & Optics — An optical fibre has a high-index core surrounded by a lower-index cladding. When light hits the core–cladding boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle, it undergoes total internal reflection and stays trapped inside the core. This lets fibres carry signals over long distances with very low loss, which is why all modern undersea and long-haul internet cables use them.

cards.front:
A rainbow is formed by which combination of optical phenomena acting on sunlight in water droplets?

(A) Reflection and absorption
(B) Refraction, dispersion, and internal reflection
(C) Diffraction and polarisation
(D) Scattering and absorption
cards.back:
(B) Refraction, dispersion, and internal reflection

Light & Optics — Sunlight enters a water droplet (refraction), different wavelengths bend by different amounts (dispersion), reflects once off the back of the droplet (internal reflection), and refracts again on exit. The primary rainbow shows red outside and violet inside. A fainter secondary rainbow forms when light undergoes two internal reflections — in it the colour order is reversed.
cards.storedExplanation: Sunlight enters a water droplet (refraction), different wavelengths bend by different amounts (dispersion), reflects once off the back of the droplet (internal reflection), and refracts again on exit. The primary rainbow shows red outside and violet inside. A fainter secondary rainbow forms when light undergoes two internal reflections — in it the colour order is reversed.

cards.front:
The apparent depth of a coin seen through still water is less than its real depth because of:

(A) Reflection at the surface
(B) Refraction at the water surface
(C) Dispersion of light
(D) Diffraction around the coin
cards.back:
(B) Refraction at the water surface

Light & Optics — Light from the coin bends away from the normal on leaving the water, so to the observer the coin appears shallower. The relation is Apparent depth = Real depth / n, where n is the refractive index of water (~1.33). This is the same reason a straw in a glass of water looks bent at the surface.

The relation is Apparent depth = Real depth / n, where n is the refractive index of water (~1.33). This is the same reason a straw in a glass of water looks bent at the surface.

cards.front:
The speed of light in vacuum is:

(A) 3 × 10⁵ m/s
(B) 3 × 10⁸ m/s
(C) 3 × 10⁶ m/s
(D) 3 × 10¹⁰ m/s
cards.back:
(B) 3 × 10⁸ m/s

Light & Optics — c = 299,792,458 m/s ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Fundamental constant; upper speed limit for information in SR.
cards.storedExplanation: c = 299,792,458 m/s ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Fundamental constant; upper speed limit for information in SR.

cards.front:
The image formed by a PLANE mirror is:

(A) Real, inverted, same size
(B) Virtual, erect, same size, laterally inverted
(C) Real, erect, magnified
(D) Virtual, inverted, diminished
cards.back:
(B) Virtual, erect, same size, laterally inverted

Light & Optics — Plane mirror forms a virtual (behind-mirror) image, erect, same size, laterally inverted (LEFT↔RIGHT). Distance of image = distance of object.
cards.storedExplanation: Plane mirror forms a virtual (behind-mirror) image, erect, same size, laterally inverted (LEFT↔RIGHT). Distance of image = distance of object.

cards.front:
A person suffers from MYOPIA (short-sightedness). To correct the vision, the lens used is:

(A) Convex
(B) Concave
(C) Cylindrical
(D) Bifocal
cards.back:
(B) Concave

Light & Optics — Myopia — image forms in front of retina because eyeball is too long or lens too strong. A CONCAVE (diverging) lens diverges rays outward so they converge on the retina. Hypermetropia uses CONVEX lens; astigmatism uses CYLINDRICAL.

cards.front:
Rainbow is formed due to:

(A) Reflection only
(B) Refraction + dispersion + total internal reflection of light in water droplets
(C) Scattering of light
(D) Polarisation
cards.back:
(B) Refraction + dispersion + total internal reflection of light in water droplets

Light & Optics — Light enters droplet (refraction + dispersion — separating colours), reflects off the back surface (TIR), and exits (refraction again). Primary rainbow: red outside, violet inside. Secondary rainbow is fainter, colours reversed.
cards.storedExplanation: Light enters droplet (refraction + dispersion — separating colours), reflects off the back surface (TIR), and exits (refraction again). Primary rainbow: red outside, violet inside. Secondary rainbow is fainter, colours reversed.

cards.front:
The BLUE COLOUR OF THE SKY is primarily due to:

(A) Diffraction of light around clouds
(B) Rayleigh scattering
(C) Absorption of red wavelengths by oxygen
(D) Reflection of blue ocean surface
cards.back:
(B) Rayleigh scattering

Light & Optics — Rayleigh scattering ∝ 1/λ⁴. Blue light (λ ≈ 450 nm) is scattered ~10× more strongly than red (~700 nm). Hence the scattered blue reaches our eyes from all directions. At sunset, light passes through a longer atmospheric path — blues are scattered OUT, leaving red-orange directly visible. shorter wavelengths scattered more strongly by atmospheric molecules.
cards.option2: Absorption of red wavelengths by oxygen

cards.front:
A convex lens of focal length 20 cm forms a real image at a distance of 40 cm. The object distance is:

(A) 20 cm
(B) 40 cm
(C) 60 cm
(D) 30 cm
cards.back:
(B) 40 cm

Light & Optics — Lens formula 1/v − 1/u = 1/f with sign convention (real image on far side → v = +40 cm, f = +20 cm; object on incoming side → u is negative). 1/40 − 1/u = 1/20 → 1/u = 1/40 − 1/20 = −1/40 → u = −40 cm. Magnitude 40 cm. (Special case: u = v = 2f → m = −1, same-size real inverted image.)

Magnitude 40 cm. (Special case: u = v = 2f → m = −1, same-size real inverted image.)

cards.front:
The mirage phenomenon observed in deserts is due to:

(A) Reflection on wet sand
(B) Total internal reflection of light in layers of air at different temperatures/densities
(C) Diffraction of sunlight
(D) Optical illusion caused by thirst
cards.back:
(B) Total internal reflection of light in layers of air at different temperatures/densities

Light & Optics — Hot sand heats the air layer above → lower density → lower refractive index. Light coming from the sky bends upward via continuous refraction; at the critical angle, TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION occurs — observer sees a shimmering 'water' image. Same principle (inverted) produces 'water on the road' on a hot day.

Light coming from the sky bends upward via continuous refraction; at the critical angle, TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION occurs — observer sees a shimmering 'water' image. cards.front:
REFRACTION of light is the bending of a light ray when it passes from one medium to another due to:

(A) A change in the colour of the light beam itself
(B) A change in the speed of light between the media
(C) A change in the direction the light source is facing
(D) Reflection of light back into the original medium
cards.back:
(B) A change in the speed of light between the media

Light & Optics — Refraction occurs because light travels at DIFFERENT SPEEDS in different media. In vacuum c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s; in water ~ 2.25 × 10⁸ m/s; in glass ~ 2 × 10⁸ m/s; in diamond ~ 1.24 × 10⁸ m/s. The bending follows Snell's law: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂. When light enters a DENSER medium it bends TOWARD the normal; entering a less dense medium it bends AWAY from the normal. Distractor 1 — colour can disperse but isn't the cause. Distractor 3 — source direction is irrelevant. Distractor 4 — reflection is a separate phenomenon.
cards.option1: A change in the colour of the light beam itself
cards.option2: A change in the direction the light source is facing
cards.option3: Reflection of light back into the original medium

In vacuum c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s; in water ~ 2.25 × 10⁸ m/s; in glass ~ 2 × 10⁸ m/s; in diamond ~ 1.24 × 10⁸ m/s. The bending follows Snell's law: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂. cards.front:
TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION (TIR) occurs when:

(A) Light strikes a denser medium at any angle of incidence
(B) Light tries to leave a denser medium at angle exceeding the critical angle
(C) Light is reflected back from a thick mirror surface to viewer
(D) Two beams of light combine to produce a single brighter beam
cards.back:
(B) Light tries to leave a denser medium at angle exceeding the critical angle

Light & Optics — TIR — light traveling FROM a denser TO a less dense medium (e.g., glass to air) at an angle greater than the CRITICAL ANGLE bounces entirely back. Critical angle θ_c is given by sin θ_c = 1/n (n = refractive index of denser medium). For glass (n ≈ 1.5), θ_c ≈ 42°. For water (n ≈ 1.33), θ_c ≈ 49°. For diamond (n ≈ 2.42), θ_c ≈ 24° (gives diamonds their brilliance — light bounces around inside before exiting). Applications: OPTICAL FIBRES (light travels via TIR through cladded glass strands — basis of telecom + endoscopes), prismatic binoculars / periscopes.

cards.option2: Light is reflected back from a thick mirror surface to viewer
cards.option3: Two beams of light combine to produce a single brighter beam

cards.front:
When white light passes through a glass PRISM, it splits into seven colours because:

(A) The prism adds new colours not present in white light
(B) Different colours of light bend by different amounts on entry
(C) Prisms randomly select colours to allow through the medium
(D) Heat from the prism alters the wavelength of the light
cards.back:
(B) Different colours of light bend by different amounts on entry

Light & Optics — DISPERSION — refractive index of glass varies slightly with wavelength (n is highest for VIOLET, lowest for RED). So violet bends most, red bends least → white splits into the visible spectrum (VIBGYOR — violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red). Newton (1666) demonstrated this and showed a SECOND prism could re-combine the colours into white — proving white light is a mixture, not pure. Distractor 1 — colours are PRESENT in white, just unseen until separated. Distractor 3 — prism doesn't 'select'. Distractor 4 — heat doesn't change wavelength meaningfully.
cards.option1: The prism adds new colours not present in white light
cards.option2: Prisms randomly select colours to allow through the medium
cards.option3: Heat from the prism alters the wavelength of the light
cards.storedExplanation: DISPERSION — refractive index of glass varies slightly with wavelength (n is highest for VIOLET, lowest for RED). So violet bends most, red bends least → white splits into the visible spectrum (VIBGYOR — violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red). Newton (1666) demonstrated this and showed a SECOND prism could re-combine the colours into white — proving white light is a mixture, not pure. Distractor 1 — colours are PRESENT in white, just unseen until separated. Distractor 3 — prism doesn't 'select'. Distractor 4 — heat doesn't change wavelength meaningfully.

cards.front:
If the absolute refractive index of a medium is 1.5, the SPEED of light in that medium is approximately:

(A) 4.5 × 10⁸ m/s
(B) 2 × 10⁸ m/s
(C) 3 × 10⁸ m/s
(D) 1 × 10⁸ m/s
cards.back:
(B) 2 × 10⁸ m/s

Light & Optics — Refractive index n = c / v → v = c / n = (3 × 10⁸) / 1.5 = 2 × 10⁸ m/s. Distractor 4.5 × 10⁸ multiplies (faster than light, impossible). Distractor 3 × 10⁸ is c itself (vacuum value). Distractor 1 × 10⁸ uses n = 3.
cards.storedExplanation: Refractive index n = c / v → v = c / n = (3 × 10⁸) / 1.5 = 2 × 10⁸ m/s. Distractor 4.5 × 10⁸ multiplies (faster than light, impossible). Distractor 3 × 10⁸ is c itself (vacuum value). Distractor 1 × 10⁸ uses n = 3.

cards.front:
A CONVEX LENS forms an image of a distant object at its:

(A) Centre of curvature, twice the focal-length distance
(B) Focal point, on the side opposite to the source
(C) Optical centre, just inside the body of the lens
(D) Pole of the lens, exactly at the front surface
cards.back:
(B) Focal point, on the side opposite to the source

Light & Optics — Parallel rays from a distant object converge at the FOCAL POINT (F) of a convex lens. Image is real, inverted, highly diminished. The focal length f is the distance from the optical centre to F. Used in telescopes (objective lens converges starlight at F), camera lenses, the eye's lens (forms image on retina). Distractor 1 = centre of curvature is for spherical mirrors, not directly for lenses. Distractor 3 = optical centre is inside the lens. Distractor 4 = pole is for mirrors.
cards.option1: Centre of curvature, twice the focal-length distance
cards.option2: Optical centre, just inside the body of the lens
cards.option3: Pole of the lens, exactly at the front surface

cards.front:
A pencil partly dipped in water appears BENT at the water surface because of:

(A) Reflection of light from the water's flat surface
(B) Refraction as light bends entering and leaving water
(C) Diffraction of light around the pencil's edges
(D) Polarisation of light at the air-water boundary
cards.back:
(B) Refraction as light bends entering and leaving water

Light & Optics — Light from the submerged part of the pencil bends as it leaves water (n=1.33) into air (n=1.00) — bends AWAY from the normal. Our brain projects the light back along straight lines, so the underwater part appears displaced (and so the pencil seems 'bent'). Same reason: a coin in a glass of water seems shallower than it is; rivers look less deep. Distractor 1 — reflection is from the surface (image flipped) but not the bend. Distractor 3 — diffraction is wave-spreading, different effect. Distractor 4 — polarisation does occur (Brewster's angle) but does not cause the bending appearance.

cards.option2: Diffraction of light around the pencil's edges
cards.option3: Polarisation of light at the air-water boundary

cards.front:
OPTICAL FIBRES used in long-distance telecommunication transmit light by exploiting:

(A) Reflection from a polished metal coating outside the fibre
(B) Total internal reflection inside the fibre's glass core
(C) Diffraction of light around the fibre's circular cross-section
(D) Scattering of light by particles dissolved within the glass
cards.back:
(B) Total internal reflection inside the fibre's glass core

Light & Optics — Optical fibre = glass CORE (high n) surrounded by glass CLADDING (lower n). Light injected into the core hits the core-cladding boundary at an angle GREATER than the critical angle → totally internally reflected → bounces along the fibre with very low loss (~0.2 dB/km in modern silica fibres). Backbone of internet, undersea cables (e.g., the SEA-ME-WE network), endoscopes, hi-fi audio (TOSLINK). Distractor 1 — fibres don't use metal coating. Distractor 3 — diffraction is a different phenomenon. Distractor 4 — scattering would attenuate the signal, the OPPOSITE of what we want.

cards.option2: Diffraction of light around the fibre's circular cross-section
cards.option3: Scattering of light by particles dissolved within the glass

Light injected into the core hits the core-cladding boundary at an angle GREATER than the critical angle → totally internally reflected → bounces along the fibre with very low loss (~0.2 dB/km in modern silica fibres). cards.front:
SOUND requires a MEDIUM to travel because sound is:

(A) An electromagnetic wave (no medium needed)
(B) A mechanical wave (needs particles to vibrate)
(C) A transverse wave like light fully
(D) A standing wave that doesn't move
cards.back:
(B) A mechanical wave (needs particles to vibrate)

Sound & Waves — Sound = MECHANICAL LONGITUDINAL wave; needs medium (air, water, solid) — particles compress + rarefy + transmit energy. Cannot travel through VACUUM. Light + radio = ELECTROMAGNETIC waves; CAN travel through vacuum (sun's light reaches us through space). LONGITUDINAL = particles oscillate parallel to wave direction. Compare TRANSVERSE = perpendicular (light, water surface waves).
cards.option2: A transverse wave like light fully
cards.option3: A standing wave that doesn't move

Light + radio = ELECTROMAGNETIC waves; CAN travel through vacuum (sun's light reaches us through space). LONGITUDINAL = particles oscillate parallel to wave direction. Compare TRANSVERSE = perpendicular (light, water surface waves).

cards.front:
Speed of sound in AIR at room temperature (~20°C) is approximately:

(A) 330 m/s in cold dry air
(B) 343 m/s (~1235 km/h)
(C) 1500 m/s in dry warm air
(D) 300,000 km/s like light
cards.back:
(B) 343 m/s (~1235 km/h)

Sound & Waves — Speed of sound in dry air at 20°C = 343 m/s (~1235 km/h, ~767 mph, ~Mach 1). Increases with temperature (~0.6 m/s per °C). At 0°C = 331 m/s. WATER = ~1500 m/s (~4.4× faster than air). STEEL / IRON = ~5000 m/s (~15× faster). Speed depends on medium's elasticity + density — DENSER + MORE ELASTIC media transmit faster (counter-intuitive). Distractor 4 = speed of light (~10⁶ × faster than sound).

cards.front:
PITCH of a sound is determined by its:

(A) Amplitude (height of wave only)
(B) Frequency (number of vibrations / sec)
(C) Speed of travel only through medium
(D) Wavelength alone, not frequency
cards.back:
(B) Frequency (number of vibrations / sec)

Sound & Waves — PITCH (high or low note) = subjective perception of FREQUENCY (Hz). High frequency → high pitch; low frequency → low pitch. Human range: ~20 Hz - 20 kHz (declines with age). Below 20 Hz = INFRASOUND (elephants, whales communicate); above 20 kHz = ULTRASOUND (bats, dolphins, medical imaging). Distractor 1 — amplitude = LOUDNESS (dB). Distractor 3 — speed determined by medium, not source. Distractor 4 — wavelength = speed/frequency; in same medium, frequency uniquely determines wavelength.
cards.option2: Speed of travel only through medium

Distractor 3 — speed determined by medium, not source. Distractor 4 — wavelength = speed/frequency; in same medium, frequency uniquely determines wavelength.

cards.front:
ULTRASOUND has frequency:

(A) Below 20 Hz (infrasound range here)
(B) Above 20,000 Hz (above human hearing)
(C) Between 1000 and 5000 Hz only here
(D) Same as visible-light frequency band
cards.back:
(B) Above 20,000 Hz (above human hearing)

Sound & Waves — ULTRASOUND = > 20 kHz (above human upper hearing limit). USES: medical imaging (gestational ultrasound, echocardiography); SONAR (ships, submarines, fish-finding); industrial flaw detection (NDT — non-destructive testing); cleaning (ultrasonic cleaners for jewellery, dental tools); pest repellers; ultrasonic welding. ANIMALS using ultrasound: BATS (echolocation, up to 200 kHz); DOLPHINS, WHALES; MOTHS detect bat ultrasound. INFRASOUND (< 20 Hz) — elephants, earthquakes, large explosions. Distractor 4 — light is ~10¹⁴ Hz, completely different (electromagnetic, not mechanical).

cards.front:
DOPPLER EFFECT explains why an ambulance siren sounds:

(A) Same pitch when approaching + leaving
(B) Higher when approaching, lower when leaving
(C) Lower when approaching, higher when leaving
(D) Distorted but at constant frequency
cards.back:
(B) Higher when approaching, lower when leaving

Sound & Waves — DOPPLER EFFECT (1842, Christian Doppler): apparent frequency change due to relative motion between source + observer. SOURCE APPROACHING → wavefronts compressed → higher frequency → HIGHER PITCH. SOURCE RECEDING → wavefronts stretched → lower frequency → LOWER PITCH. Sudden drop as siren passes. Used in: RADAR speed guns (police), weather radar (storm tracking), medical Doppler (blood flow), astronomy (RED SHIFT — galaxies receding → expanding universe — Hubble's discovery, 1929).

cards.front:
ECHO is heard distinctly when minimum reflection time is:

(A) 0.05 second from the wall surface
(B) 0.1 second (persistence of hearing)
(C) 1 second of delay from the wall
(D) Instantly without any delay at all
cards.back:
(B) 0.1 second (persistence of hearing)

Sound & Waves — Echo = reflected sound heard distinctly. Minimum gap = 0.1 s (persistence of hearing) → minimum reflector distance = (speed × time)/2 = (343 × 0.1)/2 ≈ 17 m. Less than this → original + echo overlap (heard as a single, lingering sound — REVERBERATION, common in halls). Echoes used in: SONAR (ship → seabed), animal echolocation (bats, dolphins). Distractor 4 — instant reflection = no echo perceived.

cards.option3: Instantly without any delay at all

cards.front:
A 'SONIC BOOM' is created when an aircraft:

(A) Lands or takes off from runway
(B) Exceeds the speed of sound (Mach 1)
(C) Flies at low altitude over cities
(D) Cuts through clouds at any speed
cards.back:
(B) Exceeds the speed of sound (Mach 1)

Sound & Waves — SONIC BOOM = shock wave heard as loud bang/clap when aircraft exceeds SPEED OF SOUND (Mach 1, ~343 m/s at SL). Compressed air waves accumulate at nose of aircraft; can't get out of the way → form a CONE (Mach cone) trailing behind. When the cone passes over an observer = the boom. Concorde (1976-2003) was supersonic civilian jet — banned from supersonic flight over land due to noise. Modern fighter jets (F-22, Su-30, Rafale, Tejas Mk2) routinely supersonic. Mach 2 = twice speed of sound; Mach 3 = thrice; etc.

The approximate speed of sound in dry air at 20 °C is:

(A) 130 m/s
(B) 343 m/s
(C) 1,500 m/s
(D) 3 × 10⁸ m/s
cards.back:
(B) 343 m/s

cards.front:
Sound CANNOT travel through:

(A) Water
(B) Vacuum
(C) Air
(D) Steel
cards.back:
(B) Vacuum

Sound & Waves — Sound is a mechanical wave — it needs a medium (solid, liquid or gas) to propagate. In a vacuum there are no particles to vibrate, so sound cannot travel — this is why the Moon (with no atmosphere) is silent. Sound travels fastest in solids (close molecular packing), slower in liquids, slowest in gases. Light, a transverse EM wave, does not need a medium.

cards.front:
The pitch of a sound is determined by its:

(A) Amplitude
(B) Frequency
(C) Wavelength
(D) Speed
cards.back:
(B) Frequency

Sound & Waves — Pitch (how 'high' or 'low' a sound seems) is set by frequency — higher frequency → higher pitch. A woman's voice is higher-pitched than a man's because it has more cycles per second (~200 Hz vs ~125 Hz). Amplitude determines loudness. Wavelength is inversely related to frequency (v = fλ) but pitch itself is directly linked to frequency, not wavelength as the controlled variable.

cards.front:
The apparent change in the frequency of a sound as its source moves towards or away from an observer is called the:

(A) Raman effect
(B) Doppler effect
(C) Tyndall effect
(D) Zeeman effect
cards.back:
(B) Doppler effect

Sound & Waves — Doppler effect — the siren of a passing ambulance sounds higher in pitch as it approaches and lower as it recedes. Named after Christian Doppler (1842). Also applies to light: 'red-shift' of receding galaxies (evidence of an expanding universe). Raman effect — inelastic scattering of light. Tyndall effect — scattering of light by colloidal particles. Zeeman effect — splitting of spectral lines in a magnetic field.

(B) Decibels

cards.back:

A normal conversation is ~60 dB, city traffic ~80 dB; continuous exposure above 85 dB damages hearing; 130 dB is the threshold of pain. Hertz measures frequency (pitch). Pascal measures pressure (and sound pressure itself is in Pa, but loudness is expressed in dB).

cards.front:
An echo is heard when the reflecting surface is at least at what minimum distance?

(A) 8.5 m
(B) 17 m
(C) 34 m
(D) 343 m
cards.back:
(B) 17 m

Sound & Waves — The human ear needs at least 0.1 s gap to distinguish the echo from the original sound. In that time sound travels 343 × 0.1 ≈ 34 m round-trip, so the reflector must be at least ~17 m (one-way) away. Distances less than 17 m produce reverberation rather than a distinct echo. Caves, deep wells and large auditoriums demonstrate the effect clearly.

(B) 17 m
(C) 34 m
(D) 100 m

(B) 17 m

(A) Transverse
(B) Longitudinal
(C) Electromagnetic
(D) Neither transverse nor longitudinal
cards.back:

(A) 343 m/s
(B) 3 × 10⁸ m/s
(C) 1500 m/s
(D) 5 × 10⁵ m/s
cards.back:
(A) 343 m/s

Sound & Waves — SPEED OF SOUND in AIR: ~343 m/s at 20°C (~1235 km/h). Increases with temperature (~0.6 m/s per °C rise). Formula: v = 331 + 0.6 × T (T in °C). SPEED OF SOUND in DIFFERENT MEDIA: AIR ~343 m/s; WATER ~1480 m/s (~4.3× air); STEEL ~5960 m/s (~17× air); DIAMOND ~12000 m/s. General rule: faster in SOLIDS than LIQUIDS than GASES (because molecules are closer in solids, transmitting vibrations faster). VACUUM — SOUND CANNOT travel (no medium). SPEED OF LIGHT in vacuum: c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s — ~874,000× faster than sound in air. This is why thunder FOLLOWS lightning (flash first, bang later — 3s per km). SONIC BOOM: aircraft exceeding sound speed (Mach 1, 1235 km/h sea level). MACH NUMBER = ratio of object speed to speed of sound (Mach 1, 2, 3...). HYPERSONIC: Mach 5+. Concorde flew Mach 2.04. First supersonic flight: Chuck Yeager 14 Oct 1947 (Bell X-1).

cards.front:
The DOPPLER EFFECT — apparent change in frequency of a wave as the source or observer moves — was first formulated by:

(A) Albert Einstein
(B) Christian Doppler
(C) Isaac Newton
(D) Michael Faraday
cards.back:
(B) Christian Doppler

Sound & Waves — DOPPLER EFFECT: proposed by Christian Andreas DOPPLER (Austrian physicist, 1842). Observed frequency > emitted when source approaches observer; < when moving away. Everyday example: AMBULANCE siren — sounds higher pitch as it approaches, lower as it recedes. Formula (non-relativistic): f_observed = f_source × (v ± v_observer) / (v ± v_source), where v = speed of wave in medium. APPLICATIONS: (1) DOPPLER RADAR — police speed guns; weather radar (measures wind speed); (2) RED SHIFT in astronomy — light from distant galaxies shifts to red (longer wavelength) = receding; Edwin Hubble's 1929 work showed galaxies receding proportional to distance → Universe is expanding → Big Bang evidence. (3) MEDICAL DOPPLER — blood flow velocity via ultrasound. (4) SONAR, bat echolocation, air traffic control. RELATIVISTIC DOPPLER EFFECT: Einstein's generalisation accounting for time dilation. Doppler predicted applicability to light — proven experimentally only 3 years later. 1842, Austrian physicist.

The ELECTROMAGNETIC SPECTRUM (in order of INCREASING frequency / DECREASING wavelength) is:

(A) Radio → Microwaves → Infrared → Visible light → UV → X-rays → Gamma rays
(B) Gamma → X-rays → UV → Visible → Infrared → Microwaves → Radio
(C) Random order — no arrangement
(D) Sound → Light → Radio → Microwaves
cards.back:
(A) Radio → Microwaves → Infrared → Visible light → UV → X-rays → Gamma rays

Sound & Waves — EM SPECTRUM (low to high frequency): RADIO WAVES (long wavelength, low frequency, low energy; AM/FM radio, TV, WiFi) → MICROWAVES (ovens, cell phones, radar, satellite comms) → INFRARED (heat, remote controls, thermography) → VISIBLE LIGHT (tiny slice humans see: red→orange→yellow→green→blue→indigo→violet = VIBGYOR in reverse) → ULTRAVIOLET (sunburn, vitamin D, sterilisation) → X-RAYS (medical imaging, airport scanners) → GAMMA RAYS (shortest wavelength, highest energy; nuclear reactions, cosmic rays — very penetrating). ALL travel at SPEED OF LIGHT in vacuum (c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s). c = λf (wavelength × frequency). Visible light: 400-700 nm wavelength; 430-770 THz. Discovered by MAXWELL (theoretical predictions, 1865), HEINRICH HERTZ (radio waves, 1887), W.C. RÖNTGEN (X-rays, 1895, Nobel 1901 first-ever). Photons carry energy E = hf = hc/λ (h = Planck's constant). EM waves don't need a medium (can travel in vacuum, unlike sound).

cards.front:
ECHOES are produced when sound reflects off a surface. For the reflected sound to be perceived as a distinct echo (not just reverberation), the reflecting surface must be AT LEAST how far away from the source?

(A) 5 metres
(B) ~17 metres
(C) 100 metres
(D) 1 kilometre
cards.back:
(B) ~17 metres

Sound & Waves — ECHO REQUIREMENT: the reflected sound must reach the listener's ear at LEAST 0.1 seconds AFTER the original sound (persistence of hearing / auditory resolution). Time = distance/speed → in air (v=343 m/s): 0.1 s means round trip ≥ 34 m → reflector must be ≥ 17 m away. Below that distance, sound blurs into REVERBERATION. Examples: WHISPERING GALLERIES (St. Paul's Cathedral London, Gol Gumbaz Bijapur, US Capitol) — sound travels along curved walls. SONAR (SOund Navigation And Ranging): uses ultrasonic waves + echo timing to measure ocean depth or locate objects underwater. BAT ECHOLOCATION: emit 50-200 kHz pulses, listen for echoes. RADAR (RAdio Detection And Ranging): EM waves + echo for aircraft/weather tracking. ULTRASOUND IMAGING: uses ~1-20 MHz ultrasound + echo to image internal body organs (prenatal, cardiac). Reverberation: useful in concert halls (designed for ~1.5-2s reverberation time); but poor in classrooms or homes where clarity is needed. so total travel time ≥ 0.1 seconds, the human ear's resolution.

cards.front:
Sound INTENSITY is measured on a LOGARITHMIC scale called:

(A) Hertz (Hz)
(B) Decibel (dB)
(C) Newton (N)
(D) Watt (W)
cards.back:
(B) Decibel (dB)

Sound & Waves — DECIBEL (dB) = log-scale unit for sound intensity. Named after Alexander Graham BELL (inventor of the phone; B = bel; dB = decibel, 1/10th). Formula: dB = 10 × log₁₀(I/I₀), where I₀ = reference = 10⁻¹² W/m² (threshold of human hearing). Every 10 dB = 10× intensity. 20 dB = 100× intensity. COMMON SOUND LEVELS: 0 dB — threshold of hearing; 10 dB — breathing; 20-30 dB — whisper; 40 dB — library; 60 dB — normal conversation; 70 dB — vacuum cleaner; 80-90 dB — city traffic; 90-100 dB — subway, motorcycle; 100 dB — chainsaw; 110 dB — rock concert, baby crying close; 120 dB — jet takeoff at 60 m; 130 dB — threshold of PAIN; 140 dB — jet engine at 30 m; >140 dB — immediate hearing damage. NOISE POLLUTION in India regulated by Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules 2000 — day/night limits in industrial/commercial/residential/silence zones. Noise-induced hearing loss (NIHL) is permanent above 85 dB sustained exposure.

cards.front:
When light passes from a LESS DENSE medium (air) to a MORE DENSE medium (water or glass), it:

(A) Speeds up and bends AWAY from the normal
(B) Slows down and bends TOWARDS the normal
(C) Continues in a straight line with no change
(D) Reflects completely back
cards.back:
(B) Slows down and bends TOWARDS the normal

Sound & Waves — REFRACTION of LIGHT: when a light ray passes from one medium to another with different optical density, it CHANGES DIRECTION (bends) at the interface AND changes speed. From LESS DENSE (e.g., air) to MORE DENSE (e.g., water/glass): light SLOWS DOWN and bends TOWARDS the normal (the perpendicular to the surface). Vice versa: from dense to less dense, light SPEEDS UP and bends AWAY from the normal. SNELL'S LAW: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, where n = refractive index (n_vacuum = 1, n_air ≈ 1.0003, n_water ≈ 1.33, n_glass ≈ 1.5, n_diamond ≈ 2.42). SPEED OF LIGHT in a medium: v = c/n. TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION (TIR): when light tries to move from dense to less dense medium at an angle > CRITICAL ANGLE, ALL light reflects back. Applications: OPTICAL FIBRES (internet cables), MIRAGE (hot air acts as less dense; road appears wet), SPARKLE OF DIAMOND (high n + cutting causes TIR from many facets). Critical angle for water-air: ~48.6°; glass-air: ~42°; diamond-air: ~24.4°.

cards.option2: Continues in a straight line with no change

cards.front:
A RAINBOW is formed by THREE optical phenomena acting on sunlight interacting with water droplets. These are:

(A) Refraction, total internal reflection, and dispersion
(B) Only diffraction
(C) Polarisation, scattering, absorption
(D) Gravity + reflection
cards.back:
(A) Refraction, total internal reflection, and dispersion

Sound & Waves — RAINBOW formation: (1) SUNLIGHT enters water droplet — REFRACTION at entry surface (white light bends into droplet); (2) hits back wall of droplet — TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION (if within critical angle limits); (3) exits droplet — another REFRACTION. Throughout, DISPERSION (different wavelengths bend by slightly different amounts — because refractive index depends on wavelength) separates white light into COLOURS: VIBGYOR (Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red). RED on OUTER edge (least bent, ~42° from sun-anti point); VIOLET on INNER (most bent, ~40°). OBSERVER is between sun and raindrops — must have sun BEHIND + rain in front; rainbow appears in an arc centred on the anti-solar point. DOUBLE RAINBOW: faint outer rainbow with REVERSED colours, formed by 2 internal reflections (~51°-54°). Alexander's dark band between them (no light bounces into it). Colours are continuous, not discrete 7 — we see 7 by convention (Newton's division). No two people see the SAME rainbow — position-dependent optical illusion.

cards.front:
The relation between wave speed (v), frequency (f), and wavelength (λ) is:

(A) v = f × λ (universal wave equation)
(B) v = f / λ (a wrong form here)
(C) v = f + λ (an addition form)
(D) v = f − λ (a subtraction form)
cards.back:
(A) v = f × λ (universal wave equation)

Sound & Waves — WAVE EQUATION: v = f × λ, where v = wave speed (m/s), f = frequency (Hz = 1/s), λ = wavelength (m). UNIVERSAL: applies to ALL waves — sound, light, water, electromagnetic, seismic. EXAMPLES: (1) SOUND in AIR: v ≈ 343 m/s; if f = 440 Hz (musical note A), λ = 343/440 ≈ 0.78 m. (2) LIGHT in vacuum: v = c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s; visible light frequency ~5 × 10¹⁴ Hz, λ ~600 nm. (3) AM RADIO: 1 MHz, λ = 300 m; FM at 100 MHz, λ = 3 m. KEY DEFINITIONS: WAVELENGTH (λ) = distance between consecutive crests (or troughs); FREQUENCY (f) = cycles per second (Hz); PERIOD (T) = time per cycle = 1/f; AMPLITUDE = max displacement from equilibrium (loudness for sound, brightness for light). RELATIONSHIPS: f × T = 1; v = λ/T; v = f × λ. INSIGHT — different colors of light have DIFFERENT frequencies (and wavelengths) but ALL travel at SAME speed c in vacuum. RED light: λ ~700 nm; violet: λ ~400 nm. RAINBOW: visible spectrum split by prism/raindrops. PYQ FREQUENCY: wave equation v=fλ in NEET, JEE-Main 2-3× per paper, NCERT-driven SSC 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
SOUND waves in air are classified as:

(A) Longitudinal mechanical waves
(B) Transverse mechanical waves
(C) Electromagnetic waves now
(D) Standing waves only here
cards.back:
(A) Longitudinal mechanical waves

Sound & Waves — SOUND in AIR: LONGITUDINAL — particles oscillate ALONG the direction of wave propagation (compressions and rarefactions). MECHANICAL — needs a medium (cannot travel in vacuum). DEFINITIONS: (1) TRANSVERSE WAVES — particles oscillate PERPENDICULAR to wave direction (e.g., light, water waves on surface, EM waves, seismic S-waves). (2) LONGITUDINAL WAVES — particles oscillate PARALLEL to wave direction (e.g., sound, seismic P-waves). (3) MECHANICAL WAVES — need medium (sound, water, seismic, slinky). (4) ELECTROMAGNETIC WAVES — DON'T need medium (light, radio, X-rays — propagate as oscillating electric+magnetic fields). KEY DIFFERENCES: SOUND speed in air ~343 m/s (depends on T, density). SOUND in WATER: ~1,500 m/s (~4× faster). SOUND in STEEL: ~5,100 m/s (~15× faster than air). SOUND in VACUUM: cannot propagate (no particles). SHOUTING ON THE MOON: would be silent — no atmosphere; astronauts use radios. AUDIBLE RANGE: humans hear ~20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz). Below 20 Hz = INFRASOUND (elephants, whales communicate with infrasound). Above 20 kHz = ULTRASOUND (bats, dolphins, medical imaging). PYQ FREQUENCY: sound-wave properties in NEET, NCERT, JEE-Main 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
LIGHT waves are EM (electromagnetic) waves and:

(A) Can travel through vacuum
(B) Need a material medium always
(C) Are only longitudinal in nature
(D) Have lowest speed of any wave
cards.back:
(A) Can travel through vacuum

Sound & Waves — LIGHT (and all EM waves) — TRANSVERSE in nature, can travel through VACUUM. SPEED in VACUUM: c = 299,792,458 m/s ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s. KEY: EM waves are oscillating ELECTRIC + MAGNETIC fields propagating perpendicular to each other AND to direction of motion. NO MEDIUM needed (a key 19th-century debate; Michelson-Morley experiment 1887 disproved 'aether'). EM SPECTRUM (low to high frequency / long to short wavelength): RADIO → MICROWAVES → INFRARED → VISIBLE LIGHT (red→violet) → ULTRAVIOLET → X-RAYS → GAMMA RAYS. ALL TRAVEL AT c in vacuum. WAVELENGTHS: radio ~m to km; microwaves ~cm; IR ~µm; visible 400-700 nm; UV ~10-400 nm; X-rays ~0.01-10 nm; gamma < 0.01 nm. EVERYDAY EMISSIONS: (1) Sun — full spectrum. (2) Lightbulb — visible + IR. (3) WiFi — microwaves (~2.4 GHz). (4) X-ray machine — X-rays. SPEED IN MEDIUM: light SLOWS in glass, water (refractive index n; v = c/n). Glass n ~1.5; water n ~1.33; diamond n ~2.4 → light is 2.4× slower in diamond. EINSTEIN's special relativity (1905): c is the universal speed limit; nothing material can travel faster than c. PYQ FREQUENCY: EM wave properties in NEET, JEE-Main 2× per paper.

cards.front:
The DOPPLER EFFECT is observed when:

(A) Source and observer move relative to each other
(B) Wave passes through a denser medium (option here)
(C) Wave reflects off a flat surface (option here)
(D) Two waves combine in same direction (option here)
cards.back:
(A) Source and observer move relative to each other

Sound & Waves — DOPPLER EFFECT (Christian Doppler, 1842): apparent CHANGE IN FREQUENCY (or wavelength) observed when SOURCE and OBSERVER are in RELATIVE MOTION. APPROACHING source/observer → frequency INCREASES (shorter wavelength). RECEDING → frequency DECREASES (longer wavelength). EVERYDAY EXAMPLES: (1) AMBULANCE SIREN: pitch HIGHER as it APPROACHES, LOWER as it RECEDES — same physical sound from siren. (2) FORMULA 1 RACING — engine pitch shifts dramatically as cars whiz by. APPLICATIONS: (1) RADAR speed guns — measure vehicle speed via Doppler shift in reflected radio waves. (2) MEDICAL ULTRASOUND — Doppler probes measure blood flow rates. (3) WEATHER RADAR — Doppler radar tracks storm motion. (4) ASTRONOMY — REDSHIFT: galaxies' light shifts to red (longer λ) as they recede; basis for Hubble's discovery (1929) that universe is EXPANDING. (5) BLUESHIFT — galaxies/stars approaching us. KEY FORMULA (sound, source moving): f' = f × v / (v − v_source) — for approaching source. EXAM TIP: 'siren pitch change' is the universal example. IS DOPPLER for LIGHT: yes — relativistic Doppler effect; foundation of cosmology, satellite tracking. PYQ FREQUENCY: Doppler effect in NEET, JEE-Main 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
The frequency RANGE of AUDIBLE sound for humans is approximately:

(A) 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz)
(B) 1 Hz to 1,000 Hz only here
(C) 100 Hz to 1 GHz approximately
(D) 200,000 Hz to 1 MHz only
cards.back:
(A) 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz)

Sound & Waves — HUMAN AUDIBLE RANGE: ~20 Hz (lowest, deep bass) to ~20,000 Hz (highest, very high pitch). DECLINES WITH AGE (PRESBYCUSIS): adults' upper limit drops to ~12-15 kHz by age 30-40; high-frequency hearing loss is universal with aging. INFRASOUND: < 20 Hz — felt rather than heard (vibrations); whales, elephants, hippos communicate using infrasound (travels far). Used by DEFENSE for long-range comm. ULTRASOUND: > 20 kHz — used by BATS (echolocation, ~20-200 kHz), DOLPHINS, CATS, DOGS (up to ~45 kHz — dog whistles emit at 20-25 kHz, human-inaudible but dogs hear). MEDICAL ULTRASOUND: ~1-20 MHz; pregnancy scans, abdominal scans, echocardiography. PHYSICAL EFFECT: low frequencies reach FAR; high frequencies attenuate over distance (why distant thunder sounds 'rumbly' — high frequencies absorbed). INDIA NOISE STANDARDS (CPCB): residential limits 55 dB day / 45 dB night; commercial 65/55; industrial 75/70; silence zones (near schools/hospitals) 50/40. NOISE POLLUTION: > 85 dB prolonged exposure causes hearing damage. PYQ FREQUENCY: human hearing range in NEET, NCERT-driven SSC GA 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Speed of sound in AIR at room temperature is approximately:

(A) 343 m/s (~1235 km/h)
(B) 3 × 10⁸ m/s (speed of light)
(C) 1500 m/s (sound in water)
(D) 10 m/s (very slow rate)
cards.back:
(A) 343 m/s (~1235 km/h)

Sound & Waves — SPEED OF SOUND in AIR at 20°C and 1 atm: ~343 m/s = ~1235 km/h. AT 0°C: ~331 m/s. AT 100°C: ~387 m/s. INCREASES with TEMPERATURE: roughly v ≈ 331 + 0.6T (T in °C). WHY: warmer air = faster molecular motion = faster transmission of pressure waves. SPEED of SOUND in OTHER MEDIA: (1) FRESH WATER (20°C): ~1480 m/s. (2) SEA WATER: ~1530 m/s (slightly faster due to salinity). (3) STEEL: ~5100 m/s (~15× faster than air). (4) GLASS: ~5500 m/s. (5) DIAMOND: ~12,000 m/s (highest known). REASON: solids are more INCOMPRESSIBLE; sound transmits via pressure waves in atomic lattice. CONTRAST WITH LIGHT: light is much faster (3 × 10⁸ m/s) — that's why we see lightning before hearing thunder. RULE: count seconds between flash and thunder; divide by 3 to estimate distance in km. SUPERSONIC: above speed of sound (Mach 1). MACH NUMBER = velocity / speed of sound. SUPERSONIC AIRCRAFT: Concorde (Mach 2.04), SR-71 Blackbird (Mach 3.3+), HYPERSONIC missiles (Mach 5+). SONIC BOOM occurs when aircraft crosses Mach 1 — pressure waves merge into shock front. PYQ FREQUENCY: sound speed in NEET, NCERT, SSC physics 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
A sound wave has frequency 500 Hz and wavelength 0.7 m in air. The speed is:

(A) 350 m/s (close to standard 343)
(B) 3500 m/s (over-shot value)
(C) 35 m/s (too slow value)
(D) 5000 m/s (steel speed value)
cards.back:
(A) 350 m/s (close to standard 343)

Sound & Waves — Apply WAVE EQUATION: v = f × λ. Plug: v = 500 × 0.7 = 350 m/s. CONSISTENT with sound in air (typical 343 m/s); slight variation OK due to room T. NUMERICAL CHECK: 500 Hz means 500 cycles/sec. Each cycle has wavelength 0.7 m. So in 1 second, wave covers 500 × 0.7 = 350 m. KEY METHOD: identify which two of (v, f, λ) are given; compute the third. PRACTICE: (1) f = 1000 Hz, λ = 0.34 m → v = 340 m/s (sound in air). (2) v = 1500 m/s (water), f = 600 Hz → λ = 2.5 m. (3) Light: c = 3×10⁸, f = 6×10¹⁴ → λ = 5×10⁻⁷ m = 500 nm (green light). UNIT CHECKS: m/s = (1/s) × m ✓. Always verify units! REAL-WORLD: opera singer hits high C ~1046 Hz; air wavelength ~0.33 m; double bass low E ~41 Hz; air wavelength ~8.4 m. INSIGHT — INSTRUMENTS: long instruments (organ pipes, double bass) produce LOW frequencies (long wavelengths fit better); short instruments (piccolo, violin) high frequencies. PYQ FREQUENCY: simple v=fλ calculations 2-3× per JEE-Main, NEET; 1× per SSC CGL Tier 2.

(B) Vacuum (no medium for it)

cards.back:

Sound & Waves — Sound NEEDS a material medium (solid/liquid/gas). VACUUM has no particles → no compression-rarefaction → no sound transmission. 'In space, no one can hear you scream.' Famous demo: ringing bell in a glass jar; as air is pumped out, sound fades. Distractor 1 — sound DOES travel through water (4× faster than air). Distractor 3 — even cold air conducts sound. Distractor 4 — sound travels FASTEST in solids. Light, in contrast, travels best in vacuum.

cards.front:
ULTRASOUND in medical imaging uses sound waves of frequency typically:

(A) 20 to 20,000 Hz, the audible range only
(B) 1 to 20 MHz, well above the audible limit
(C) Below 20 Hz, in the infrasound range
(D) Same as the radio waves used in FM band
cards.back:
(B) 1 to 20 MHz, well above the audible limit

Sound & Waves — Medical ultrasound: typically 2-15 MHz (general); 1-3 MHz for deeper imaging; 7-15 MHz for superficial. ULTRASOUND = sound above 20 kHz. Used for: fetal ultrasound, abdominal scans, echocardiography, kidney/gallbladder stones, FAST scans (trauma). Non-ionising, safe (unlike X-rays/CT). Doppler ultrasound shows blood flow. Industrial uses: cleaning, welding, distance sensors. Bats + dolphins navigate using ultrasonic echolocation. Distractor 4 — radio waves are EM, different physical phenomenon.

cards.front:
If the WAVELENGTH of a sound wave is 0.5 m and its FREQUENCY is 686 Hz, the speed of sound in that medium is:

(A) 1372 m/s, twice the actual speed
(B) 343 m/s, matching speed in air at 20°C
(C) 171.5 m/s, half of the actual speed
(D) 686 m/s, equal to its frequency only
cards.back:
(B) 343 m/s, matching speed in air at 20°C

Sound & Waves — Wave speed: v = f × λ = 686 × 0.5 = 343 m/s — matches the speed of sound in dry air at 20°C. Universal wave equation. Distractor 1 = frequency × 2 × wavelength. Distractor 3 = halved (used 0.25 m). Distractor 4 = frequency value alone. Useful: humans speaking ~100-3000 Hz, with wavelengths in air ~3.4 m to 11 cm.

cards.option3: 686 m/s, equal to its frequency only

cards.front:
OHM'S LAW states that the current (I) through a conductor between two points is directly proportional to the voltage (V) across it, with resistance (R) as the constant of proportionality. Mathematically:

(A) V = I × R
(B) V = I / R
(C) V = I² × R
(D) V = R / I
cards.back:
(A) V = I × R

Electricity & Magnetism — OHM'S LAW: V = IR, where V = voltage (volts, V), I = current (amperes, A), R = resistance (ohms, Ω). Given by Georg Simon OHM (German, 1827). Applies to ohmic conductors (metal wires, resistors at constant temperature). Non-ohmic: diodes, transistors, filament bulbs at high current (resistance changes with temperature), electrolytes. POWER equations: P = VI = I²R = V²/R (watts). ENERGY = P × t (joules). 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J. Units in SI: VOLT (V) — potential difference; AMPERE (A) — current; OHM (Ω) — resistance; WATT (W) — power; COULOMB (C) — charge. I = Q/t (charge per unit time).

cards.front:
Three resistors of 2Ω, 4Ω, and 6Ω are connected in SERIES. The equivalent resistance is:

(A) 12 Ω
(B) 12/11 Ω
(C) 8/3 Ω
(D) 6 Ω
cards.back:
(A) 12 Ω

Electricity & Magnetism — SERIES connection: resistances ADD. R_series = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ = 2 + 4 + 6 = 12 Ω. Same current through all (I_total = I₁ = I₂ = I₃), voltages add (V_total = V₁ + V₂ + V₃). PARALLEL connection: 1/R_parallel = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃ = 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/6 = 6/12 + 3/12 + 2/12 = 11/12 → R_parallel = 12/11 ≈ 1.09 Ω (so parallel equivalent is LESS than the smallest resistor). Parallel: same voltage across all (V_total = V₁ = V₂ = V₃), currents add (I_total = I₁ + I₂ + I₃). Domestic wiring uses parallel (each appliance gets same voltage, independent on/off). Christmas tree lights can be series (one fails → all out) or parallel.

cards.front:
A 60 W light bulb operates on 220 V mains. What is the current flowing through it?

(A) 0.27 A
(B) 3.67 A
(C) 13200 A
(D) 0.036 A
cards.back:
(A) 0.27 A

Electricity & Magnetism — Use P = VI → I = P/V = 60/220 = 0.2727 A ≈ 0.27 A (or 273 mA). Working: power 60 W, voltage 220 V, so I = 60 W / 220 V = 3/11 A. Resistance: R = V/I = 220 / 0.27 ≈ 806 Ω (or R = V²/P = 220²/60 = 48400/60 ≈ 807 Ω — same answer). 3.67 A would be wrong — that's V/P; 13200 A comes from V×P (wrong formula). Indian mains: 220-240V, 50 Hz. European: 230V, 50Hz. US: 110-120V, 60 Hz. A typical home has 15-30 A per circuit. Circuit breaker trips if exceeded. Higher voltage → less current for same power → thinner wires feasible → less I²R loss in transmission — rationale for HIGH-VOLTAGE power transmission (132 kV, 220 kV, 400 kV, 765 kV).

cards.front:
The unit of ELECTRIC CHARGE in the SI system is:

(A) Ampere
(B) Coulomb
(C) Volt
(D) Farad
cards.back:
(B) Coulomb

Electricity & Magnetism — COULOMB (C) — SI unit of electric charge, named after Charles-Augustin de Coulomb (French, 1736-1806). Defined: 1 C = charge transported by a current of 1 A in 1 s (Q = I × t). One electron: e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (elementary charge). One Coulomb ≈ 6.24 × 10¹⁸ electrons. AMPERE (A) = current = C/s. VOLT (V) = electric potential = J/C (work done per unit charge). FARAD (F) = capacitance = C/V. OHM (Ω) = V/A. WATT (W) = V × A = J/s. TESLA (T) = magnetic flux density = V·s/m². WEBER (Wb) = magnetic flux = V·s. HENRY (H) = inductance = V·s/A. COULOMB'S LAW: F = kQ₁Q₂/r², where k ≈ 9 × 10⁹ Nm²/C². Compare with Newton's gravity: F = Gm₁m₂/r², G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹. Coulomb force is ~10⁴⁰ stronger than gravity between charged particles.

cards.front:
KIRCHHOFF'S CURRENT LAW (KCL) states that:

(A) The sum of voltages around a closed loop is zero
(B) The sum of currents entering a junction equals the sum of currents leaving it
(C) Current is proportional to voltage
(D) Resistance in series is additive
cards.back:
(B) The sum of currents entering a junction equals the sum of currents leaving it

Electricity & Magnetism — KIRCHHOFF'S TWO LAWS (1845, Gustav Kirchhoff, German): (1) CURRENT LAW (KCL / Junction Rule): Σ I_in = Σ I_out at any junction. Based on conservation of CHARGE. (2) VOLTAGE LAW (KVL / Loop Rule): Σ V = 0 around any closed loop. Based on conservation of ENERGY. These laws allow analysis of complex multi-loop circuits that Ohm's law alone can't handle. Example multi-loop: Wheatstone bridge, star-delta networks. Sign convention: current entering junction positive, leaving negative. For voltage: going through EMF source negative-to-positive terminal = +EMF; in direction of current through resistor = -IR. Kirchhoff also worked on black-body radiation (another 'Kirchhoff's law' in thermodynamics: good emitter = good absorber).

cards.front:
A FUSE wire in an electrical circuit is made of a material with:

(A) High melting point + low resistance
(B) Low melting point + high resistance
(C) Zero resistance (superconductor)
(D) Very high melting point + high resistance
cards.back:
(B) Low melting point + high resistance

Electricity & Magnetism — FUSE — safety device that melts when excessive current (overcurrent/short circuit) flows, breaking the circuit. Material: TIN-LEAD ALLOY (typically 37% Pb + 63% Sn), with LOW melting point (~200°C) + relatively HIGH resistance — so it heats up (I²R) and melts BEFORE the wiring or appliance does. Rated in amperes (e.g., 5A, 15A household fuses). Must be placed in the LIVE (phase) wire, not neutral. CIRCUIT BREAKERS (MCB — Miniature Circuit Breakers) have replaced fuses in modern wiring — resettable, uses electromagnet or bimetallic strip. ELCB/RCCB = Earth Leakage Circuit Breaker — detects current mismatch between live + neutral (leakage through human body or earth) and trips within 30ms. Fuse DIFFERS from a resistor (which limits but doesn't break). 'Fuse blown' = fuse has melted; must be replaced with the same rating. so heat generated by excess current melts it.

cards.front:
Which material is considered the BEST conductor of electricity at room temperature (highest conductivity)?

(A) Copper
(B) Silver
(C) Gold
(D) Aluminium
cards.back:
(B) Silver

Electricity & Magnetism — ELECTRICAL CONDUCTIVITY (at 20°C): Silver (6.3 × 10⁷ S/m) > Copper (5.96) > Gold (4.52) > Aluminium (3.77) > Tungsten (1.79) > Iron (1.00) > Lead (0.48). SILVER is the best, but TOO EXPENSIVE for general wiring → COPPER is the industry standard (good conductivity + affordability + ductility). ALUMINIUM is used for overhead power lines (lighter weight — reduces tower spacing costs, despite being ~60% as conductive as copper). GOLD is used in fine electronics (phone connectors, PCB plating) because of corrosion resistance. SUPERCONDUCTORS have ZERO electrical resistance below critical temperature (Tc): Mercury Tc = 4.2K (Kamerlingh Onnes, 1911, Nobel 1913); YBa₂Cu₃O₇ (YBCO) Tc = 92K (high-Tc cuprate, above liquid nitrogen 77K); recent room-temperature superconductor claims (LK-99, 2023) remain disputed.

cards.front:
In a HOUSEHOLD electric circuit, the three wires typically supplied by the mains are:

(A) Live (phase), Neutral, Earth
(B) Positive, Negative, Ground
(C) DC+, DC−, AC
(D) Source, Sink, Bypass
cards.back:
(A) Live (phase), Neutral, Earth

Electricity & Magnetism — Indian household mains wires (3-pin plug): (1) LIVE (phase) — RED (old) or BROWN (new standard) — carries current at 220-240V AC relative to neutral. (2) NEUTRAL — BLACK (old) or BLUE — completes the circuit, should ideally be at 0V. (3) EARTH (ground) — GREEN / GREEN-YELLOW — connects metal casings to ground to prevent shock if live wire touches casing. Frequency: 50 Hz (60 Hz in US, Canada, parts of Japan). AC (Alternating Current) used for distribution because of ease of voltage transformation (step-up for transmission, step-down for consumption). 3-phase vs single-phase: commercial/industrial use 3-phase (three live wires 120° phase apart + neutral), residences get one phase. MCB trips if current exceeds its rating; ELCB trips on leakage.

cards.front:
A transformer works on the principle of:

(A) Mutual electromagnetic induction
(B) Ohm's law
(C) Kirchhoff's laws
(D) Joule heating
cards.back:
(A) Mutual electromagnetic induction

Electricity & Magnetism — TRANSFORMER works on MUTUAL INDUCTION — Michael Faraday's law (1831): a changing magnetic flux in one coil induces an EMF in a nearby coil. Only works with AC (not DC, since DC doesn't produce a changing flux). Structure: two coils (PRIMARY + SECONDARY) wound on a common laminated iron CORE. V_primary / V_secondary = N_primary / N_secondary (turns ratio). If N_secondary > N_primary → STEP-UP (raises voltage, lowers current). If N_secondary < N_primary → STEP-DOWN. Power conservation (ideal): V₁I₁ = V₂I₂. Real transformers have ~95-99% efficiency (losses: copper = I²R, iron = eddy currents + hysteresis). Used in: power distribution (11kV → 415V/220V), phone chargers, doorbells. Invented by William Stanley (1885) + Zipernowsky-Déri-Bláthy in Hungary (1884-85).

cards.front:
Who invented the electric BATTERY (the first reliable source of continuous electric current) in 1800?

(A) Benjamin Franklin
(B) Alessandro Volta
(C) Thomas Edison
(D) Michael Faraday
cards.back:
(B) Alessandro Volta

Electricity & Magnetism — ALESSANDRO VOLTA (Italian, 1745-1827) invented the VOLTAIC PILE in 1800 — alternating discs of zinc + copper separated by brine-soaked cloth. First reliable source of steady electric current. UNIT 'VOLT' named after him. Earlier, Luigi Galvani had observed 'animal electricity' in frog legs (1780), but Volta proved it was chemistry-based (not biological). Volta demonstrated his pile to Napoleon (1801) who ennobled him. Subsequent developments: DANIELL CELL (1836, John Daniell — more stable); LECLANCHÉ CELL (1866, carbon-zinc — basis of modern dry cells); LEAD-ACID BATTERY (1859, Planté — first rechargeable, still in cars); NICKEL-CADMIUM (1899); LITHIUM-ION (1985, John Goodenough + Stanley Whittingham + Akira Yoshino — Nobel 2019; powers phones + EVs). BENJAMIN FRANKLIN's famous kite experiment (1752) proved lightning is electrical — but he didn't invent the battery. FARADAY's work on electromagnetic induction enabled generators.

cards.front:
A 60 W bulb and a 100 W bulb designed for 220 V are connected in SERIES across a 220 V supply. Which will be BRIGHTER and why?

(A) The 100 W bulb, because its power rating is higher
(B) The 60 W bulb, because its resistance is higher and more power dissipates in it
(C) Both will glow equally
(D) Neither will glow in series
cards.back:
(B) The 60 W bulb, because its resistance is higher and more power dissipates in it

Electricity & Magnetism — Resistance R = V²/P. 60 W bulb has R = 220²/60 ≈ 807 Ω. 100 W bulb has R = 220²/100 = 484 Ω. In SERIES, same current flows through both; power dissipated P = I²R → the HIGHER-resistance (60 W, the lower-rated) bulb dissipates more power and glows brighter. Counter-intuitive result — classic exam trap.

cards.front:
Consider the following about ELECTRIC POWER in a purely RESISTIVE circuit. 1. P = V²/R. 2. P = I²R. 3. P = V·I. 4. In an AC purely resistive circuit, RMS values are used for V and I in power calculations. Which are correct?

(A) 1, 2 and 3 only
(B) 1, 2, 3 and 4
(C) 1 and 3 only
(D) 3 and 4 only
cards.back:
(B) 1, 2, 3 and 4

Electricity & Magnetism — All four correct. The three power formulae are equivalent through V = IR. For AC resistive circuits, average power = V_rms × I_rms (with V_rms = V_peak/√2 for sinusoidal). In reactive circuits add the cosφ (power factor).

cards.front:
Three resistors of 4 Ω, 6 Ω and 12 Ω are connected in PARALLEL across a 12 V battery. The total current drawn is:

(A) 1 A
(B) 6 A
(C) 4 A
(D) 3 A
cards.back:
(B) 6 A

Electricity & Magnetism — 1/R_eq = 1/4 + 1/6 + 1/12 = 3/12 + 2/12 + 1/12 = 6/12 → R_eq = 2 Ω. I = V/R = 12/2 = 6 A. Always compute R_eq first, then I = V/R_eq.

cards.front:
Match the instrument with its PRINCIPLE of operation. A. Electric motor. B. Transformer. C. Electric generator (dynamo). D. Galvanometer. List-II: 1. A current-carrying coil in a magnetic field experiences a torque (motor effect). 2. Mutual induction. 3. Electromagnetic induction (moving conductor in magnetic field). 4. Deflection of a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field.

(A) A-1, B-2, C-3, D-4
(B) A-1, B-3, C-2, D-4
(C) A-3, B-2, C-1, D-4
(D) A-4, B-2, C-3, D-1
cards.back:
(A) A-1, B-2, C-3, D-4

Electricity & Magnetism — Motor — motor effect (Fleming's Left-Hand rule). Transformer — mutual induction (Faraday). Generator — electromagnetic induction (Fleming's Right-Hand rule). Galvanometer — torque on coil causes deflection proportional to current. Note 1 vs 4 are subtly different: motor converts to mechanical rotation; galvanometer produces a measured deflection.

cards.front:
Ohm's law states that in a metallic conductor at constant temperature, the current is:

(A) Inversely proportional to the voltage
(B) Directly proportional to the voltage
(C) Independent of the voltage
(D) Proportional to voltage squared
cards.back:
(B) Directly proportional to the voltage

Non-ohmic devices — diodes, filament lamps, thermistors — do not satisfy this relation. Wire resistance itself grows with temperature, which is why long-run steady-state currents in heaters are lower than their cold-start value.

cards.front:
An electrical appliance rated 2 kW is run for 5 hours. The electrical energy consumed is:

(A) 2 kWh
(B) 10 kWh
(C) 5 kWh
(D) 10 W
cards.back:
(B) 10 kWh

The filament of an incandescent bulb is made of which metal?

(A) Copper
(B) Tungsten
(C) Iron

cards.front:
The equivalent resistance of two 6 Ω resistors connected in parallel is:

(A) 12 Ω
(B) 3 Ω
(C) 6 Ω
(D) 1 Ω
cards.back:

cards.back:

Domestic alternating current supply in India has a standard frequency of:

When two resistors of resistance 6 Ω and 3 Ω are connected in PARALLEL, the equivalent resistance is:

An electric heater rated 1500 W operates on a 230 V supply. The current drawn is approximately:

(A) 3.4 A
(B) 6.5 A

cards.back:

cards.front:
Kirchhoff's current law (KCL) states that at any junction in an electric circuit:

(A) Total energy is conserved
(B) Algebraic sum of currents = 0 (currents in = currents out)
(C) Voltage drops add up to EMF
(D) Resistance equals voltage
cards.back:
(B) Algebraic sum of currents = 0 (currents in = currents out)

Electricity & Magnetism — Kirchhoff's two laws: (1) KCL (current law / junction rule): ∑I = 0 at any node — conservation of charge. (2) KVL (voltage law / loop rule): ∑V = 0 around any closed loop — conservation of energy. KCL implies whatever flows in must flow out. KVL implies the total potential gain (EMF) around a loop equals total potential drop (across resistors). Together they enable analysis of any DC circuit, however complex.

cards.front:
If the same current flows through two resistors connected in series, the larger resistor:

(A) Dissipates less power
(B) Dissipates more power (P = I²R, so larger R → more heat)
(C) Always blows the fuse
(D) Carries less current

In parallel: voltage is the same across both, current divides; P = V²/R, so the SMALLER resistor dissipates more power. This is the underpinning of why nichrome (high R) is used in heaters but copper (low R) in connecting wires.

cards.front:
What is the SI unit of electric field intensity?

(A) Newton per Coulomb (N/C)
(B) Coulomb per Newton (C/N)
(C) Joule per Coulomb (J/C) alone
(D) Coulomb per second (C/s).
cards.back:
(A) Newton per Coulomb (N/C)

Electricity & Magnetism — ELECTRIC FIELD E is defined as force per unit positive test charge: E = F/q. SI UNIT: Newton/Coulomb (N/C), equivalent to Volt/metre (V/m) — the EQUIVALENT unit. DERIVATION OF V/m: V = J/C, and J = N·m, so V/m = (N·m/C)/m = N/C ✓. KEY FORMULAS: (1) For a point charge Q at distance r: E = kQ/r² (where k = 1/(4πε₀) ≈ 9×10⁹ Nm²/C²). APPLICATION: lightning discharge happens when atmospheric E exceeds ~3 MV/m (megavolt/metre). EXAM TIP: know N/C ≡ V/m; questions often switch between units. PYQ ANGLE: definitional Qs on E-field appear in JEE-Main, NEET, NCERT-driven SSC papers.

cards.front:
Two point charges of +4 μC and −4 μC are placed 0.1 m apart. The electric DIPOLE MOMENT is:

(A) 4 × 10⁻⁷ C·m, towards positive
(B) 4 × 10⁻⁵ C·m alone alone
(C) Zero (cancelling charges) alone
(D) 0.4 C·m alone alone alone
cards.back:
(A) 4 × 10⁻⁷ C·m, towards positive

Electricity & Magnetism — DIPOLE MOMENT p = q × d, where q = magnitude of charge, d = separation distance. p = 4 × 10⁻⁶ C × 0.1 m = 4 × 10⁻⁷ C·m. DIRECTION: by convention, dipole moment points from NEGATIVE to POSITIVE charge. KEY POINTS ABOUT DIPOLES: (1) Net charge = 0, but field is NOT zero everywhere — strongest along the dipole axis. (2) Far-field E ∝ p/r³ (faster decay than point-charge 1/r²). (3) In an external uniform field, dipole experiences TORQUE τ = p × E (no net force, but rotates to align with E). REAL-WORLD: water molecule has dipole moment ~6.2 × 10⁻³⁰ C·m — that's why H₂O is a polar solvent (dissolves ionic compounds). HCl molecule = 3.6 × 10⁻³⁰ C·m. RADIO ANTENNAS: oscillating dipoles radiate EM waves — basis of all wireless communication. INSIGHT: 'Debye' (D) is a CGS unit = 3.336 × 10⁻³⁰ C·m, used in chemistry. PYQ FREQUENCY: 1 Q on dipoles per JEE-Main; less common in SSC/CGL.

(A) Cross each other anywhere in space
(B) Begin from positive charges alone
(C) End at negative charges alone
(D) Are tangent to field at every point
cards.back:
(A) Cross each other anywhere in space

Electricity & Magnetism — PROPERTIES of electric field lines (Faraday's representation): (1) START at POSITIVE charges, END at NEGATIVE charges (or extend to infinity). (2) NEVER CROSS — because at any point, E has a UNIQUE direction; two crossing lines would mean two directions, impossible. (3) Density of lines reflects field STRENGTH. (4) Tangent to a field line at any point gives the direction of E at that point. (5) Field lines are CONTINUOUS curves — no breaks. (6) They DO NOT pass THROUGH a conductor (E = 0 inside conductors at equilibrium). INSIGHT: field lines are a VISUALIZATION tool, not real physical entities — the field exists everywhere in space; lines just represent it conveniently. ANALOG: gravitational field, magnetic field also have similar field-line concepts. NCERT CLASS 12 — Ch. 1 Electric Charges and Fields. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests CONCEPTUAL understanding of field-line properties — a perennial SSC, JEE, NEET MCQ favourite. PYQ FREQUENCY: 1 Q per JEE-Main paper on field-line properties.

cards.front:
Coulomb's law states that the force between two point charges is:

(A) Inversely proportional to distance squared
(B) Directly proportional to distance.
(C) Inversely proportional to distance.
(D) Proportional to charge sum only.
cards.back:
(A) Inversely proportional to distance squared

Electricity & Magnetism — COULOMB'S LAW: F = k·q₁·q₂/r², where k = 1/(4πε₀) ≈ 9 × 10⁹ Nm²/C². Force is: (1) DIRECTLY proportional to product of charges. (2) INVERSELY proportional to SQUARE of distance. (3) Acts along the line joining the charges. (4) ATTRACTIVE for opposite-sign charges, REPULSIVE for same-sign. HISTORY: Charles-Augustin de Coulomb (1785, France) measured this with a torsion balance — same principle Cavendish later used for gravity. STRUCTURAL SIMILARITY to NEWTON'S GRAVITY: F = G·m₁·m₂/r² — both inverse-square laws. RELATIVE STRENGTH: electric force is ~10³⁹ TIMES stronger than gravity at atomic scales — that's why atoms hold together via electrostatics, and gravity dominates only at large scales (no negative mass to cancel out). NCERT CLASS 12 — Ch. 1. PYQ FREQUENCY: Coulomb's law is a 1-mark guarantee in JEE-Main and NEET. EXAM ANGLE: 'inverse-square law' is the KEY phrase — appears in 90% of polarity-of-distance Qs.

cards.front:
Inside a CONDUCTOR in electrostatic equilibrium, the electric field is:

(A) Zero — charges redistribute to cancel
(B) Equal to surface field always.
(C) Maximum at the centre always.
(D) Inversely proportional to volume.
cards.back:
(A) Zero — charges redistribute to cancel

Electricity & Magnetism — INSIDE a conductor at electrostatic equilibrium, E = 0. WHY? Free electrons redistribute themselves on the SURFACE such that internal fields cancel (otherwise charges would keep moving — not equilibrium). KEY CONSEQUENCES: (1) NO charge inside a solid conductor — all excess charge resides on the OUTER SURFACE. (2) Field just outside conductor's surface = σ/ε₀ (perpendicular to surface). (3) FARADAY CAGE: a hollow conductor SHIELDS its interior from external E-fields — used in MRI rooms, sensitive electronics, lightning protection on aircraft. (4) Cars are essentially Faraday cages — relatively safe in a lightning strike (current flows over the metal body, not through occupants). NCERT CLASS 12 — Ch. 1, 2. APPLICATION: COAXIAL CABLES use a conductor-shield to keep signals undistorted by external E-fields. INSIGHT: this property is unique to ELECTROSTATIC (not dynamic) — under AC currents, internal E can be non-zero. PYQ ANGLE: a perennial SSC, JEE-Main MCQ — 1-2 Qs per paper. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests conductor-property fundamentals.

cards.front:
What is the electric field at a distance of 1 metre from a point charge of +1 microcoulomb?

(A) 9000 N/C towards outward radial
(B) 900 N/C alone alone alone
(C) 9 × 10⁻³ N/C alone alone
(D) 9 × 10⁵ N/C alone alone alone
cards.back:
(A) 9000 N/C towards outward radial

Electricity & Magnetism — FIELD due to point charge: E = kQ/r². Plug: k = 9 × 10⁹ Nm²/C²; Q = 1 × 10⁻⁶ C; r = 1 m. E = (9 × 10⁹ × 10⁻⁶) / 1² = 9 × 10³ = 9000 N/C. DIRECTION: radially OUTWARD from positive charge. SCALE-CHECK: 9000 N/C is a moderate field; air breakdown is ~3 × 10⁶ N/C, so this charge wouldn't ionize air at 1 m. SHORTCUT MNEMONIC: for any point charge, when you know Q in microcoulombs and r in metres, E = 9000 × Q(μC) / r²(m²) — a fast-recall formula. PRACTICE: at 0.5 m, E quadruples to 36,000 N/C (because 1/r²). At 2 m, E becomes 2250 N/C (1/4 of original). INVERSE-SQUARE FALLOFF: doubling distance reduces field to 1/4. EXAM ANGLE: standard 'plug-and-chug' Coulomb's law / E-field Q in JEE-Main, NEET, NDA. PYQ FREQUENCY: 2-3 such numerical Qs per JEE-Main physics section. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests formula recall + unit-handling discipline.

cards.front:
The relationship between electric field E and electric potential V in a uniform field is:

(A) E = −dV/dx (negative gradient)
(B) E = V × distance always alone
(C) E = +dV/dx (positive gradient)
(D) E and V are unrelated.
cards.back:
(A) E = −dV/dx (negative gradient)

Electricity & Magnetism — RELATION: E = −∇V (negative gradient of potential). In 1-D: E = −dV/dx. In 3-D: E_x = −∂V/∂x, E_y = −∂V/∂y, E_z = −∂V/∂z. NEGATIVE SIGN: E points in the direction of DECREASING potential — high V to low V (just as water flows from high to low gravitational potential). SIMPLE CASE — UNIFORM FIELD: V = E·d (or magnitude V = E×d in a parallel-plate capacitor where E is uniform). FORMULA RELATIONSHIPS: V (volts) = J/C; E (V/m) = volt per metre. EXAMPLE: parallel-plate capacitor with V = 100 V across d = 1 mm gap → E = V/d = 10⁵ V/m. ENERGY: work done MOVING a charge q against E from A to B = q(V_B − V_A) = q·ΔV. CONSERVATIVE FIELD: electrostatic field is conservative — work depends only on endpoints, not path. PYQ ANGLE: 'E = −dV/dx' is a JEE-Main, NEET, NCERT class 12 staple — 1-2 Qs per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests calculus-based understanding of E-V relation.

cards.front:
Earth has a MAGNETIC FIELD because of:

(A) Liquid iron-nickel core motion (geodynamo)
(B) Solid iron core's magnetism only
(C) Sun's solar wind interaction here
(D) Moon's gravity affecting Earth.
cards.back:
(A) Liquid iron-nickel core motion (geodynamo)

Electricity & Magnetism — Earth's magnetic field generated by GEODYNAMO — convection in MOLTEN OUTER CORE (liquid iron + nickel). Self-sustaining electromagnetic process. PROTECTS Earth from solar wind / cosmic rays — without it, atmosphere would be stripped (Mars lost its magnetic field 4 BYA → atmosphere blown away → cold + dry today). MAGNETIC POLES drift; OCCASIONALLY reverse (geomagnetic reversal, every ~hundreds of thousands of years). Field strength ~25-65 microtesla. Compass N-pole points to MAGNETIC NORTH (which is geomagnetic SOUTH due to naming convention).

An ELECTROMAGNET is made by:

(A) Wrapping coil of wire around iron core, passing current
(B) Heating a metal rod in fire too alone (option here)
(C) Rubbing iron with permanent magnet only alone
(D) Mixing iron filings with chemicals (option here)
cards.back:
(A) Wrapping coil of wire around iron core, passing current

Electricity & Magnetism — ELECTROMAGNET = solenoid (coil) wound on soft iron core; magnetic field exists only when CURRENT flows. Discovered by ØRSTED (1820). ADVANTAGES: (1) STRENGTH ADJUSTABLE; (2) ON/OFF switchable; (3) Much STRONGER than permanent magnets achievable. USES: motors, transformers, MRI, doorbells, relays, maglev trains, scrapyard cranes, particle accelerators. AMPERE'S RIGHT-HAND RULE: curl fingers in current direction → thumb points to N pole. FARADAY'S LAW (1831): changing magnetic flux induces EMF (foundation of generators). MAXWELL unified all in 4 equations (1860s).

cards.front:
ELECTROMAGNETIC INDUCTION was discovered by:

(A) Michael Faraday (1831)
(B) Albert Einstein (relativity)
(C) Isaac Newton (gravitation)
(D) Thomas Edison (DC + light bulb)
cards.back:
(A) Michael Faraday (1831)

Electricity & Magnetism — FARADAY'S LAW (1831) — changing magnetic flux induces EMF. Foundation of GENERATORS, TRANSFORMERS, MOTORS, MRI, induction cooktops, wireless chargers. EMF = -dΦ/dt; Lenz's law: induced current opposes change. JOSEPH HENRY (American) discovered induction independently around same time. Faraday also discovered: BENZENE structure, electrolysis laws (1834). MOTORS reverse the principle (current in field → force/rotation). HUGE PRACTICAL impact: India's 400 GW power grid relies entirely on Faraday's discovery (turbines spin → AC generators → transformers step up/down).

MAGLEV trains float using:

(A) Magnetic levitation (electromagnets repel rails)
(B) Air cushions (hovercraft style) too
(C) Hydraulic suspension only used alone
(D) Wheels on rails (conventional) (option here)
cards.back:
(A) Magnetic levitation (electromagnets repel rails)

Electricity & Magnetism — MAGLEV — train floats above tracks via magnetic repulsion / attraction. NO friction → very fast + smooth. Speeds: 400-600+ km/h. EXAMPLES: Shanghai Maglev (China, 431 km/h commercial); SCMaglev (Japan, world record 603 km/h test). VS BULLET TRAINS (Shinkansen, French TGV) — those use steel wheels + rails. INDIA: Mumbai-Ahmedabad bullet train (Shinkansen-tech, ~320 km/h target) under construction; Vande Bharat (160 km/h) running. MAGLEV = expensive but minimal maintenance (no wheel wear). HYPERLOOP (Elon Musk concept) — vacuum tube + maglev → ~1000 km/h (proposed Mumbai-Pune; status uncertain).
